p.seg: 1.1 *Běn Yì Dì Yī* (First Discourse on Fundamentals)
Only in the sixth year of the *Shǐ Yuán* reign period,
an imperial edict was issued, ordering the Chancellor and Imperial Censor to converse with the recommended worthies and men of letters,
inquiring about the hardships of the common people.
The men of letters replied,
"I have heard that the way to govern people
is to prevent the source of excessive indulgence,
expand the foundations of morality,
suppress minor profits and promote benevolence and righteousness,
and not show them the way to profit.
Only then can education flourish,
and customs be transformed.
Now, the commanderies and kingdoms have salt, iron, and liquor monopolies,
as well as equitable transport,
competing with the people for profit.
This scatters the simple honesty of the people
and leads to the formation of a greedy and base culture.
Therefore, few people engage in fundamental occupations,
and many pursue secondary ones.
When writing is complex, substance declines;
when secondary occupations flourish, fundamental ones are depleted.
When secondary occupations are cultivated, the people become licentious;
when fundamental occupations are cultivated, the people become honest.
When the people are honest, wealth and resources are sufficient;
when the people are extravagant, hunger and cold arise.
I wish to abolish the salt, iron, and liquor monopolies, as well as equitable transport,
in order to advance fundamental occupations and suppress secondary ones,
broadening the profits of agriculture,
which would be beneficial."
The Grandee said,
"The *Xiōngnú* have betrayed their allegiance and not submitted,
repeatedly acting as bandits and aggressors on the borders.
To prepare for them exhausts the soldiers of the central kingdom;
not to prepare for them allows their invasions to continue without end.
The late emperor grieved over the long suffering of the border people,
and the hardships of those captured by the barbarians.
Therefore, he repaired the barriers,
maintained the beacon towers,
and stationed troops to defend against them.
Border expenses were insufficient,
so he established salt and iron monopolies,
set up liquor monopolies,
and implemented equitable transport,
to enrich goods and increase wealth,
in order to assist with border expenses.
Now, those who deliberate want to abolish these,
emptying the treasury within,
and lacking the means for defense abroad,
causing the soldiers preparing for defense and guarding the walls to suffer from hunger and cold on the borders.
How will they be provided for?
To abolish these is
not beneficial."
The men of letters said,
"Confucius said,
'Those who govern a state or a family
do not worry about scarcity but worry about inequity;
they do not worry about poverty but worry about instability.'
Therefore, the Son of Heaven does not speak of quantity,
the feudal lords do not speak of profit or loss,
and the grandees do not speak of gain or loss.
Cultivate benevolence and righteousness to influence them,
and promote virtuous conduct to embrace them.
In this way, those nearby will be intimate and those far away will be pleased and submit.
Therefore, those skilled in conquering do not fight,
those skilled in fighting do not mobilize troops,
and those skilled in mobilizing troops do not form battle lines.
They cultivate these principles in the ancestral temple
and negotiate peace, returning the troops.
When a king practices benevolent governance,
he has no enemy in the world.
Why should he waste resources?"
The Grandee said,
"The *Xiōngnú* are treacherous and cunning,
presumptuously entering the passes,
offending and violating China,
killing and attacking commanderies, counties, and the Commandant of *Shuòfāng*.
They are extremely rebellious and lawless,
and it has long been appropriate to punish and exterminate them.
Your Majesty bestows great favor,
grieving over the lack of provision for the people,
and cannot bear to expose the officers and soldiers to the wilderness;
although it is difficult to be armed and wield weapons,
they have the will to turn north and subdue the *Xiōngnú* again.
Moreover, you want to abolish the salt, iron, and equitable transport,
disrupting border expenses,
reducing military strategy,
and showing no concern for the borders.
In my opinion, this is not beneficial."
The men of letters said,
"In ancient times,
value was placed on virtue, and military force was considered base.
Confucius said,
'If distant people do not submit,
then cultivate civil virtue to attract them.
Once they have come,
then pacify them.'
Now, abandoning morality and relying on weapons of war,
mobilizing troops to attack them,
stationing troops to defend against them,
exposing soldiers and revealing military strength,
in order to sustain this for a long time,
transporting grain endlessly,
causing the soldiers on the borders to suffer from hunger and cold outside,
and the common people to toil within.
Establishing salt and iron monopolies
initially expanded the offices of profit to provide for these expenses,
which is not a long-term strategy.
Therefore, abolishing them would be beneficial."
The Grandee said,
"Those who established states in ancient times
opened up paths for fundamental and secondary occupations,
and facilitated the use of what was available and what was lacking.
Markets and courts were used to satisfy people's needs,
attracting scholars and commoners,
gathering all kinds of goods.
Farmers, merchants, artisans, and teachers each obtained what they desired,
exchanging goods and then departing.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says,
'Understand the changes,
so that the people will not become weary.'
Therefore, if artisans do not produce,
then agricultural implements will be lacking;
if merchants do not trade,
then valuable goods will be cut off.
If agricultural implements are lacking,
then grain will not be grown;
if valuable goods are cut off,
then wealth and resources will be depleted.
Therefore, salt, iron, and equitable transport
are the means of distributing wealth and regulating emergency needs.
To abolish them is
not beneficial."
The men of letters said,
"Guiding the people with virtue will cause them to return to honesty;
showing the people the way to profit
will cause their customs to become superficial.
If customs become superficial, then people will turn their backs on righteousness and pursue profit;
if they pursue profit, then the common people will interact on the roads and meet in the marketplace.
*Lǎozi* said,
'A poor country seems to have abundance.
This is not because it has much wealth,
but because desires are numerous and the people are restless.'
Therefore, kings value fundamental occupations and suppress secondary ones,
using rites and righteousness to guard against the people's desires,
and stock up on beans, millet, goods, and wealth.
Markets
and merchants do not trade useless items,
and artisans do not make useless tools.
Therefore, merchants are for facilitating the flow of stagnant goods,
and artisans are for providing implements and weapons,
but these are not the fundamental tasks of governing a state."
The Grandee said,
"*Guǎnzi* said,
'If a state has fertile fields but the people do not have enough to eat,
it is because implements are not prepared.
If it has the wealth of mountains and seas but the people do not have enough wealth,
it is because merchants and artisans are not prepared.'
The cinnabar, lacquer, and yak tails of *Lǒng* and *Shǔ*,
the leather, hides, bones, and ivory of *Jīng* and *Yáng*,
the *nán* wood, *zǐ* wood, and bamboo arrows of south of the *Jiāng* (Yangtze),
the fish, salt, felt, and furs of *Yān* and *Qí*,
the lacquer, silk, fine hemp cloth, and coarse hemp cloth of *Yǎn* and *Yù*,
are provisions for nourishing life and burying the dead.
These depend on merchants to be circulated
and on artisans to be produced.
Therefore, the sages invented the use of boats and oars
to navigate rivers and valleys,
and domesticated oxen and harnessed horses
to travel across hills and plains;
they reached distant places and explored deep regions
in order to exchange all kinds of goods and benefit the common people.
Therefore, the late emperor established iron offices to provide for agricultural needs,
and opened equitable transport to satisfy the people's wealth.
Salt, iron, and equitable transport
are what the myriad people rely on and receive provisions from.
To abolish them is
not beneficial."
The men of letters said,
"If a state has fertile fields but the people do not have enough to eat,
it is because commerce and industry are flourishing and fundamental occupations are neglected;
if it has the wealth of mountains and seas but the people do not have enough wealth,
it is because they do not focus on the people's needs but engage in numerous extravagant crafts.
Therefore, rivers and springs cannot fill a leaking cup,
and mountains and seas cannot provide for streams and gullies.
Therefore, *Pán Gēng* gathered the people together,
*Shùn* hid gold,
and Emperor *Gāo* prohibited merchants from holding official positions.
These actions were intended to curb the customs of greed and baseness
and to purify the atmosphere of sincerity.
Even when suppressing the impoverished markets, guarding against and blocking the gates of profit,
the people still do wrong.
How much more so when the rulers pursue profit?
The *Zhuàn* (Commentary) says,
'If the feudal lords love profit, then the grandees will be base;
if the grandees are base, then the knights will be greedy;
if the knights are greedy, then the common people will steal.'
Opening up the channels of profit is like building a ladder for the people to commit crimes."
Dàfū said:
“In the past,
commandaries and kingdoms, and various princes, each offered tribute of local products.
The coming and going was troublesome and complicated,
the goods were often of poor quality,
and sometimes did not cover their costs.
Therefore, commandaries and kingdoms established transport officials to manage the transport,
and to facilitate the tribute from distant regions,
hence it was called Jūnshū (Equal Transport).
They opened distribution offices in the capital,
to collect goods.
Buying when prices were low,
and selling when prices were high.
Thus, the government did not lose revenue,
and merchants had no opportunity to profit,
hence it was called Píngzhǔn (Level Standard).
With Píngzhǔn, the people did not lose their occupations,
and with Jūnshū, the people shared labor and leisure equally.
Therefore, Píngzhǔn and Jūnshū
were used to equalize all things and benefit the common people,
not to open avenues of profit and create a ladder of crime for the people.”
The Wénxué said:
“In ancient times, the taxes levied on the people
were based on their skills,
not demanding what they were unskilled at.
Farmers paid with their harvests,
and female artisans contributed their handiwork.
Now, they give up what they have,
and are charged for what they do not possess.
The common people sell their goods cheaply,
to comply with the demands from above.
Recently,
some commandaries and kingdoms have ordered the people to make cloth and floss silk,
and officials arbitrarily detain and make things difficult for them,
conducting trade with them.
What the officials take in
is not only the silk fabrics of Qí and Ā,
and the cloth of Shǔ and Hàn,
but also what the common people produce.
Practicing fraud and selling at a fixed price,
the farmers suffer greatly,
and the female artisans are taxed twice.
I have not seen the equalization of transport.
When government officials dispatch goods recklessly,
and close the doors to monopolize the market,
then all goods are collected.
When all goods are collected,
then prices soar.
When prices soar,
then merchants reap profits.
Conducting the market themselves,
then officials engage in corruption.
Powerful officials and wealthy merchants hoard goods and store them to await emergencies,
while petty merchants and corrupt officials buy cheap to sell dear.
I have not seen the leveling of standards.
Indeed, the ancient Jūnshū
was to equalize labor and leisure and facilitate tribute transport,
not to seek profit and trade in all things."
1. 2 《Lì Gēng Dì Èr》
The Dàfū said:
“The king blocks natural wealth,
restricts passes and markets,
holds the standard and observes the times,
to control the people by weight and measure.
In years of abundance and good harvests,
they store up reserves to prepare for times of scarcity and hardship;
in years of famine and poor harvests,
they circulate money and goods;
diverting surpluses to adjust for deficiencies.
In the past, during the floods of Yǔ and the droughts of Tāng,
the common people were impoverished and lacking,
and they borrowed from each other to sustain themselves with clothing and food.
Yǔ used the gold of Lìshān,
and Tāng used the copper of Zhuāngshān,
to mint coins to redeem his people,
and the world praised him as benevolent.
In the past, when financial resources were insufficient,
soldiers sometimes did not receive their pay,
and Shāndōng was afflicted by disaster,
and Qí and Zhào suffered great famine,
relying on the reserves of the Jūnshū,
and the accumulation in the granaries,
soldiers were provided for,
and famine victims were relieved.
Therefore, the goods of the Jūnshū,
and the wealth of the treasury,
were not only for trading with the myriad people and exclusively supporting the military,
but also for relieving the distressed and preparing for floods and droughts.”
The Wénxué said:
“In ancient times,
the tax was one-tenth,
the marshes and weirs were open for seasonal use without restrictions,
and the common people were all engaged in agriculture without neglecting their duties.
Therefore, three years of cultivation provided one year of reserves,
and nine years of cultivation provided three years of reserves.
This is how Yǔ and Tāng prepared for floods and droughts and secured the well-being of the people.
If the wilderness is not reclaimed,
and the fields are not cultivated,
even if one monopolizes the wealth of mountains and seas,
and controls the profits of all trades,
it still will not be enough to sustain them.
Therefore, in ancient times, they valued labor and emphasized agriculture, planting trees extensively,
and personally engaged in farming according to the seasons, ensuring sufficient food and clothing,
so that even in years of repeated famine, the people did not suffer.
Therefore, clothing and food are the foundation of the people,
and farming and harvesting are the duties of the people.
If these two are cultivated,
then the country will be rich and the people will be secure.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
‘When the hundred families are full,
the wives and children are at peace.’”
The Dàfū said:
“Sages and worthies do not manage their families with just one treasure,
nor do they enrich a country with just one method.
In the past, Guǎn Zhòng achieved hegemony through expediency and deception,
while the Jǐ clan perished by focusing solely on agriculture.
If managing a family and maintaining life necessarily depended on farming,
then Shùn would not have made pottery and Yī Yǐn would not have been a cook.
Therefore, those who are good at governing a country
make what the world considers low as my high,
and what the world considers light as my heavy.
They use the non-essential to exchange for the essential,
and use the empty to fill the solid.
Now, the wealth of mountains and marshes,
and the reserves of the Jūnshū,
are used to control the light and heavy and to employ the feudal lords.
The gold of the Rǔ and Hàn rivers,
and the slightest tribute,
are how we entice foreign countries and obtain the treasures of the Qiāng and Hú.
For every piece of silk gauze from China,
we obtain from the Xiongnu accumulated gold,
and diminish the resources of enemy states.
Therefore, the mules and Bactrian camels,
enter the passes in a continuous line,
and the Dátuó horses, Xiè horses, and Yuán horses,
all become our livestock,
while the otter, the sable, the fox, and the badger,
and the colorful felt rugs,
fill our inner treasuries,
and jade, coral, and lapis lazuli,
all become treasures of the state.
Thus, the goods of foreign countries flow inward,
and profits do not leak outward.
When foreign goods flow inward, the state's resources are abundant,
and when profits do not leak outward, the people's needs are met.
The *Shī* says:
‘When the hundred families are full,
the wives and children are at peace.’”
The Wénxué said:
“In ancient times,
merchants exchanged goods without speculation,
and artisans produced solid goods without deception.
Therefore, gentlemen engaged in farming, cultivation, and fishing,
and their aims were the same.
Merchants are prone to deception,
and artisans adorn their products with fraud,
harboring secret desires and feeling no shame in their hearts,
so that the shallow deceive the honest.
In the past, Jié filled his palace with female musicians,
and embroidered clothes,
so Yī Yǐn left and traveled to Bó,
and the female musicians ultimately ruined his state.
Now, the use of mules
is not as effective as the labor of oxen and horses,
and otter skins and felt rugs
do not add to the quality of brocade and silk.
Beautiful jade and coral come from the Kūnshān Mountains,
and pearls, rhinoceros horns, and elephants come from the Guìlín region,
which are more than ten thousand *lǐ* away from Hàn.
Calculating the effort of farming and mulberry cultivation,
and the cost of materials,
one item is sold for a hundred times its price,
and one greeting is worth ten thousand *zhōng* of grain.
If those above favor rare and strange things,
then extravagant clothing will flow below,
and if they value goods from distant places,
then wealth will flow outward.
Therefore, the king does not value useless things to economize for his people,
nor does he love rare goods to enrich his country.
Therefore, the way to govern the people
lies in frugality and emphasizing agriculture,
and dividing the land into well-field system.”
The Dàfū said:
“From the capital in the east, west, south, and north,
passing through mountains and rivers,
and traversing commandaries and kingdoms,
all the wealthy and populous cities
have streets that are open in five directions,
where merchants gather,
and all things flourish.
Therefore, the sage takes advantage of the seasons,
the wise man takes advantage of the land's resources,
the superior man takes from the people,
and the average man labors with his body.
Chángjǔ and Jiénì
did not accumulate hundreds of gold,
and the followers of Zhí Qiáo
did not have the wealth of Yīdùn.
The merchants of Wǎn, Zhōu, Qí, and Lǔ
traveled all over the world.
Therefore, the wealth of merchants
might accumulate to tens of thousands of gold,
which is brought about by pursuing profits through multiplication.
Why must a rich country emphasize agriculture,
or sufficient people require the Jǐngtián (井田) system?"
The Literary Man said:
"The great floods reached the heavens,
yet there was the achievement of Yǔ (禹);
the Hé (河) River overflowed,
yet there was the merit of Xuānfáng (宣房).
Shāng Zhòu (商紂) was tyrannical,
yet there was the strategy of Mèngjīn (孟津).
The world was disturbed,
yet there was the wealth from multiplying profits.
In the most well-governed ancient times,
the people were simple, valued agriculture, lived peacefully and had few desires.
At that time,
roads were rarely traveled,
and markets grew grass.
Therefore, those who did not diligently cultivate could not fill their emptiness,
and those who did not diligently weave could not cover their bodies.
Even if there were crucial opportunities for aggregation,
and the techniques of pottery and weaving,
there was no place to apply their skills.
From ancient times until now,
there has never been a case of receiving rewards without effort,
or achieving merit without labor."
1.3 *Tōng Yǒu* (通有) - Third
The Grandee said:
"The Zhuō (涿) and Jì (薊) of Yàn (燕),
the Hándān (邯鄲) of Zhào (趙),
the Wēnzhǐ (溫軹) of Wèi (魏),
the Xíngyáng (滎陽) of Hán (韓),
the Línzī (臨淄) of Qí (齊),
the Wǎn (宛) and Chén (陳) of Chǔ (楚),
the Yángdí (陽翟) of Zhèng (鄭),
the Èr Zhōu (二周) of the Sān Chuān (三川),
were the richest in the land,
and were all famous capitals,
none of which relied on cultivating the fields or farming the land.
They were located at the crossroads of the five zhū (諸),
and straddled the thoroughfares.
Therefore, where goods are plentiful, the people thrive,
and where homes are near the market, families are wealthy.
Wealth lies in strategy,
not in physical labor;
profit lies in advantageous location,
not in diligent farming."
The Literary Man said:
"Jīng (荊) and Yáng (揚) in the south have the abundance of Guìlín (桂林),
and within them are the benefits of the Jiāng (江) and Hú (湖) Rivers.
To the left is the gold of Língyáng (陵陽),
and to the right are the materials of Shǔ (蜀) and Hàn (漢).
They fell trees and plant grains,
burn weeds and sow millet,
practice slash-and-burn agriculture and water the fields;
the land is vast and rich in resources;
yet the people are lazy and seek an easy life,
enjoying fine clothes and delicious food.
Even in humble houses and thatched huts,
they sing and play music,
living from day to day,
rejoicing in the morning and grieving in the evening.
Zhào (趙) and Zhōngshān (中山) are located along the Dà Hé (大河) River,
connecting the thoroughfares of the four directions,
situated at the crossroads of the world,
with merchants crisscrossing the roads,
and lords interacting on the routes;
yet the people are licentious and fond of non-essentials,
extravagant and neglectful of fundamental tasks.
The fields are not cultivated,
men and women are preoccupied with adornment,
households lack even basic provisions,
but musical instruments are played indoors.
Therefore, the people of Chǔ (楚) and Zhào (趙)
are equally poor and lack wealth.
Sòng (宋), Wèi (衛), Hán (韓), and Liáng (梁)
value agriculture and crops,
registering households and standardizing the people,
so that every family thrives and everyone is provided for.
Therefore, profit lies in self-reliance,
not in being located at major intersections;
wealth lies in frugality and diligence, seizing the opportune time,
not in relying on the years controlled by the Yǔ Jiū (羽鳩)."
The Grandee said:
"The five elements:
the east is wood,
and Dān (丹) and Zhāng (章) have mountains of gold and copper;
the south is fire,
and Jiāozhǐ (交趾) has the great rivers of the sea;
the west is metal,
and Shǔ (蜀) and Lǒng (隴) have forests of famous timber;
the north is water,
and Yōu Dū (幽都) has lands of accumulated sand.
This is how Heaven and Earth equalize existence and non-existence and connect all things.
Today, the bamboo of Wú (吳) and Yuè (越),
and the timber of Suí (隋) and Táng (唐),
cannot be fully utilized,
while Cáo (曹), Wèi (衛), Liáng (梁), and Sòng (宋)
are collecting coffins and moving corpses;
the fish of the Jiāng (江) and Hú (湖) Rivers,
and the Tái (鮐) fish of Lái (萊) and Huáng (黃),
cannot be fully consumed,
while Zōu (鄒), Lǔ (魯), Zhōu (周), and Hán (韓)
eat vegetables.
The benefits of Heaven and Earth are not fully utilized,
and the goods of the mountains and seas are not fully enriched;
yet the people are impoverished,
and resources are insufficient,
with abundance and scarcity not being properly adjusted,
so that the wealth of the world is not distributed."
The Literary Man said:
"In ancient times,
rafters were not trimmed,
thatched roofs were not pruned,
clothes were made of coarse cloth,
food was eaten from earthen bowls,
metal was cast into hoes,
and clay was molded into vessels.
Craftsmen did not create extravagant items,
and the world did not value things that could not be worn or eaten.
Everyone was content with their dwelling,
enjoyed their customs,
savored their food,
and found their tools convenient.
Therefore, goods from distant lands were not exchanged,
and the jade of Kūnshān (昆山) did not arrive.
Today, customs have deteriorated, and people compete in extravagance.
Women pursue extreme delicacy,
and craftsmen pursue extreme skill.
They carve simple materials and value rare and strange items,
drill into mountains to seek gold and silver,
dive into deep waters to find pearls and gems,
set traps to capture rhinoceroses and elephants,
and spread nets to seek kingfishers.
They seek goods from the Mán (蠻) and Mò (貉) tribes to dazzle China,
transport the goods of Qióng (邛) and Zuó (筰),
and bring them to the East Sea,
exchanging wealth over vast distances,
wasting time and effort,
with no benefit to practical use.
Therefore, commoners, both men and women,
are weary and exhausted,
and lack sufficient clothing and food.
Therefore, rulers prohibit excessive profits
and curtail wasteful spending.
When excessive profits are prohibited, people return to fundamentals;
when wasteful spending is curtailed, the people have sufficient resources.
Therefore, people have no lack of resources in life,
and there are no corpses left unburied after death."
The Grandee said:
"In ancient times,
palaces had standards,
and carriages and clothing were appropriate for their status;
rafters and thatched roofs
were not the system of the former kings.
Gentlemen advocate frugality to critique extravagance;
frugality is solid.
Formerly, when Sūn Shū'áo (孫叔敖) was the minister of Chǔ (楚),
his wife did not wear silk,
and his horses were not fed millet.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
'That is not acceptable;
extreme frugality is the lowest.'
This is what *Xīshuài* (蟋蟀) was created for.
*Guǎnzi* (管子) says:
'If palaces are not decorated,
then timber cannot be fully utilized;
if kitchens are not filled,
then the lifespans of birds and beasts will not be shortened.
Without non-essential profits,
then fundamental industries will have no output;
without beautiful embroidery,
then women's labor will not be employed.'
Therefore, artisans and craftsmen
are essential to the state,
providing necessary equipment.
They have existed since ancient times,
not only now.
Xiángāo (弦高) traded cattle in Zhōu (周),
Wǔgǔ (五羖) rented a carriage to enter Qín (秦),
Gōngshū Zǐ (公輸子) used compasses and squares,
and Ōuyě (歐冶) used smelting and casting.
The *Yǔ* (語) says:
'The artisans reside in their workshops,
to accomplish their tasks.'
Agriculture and commerce exchange goods,
to benefit both fundamental and non-essential industries.
Those who live in the mountains or marshes,
in barren and infertile lands,
rely on the circulation of goods
to equalize their resources."
Therefore, the abundant do not become excessively so,
and the scarce do not suffer extreme famine.
If each remained in their place,
and consumed their own produce,
then oranges and pomelos would not be sold,
Qú Lǔ's 朐鹵 salt would not be exported,
felt and wool fabrics would not be traded in the markets,
and the wealth of Wú 吴 and Táng 唐 would be useless."
The Literary Man said:
"Mèngzǐ 孟子 said:
'If the farming seasons are not disrupted,
grain will be more than can be eaten.
If silkworms and hemp are cultivated in their season,
cloth and silk will be more than can be worn.
If axes and hatchets enter the forests at the right time,
timber will be more than can be used.
If fields and fishing are done in season,
fish and meat will be more than can be eaten.'
But if palaces are decorated,
and terraces and pavilions are increased,
if carpenters and artisans hew large things into small,
and make circles into squares,
so that the top reaches the clouds,
and the bottom forms forests,
then timber will not be sufficient.
If men abandon their primary occupation for secondary ones,
even if they carve and engrave elaborately,
to imitate birds and beasts,
exhausting the resources and pursuing transformation,
then grain will not be enough to eat.
If women decorate small things and refine minute details,
to create elaborate patterns,
exhausting their skills and ingenuity,
then silk and cloth will not be enough to wear.
If chefs slaughter even unborn or newly hatched creatures,
frying, roasting, and mixing flavors,
exhausting all five tastes,
then fish and meat will not be enough to eat.
In the present age,
the concern is not that birds and beasts are not diminished,
or that timber is not used up,
but that extravagance is limitless;
the concern is not the lack of felt, wool fabrics, oranges, and pomelos,
but the lack of small huts and chaff to eat."
1.4 *Cuò Bì Dì Sì* 錯幣第四 (Chapter Four: Faulty Coinage)
The Grand Secretary said:
"When currency is exchanged and circulated,
people neglect their primary occupations,
and goods become concentrated.
When fundamentals are calculated and surpluses are measured,
and people are hungry,
it is because grain is hoarded.
The wise have the labor of a hundred men,
while the foolish do not even manage their own basic tasks.
If the ruler does not regulate,
some people will have riches equal to ten thousand others.
This is why some accumulate enough to last a hundred years,
while others are not satisfied even with chaff and husks.
If the people are very rich,
they cannot be employed with stipends;
if they are very strong,
they cannot be controlled with punishments and authority.
Unless wealth is dispersed and benefits are distributed equally, there will be inequality.
Therefore, the ruler should store food,
control its use,
regulate surpluses,
adjust shortages,
prohibit excessive profits,
and restrict lucrative paths,
then the people can each have enough to provide for their families."
The Literary Man said:
"In ancient times,
virtue was valued and profit was despised,
righteousness was emphasized and wealth was belittled.
During the time of the Three Kings,
there were alternating periods of prosperity and decline.
When things declined, they were supported;
when things tilted, they were stabilized.
Therefore, Xià 夏 was loyal, Yīn 殷 was reverent, and Zhōu 周 was cultured.
The teachings of schools and academies,
and the rituals of respect and humility,
can still be clearly observed.
But later,
ritual and righteousness were relaxed and collapsed,
and customs and morals perished and ceased,
so that the gentlemen who lived off stipends
deviated from righteousness and competed for wealth,
the great and small devoured each other,
and they stirred each other to tilt and fall.
This is why some accumulate enough to last a hundred years,
while others have nothing with which to fill their emptiness and cover their bodies.
In ancient times, officials did not harvest grain,
farmers did not fish,
and gatekeepers and watchmen
all had fixed salaries,
and could not engage in multiple occupations to exhaust the resources.
In this way,
the foolish and the wise contributed equally,
and did not undermine each other.
The *Shī* 詩 (Book of Poetry) says:
'There are gleanings left by others,
here are fallen ears of grain,
these are the benefits for widows.'
This speaks of not exhausting the resources."
The Grand Secretary said:
"Tāng 湯 and Wén 文 inherited decline,
and the rise of the Hàn 漢 dynasty took advantage of corruption.
Simplicity and refinement alternate;
it is not merely a change from the norm.
Customs deteriorate, so laws are changed;
it is not that we deliberately alter the old ways,
but rather that we save what is lost and support what is failing.
Therefore, teachings change with customs,
and abuses change with the times.
The Xiàhòu 夏后 used black cowries,
the Zhōu 周 people used purple stones,
and later generations used gold coins, knives, and cloth.
Things reach their peak and then decline;
it is the cycle of beginning and end.
Therefore, if mountains and marshes are not taxed,
then ruler and subjects share the benefits;
if knives and coins are not regulated,
then treachery and honesty go hand in hand.
If subjects are rich, they will be extravagant;
if those below monopolize profit, they will undermine each other."
The Literary Man said:
"In ancient times,
there were markets but no knives or coins.
People exchanged what they had for what they lacked,
simply using cloth to trade for silk.
Later generations then had turtle shells, cowries, gold, and coins,
which were used for exchange.
As the number of currencies changed, the people became more deceitful.
To save deceit, use simplicity;
to prevent loss, use ritual.
Tāng 湯 and Wén 文 inherited decline,
reformed the laws and changed the customs,
and the ways of Yīn 殷 and Zhōu 周 flourished.
The early Hàn 漢 dynasty took advantage of corruption,
but did not change or reform,
accumulating profits and changing currencies,
wanting to return to the original state;
it is like using searing to stop a burn,
or using fire to stop boiling.
If the ruler loves ritual, the people will secretly adorn themselves;
if the ruler loves wealth, the people will die for profit."
The Grand Secretary said:
"During the time of Emperor Wéndì 文帝,
the people were allowed to cast coins, smelt iron, and boil salt.
The King of Wú 吴 monopolized the Zhàng 鄣 Sea and marshes,
and Dèng Tōng 鄧通 monopolized the Western Mountains.
Clever and cunning people from Shāndōng 山東
all gathered in the state of Wú 吴,
and the regions of Qín 秦, Yōng 雍, Hàn 漢, and Shǔ 蜀 relied on the Dèng 鄧 family.
The coins of Wú 吴 and Dèng 鄧 circulated throughout the land,
so there was a prohibition against casting coins.
When the laws of prohibition and control are established,
then deceit and falsehood will cease;
when deceit and falsehood cease,
then the people will not expect to gain by improper means,
and each will devote himself to his own duty;
if this is not returning to the original state, what is it?
Therefore, with unity,
the people will not be divided;
when currency comes from above,
then those below will not doubt."
The Literary Man said:
"In ancient times,
currency was plentiful, wealth circulated, and the people were happy.
Later,
old currencies were gradually removed,
and white gold turtle dragons were put into circulation,
and the people were skilled at making new coins.
As the number of currencies changed, the people became more doubtful.
Thereupon, all the coins in the land were abolished,
and the *Shuǐ Héng* 水衡 (Ministry of Waterways and Parks) was exclusively ordered to have its three offices make them.
Officials and artisans encroached on profits,
and some did not meet the standard,
so there were those that were thin and thick, light and heavy.
Farmers were not familiar with them,
and when they compared them to goods,
they trusted the old and doubted the new,
and did not know what was false and true.
Merchants traded good for bad,
and exchanged half for double.
Buying resulted in loss of substance,
selling resulted in loss of principle,
and their doubts grew even more.
Making counterfeit gold coins was already unlawful,
but the quality of the coins neither improved nor deteriorated compared to the past.
Selecting coins caused goods to stagnate,
and employing people became especially difficult.
The *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) says:
'Calculations that do not even reach the Mán 蠻 and Yí 夷 barbarians cannot be carried out.'
Therefore, a true king does not block the seas and marshes in order to benefit his own use,
and does not prohibit knives and coins in order to facilitate the people's exchange."
1.5 *Jìn Gēng Dì Wǔ* 禁耕第五 (Chapter Five: Prohibiting Cultivation)
The Grand Secretary said:
"If a family has a precious object,
they still put it in a box and store it away.
How much more so the mountains and seas of the ruler?
The location of these resources
must be in the deep mountains and remote marshes.
Not even powerful families can fully exploit their benefits.
In the past,
before the state controlled salt and iron,
commoners had Qú Bǐng (朐邴),
and rulers had the King of Wú (吳王).
These were the initial debates about salt and iron.
The King of Wú monopolized the abundance of mountains and marshes,
lightly taxed his people,
provided for the poor and needy,
and thereby established his own private authority.
The accumulation of private authority led to rebellious intentions.
If one does not eliminate the source early on but worries about the outcome,
it is like breaching the Mount Lǚ (呂梁),
the force of which is immense,
and what it harms will certainly be extensive.
Tàigōng (太公) said:
'One family harms a hundred families,
a hundred families harm the feudal lords,
the feudal lords harm the entire country,
and the royal law forbids it.'
Now, if we allow the people to have control over these resources,
abolish the salt and iron monopoly to benefit violent and powerful individuals,
satisfy their greedy desires,
evil elements will gather in droves,
private households will form factions,
then the strong and unruly will become increasingly uncontrollable,
and the formation of cliques dedicated to annexation and deceit will occur."
The Scholar said:
"The common people are stored within their families,
the feudal lords are stored within their states,
and the Son of Heaven is stored within the realm.
Therefore, the common people use walls as enclosures,
and the Son of Heaven uses the four seas as his case.
When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords,
he ascends from the eastern steps,
and the feudal lords submit the control and keys
and listen to his commands,
showing that there is no other master.
Therefore, the true king does not hoard,
but stores wealth among the people,
distances himself from fleeting profits,
and focuses on the righteousness of the people.
When righteousness and ritual are established,
the people will be transformed by those above.
If this is the case, even if Tāng (湯) and Wǔ (武) were still alive,
there would be no room for their concerns.
As for the matters of industry and commerce,
and the responsibilities of Ōuyě (歐冶),
how can deceit be achieved?
The Sānhuán (三桓) monopolized Lǔ (魯),
and the Six Ministers divided Jìn (晉),
but not through salt and iron.
Therefore, the source of power
is not in the mountains and seas,
but in the court;
the harm of one family to a hundred families
is within the inner walls,
and not in Qú Bǐng (朐邴)."
"If there are restrictions on the mountains and seas,
the people will not be impoverished.
If there is equality in value,
the people will have no doubts.
If the state officials set up scales and measures,
people can get what they want.
Even if you send a five-foot-tall child to the market,
no one will be able to deceive him.
If you get rid of this,
powerful families will monopolize its use and benefits.
Determining prices in the markets and alleys,
the ups and downs depend on their pronouncements,
value is inconstant,
and they become rich by sitting idly,
thereby nourishing the strong and suppressing the weak, and hoarding for Zhí (跖).
If you nourish the strong and suppress the weak,
the common people will disappear,
like the flourishing of many weeds harming the five grains.
One family harms a hundred families;
it is not in Qú Bǐng (朐邴).
How can it be otherwise?"
The Scholar said:
"Mountains and seas
are the treasure road for wealth and resources.
Ironware
is the farmers' weapon to the death.
If the weapon to the death is used,
enemies will be destroyed.
If enemies are destroyed,
the fields will be cultivated.
If the fields are cultivated, the five grains will ripen.
If the treasure road is opened,
the people will be provided for, and their needs will be met.
If the needs of the people are met, the country will be rich.
If the country is rich and they are taught with propriety,
there will be yielding on the road,
and merchants and artisans will not interfere with each other.
People will embrace sincerity and simplicity in their interactions
and not seek profit from each other.
The states of Qín (秦), Chǔ (楚), Yān (燕), and Qí (齊)
have different soil strengths
and different tendencies to be rigid or flexible.
Tools of different sizes,
and appropriate dwellings,
different customs and traditions,
each has its own convenience.
If the state controls and unifies them,
then the ironware will lose its suitability,
and the farmers will lose their convenience.
If the tools are not convenient,
then the farmers will be exhausted in the fields, and the weeds will not be cleared.
If the weeds are not cleared,
then the people will be impoverished.
The location of salt smelting,
where the big Ao are, all depends on mountains and rivers,
close to iron and coal,
and their situation is always remote and the work difficult.
The conscripted soldiers in the commanderies
often do not meet the quota,
and are charged a fee in lieu of service.
The counties and towns sometimes levy iron according to the number of households,
and lower the standard.
Respectable families hire carriages to transport salt and iron on the road,
which is troublesome and expensive,
and the people suffer.
I see one official harming a thousand *lǐ* (里),
but I do not see it in Qú Bǐng (朐邴)."
1. 6 *Fùgǔ Dìliù* (復古第六)
The Grand Secretary said:
"The former Commandant of the Water Gate, Péng Zǔníng (彭祖寧), returned
and said:
'The regulations for salt and iron
are very clear.
The soldiers and laborers are provided with food and clothing by the government,
make and cast ironware,
which is supplied in great quantities,
without hindering the people.
But the officials are sometimes corrupt,
and the prohibitions are not enforced,
so the people are troubled and suffer.'
The intention of the imperial decree is to unify the salt and iron,
not solely for profit,
but to establish the fundamental and suppress the superficial,
separate factions,
prohibit extravagance,
and cut off the path to annexation.
In ancient times,
famous mountains and large marshes were not used for enfeoffment,
because they were for the exclusive benefit of those below.
The benefits of mountains and seas,
the livestock of the wide marshes,
are the treasures of heaven and earth,
all of which should belong to the *Shàofǔ* (少府);
but Your Majesty does not keep them private,
but assigns them to the *Dà Sīnóng* (大司農)
to assist the common people.
Those floating eaters,
desire to monopolize the goods of the mountains and seas,
to achieve wealth and prosperity,
and exploit the small people,
so there are many who obstruct and debate the matter.
Ironware and weapons
are of great use to the world,
and are not suitable for the common people to handle.
In the past,
powerful and influential families
were able to control the benefits of the mountains and seas,
mine iron and stone,
and boil the sea for salt.
One family would gather a crowd
of up to a thousand people,
mostly composed of released and exiled people.
They would leave their villages,
abandon their ancestral graves,
rely on powerful families,
gather in the deep mountains and remote marshes,
engage in deceitful and fraudulent activities,
and consolidate the power of their factions.
The extent to which they commit wrongdoings is great!
Now,
we should broadly open the path to employing the wise,
select and train governors and commandants.
It is not necessary to remove salt and
iron in order to pacify the people."
The *Wénxué* said:
"What the *Shànshuǐ Dūwèi* said
concerns temporary expedients
and opportunistic tactics;
they cannot be practiced for long or passed down to future generations. This is not the way a wise ruler governs his country and cherishes his people.
The *Shī* says:
'Alas, it is done as though it were a game,
not following the example of the former people,
not taking the great norms as a guide,
but listening to what is near at hand.'
This is the poet satirizing those who do not understand the way of kings
but are good at using expedients and advantages.
*Xiàowǔ* Emperor expanded the territory of the nine *Yí* tribes
and pacified the hundred *Yuè* tribes.
Military campaigns were frequent,
and grain supplies were insufficient.
Therefore, he established agricultural officials,
set up currency,
and allowed people to exchange grain for official positions
to relieve emergencies and support the needy.
Now, Your Majesty inherits the great achievements and toils
and nourishes the weary people.
This is the time to use [policies of] clemency.
Your ministers should consider how to pacify and gather the people,
bring benefits and eliminate harm,
assist the enlightened ruler with benevolence and righteousness,
and cultivate the path of great achievements.
Since the enlightened ruler ascended the throne,
six years have passed.
The ministers have not requested the reduction of unnecessary officials
or the dismissal of those who seek personal gain.
Power has been held by individuals for too long,
and the people eagerly await the ruler above.
Your Majesty proclaims sagely virtue
and radiates enlightened brilliance,
ordering virtuous and learned scholars from the commanderies and kingdoms
to travel by relay carriage to the imperial carriage,
to discuss the way of the Five Emperors and Three Kings
and the customs of the Six Arts,
to clearly present the distinctions between safety, danger, benefit, and harm.
The intentions are perfectly clear.
Now, the ministers debate
without reaching a decision.
This is what is meant by clinging to minor details and neglecting the greater picture,
embracing small advantages and forgetting great benefits."
The *Dàfū* said:
"Within the eaves of a house,
swallows and sparrows do not know the height of the heavens;
the frog in a well
does not know the vastness of the rivers and seas;
poor men and women
do not know the concerns of the state;
merchants carrying loads
do not know the wealth of *Yīdùn*.
The late emperor calculated the benefits of foreign lands
and assessed the strength of the *Hú* and *Yuè* soldiers.
The enemy was weak and easy to control,
requiring little effort but yielding great results.
Therefore, he took advantage of the situation to dominate the four *Yí* tribes,
with the land bordering the mountains and seas
belonging to the Great Wall.
He conquered the lands beyond the Yellow River to the north
and opened roads to the lands of the *Xiōngnú*.
The work is not yet complete.
*Wén* King received the mandate to attack *Chóng*
and built a city in *Fēng*.
*Wǔ* King continued his work,
carrying the corpse of his father in his campaign,
defeating the Shang and capturing *Zhòu*,
thus completing the royal enterprise.
*Cáo Mò* cast aside the humiliation of losing three hundred *lǐ* of land
and recovered the invaded territory.
*Guǎn Zhòng* bore the burdens of his time
and established a hegemonic achievement.
Therefore, those with great ambitions overlook small matters,
and those who use expedients deviate from convention.
The officials should consider the plans of *Shī Wàng*
and continue the late emperor's enterprise,
with the ambition to cut off the *Hú* and *Mò* tribes
and capture the *Chányú*.
Therefore, they have not had time to delve into the meaning of knocking on doors
and record the opinions of confined scholars."
The *Wénxué* said:
"Swallows and sparrows leaving their nests have the worry of hawks and falcons;
frogs in wells leaving their homes have the danger of snakes and rats;
how much more so those who soar a thousand *rèn* high and travel the four seas?
Their disaster would be great indeed!
This is why *Lǐ Sī*'s wings were clipped
and *Zhào Gāo* drowned in the abyss.
I have heard that *Wén* and *Wǔ* received the mandate
to attack injustice and pacify the feudal lords and grandees,
but I have not heard of exhausting the resources of the *Zhūxià* to serve the *Yí* and *Dí* tribes.
In the past, Qin often mobilized the strength of the entire empire to serve the *Hú* and *Yuè* tribes,
depleting the wealth of the empire to provide for their needs.
Yet, the people could not meet the demands completely,
and a million soldiers
were burdened with the task of one man.
This is known by everyone in the empire.
Moreover, frequent battles exhaust the people,
and prolonged campaigns weaken the soldiers.
This is what the people suffer from
and what confined scholars worry about."
2.1 *Fēi Yǎng Dì Qī*
The *Dàfū* said:
"In the past, when *Shāng Yāng* served as minister of Qin,
he established laws and measures within the country,
enforced strict punishments,
regulated government and education,
and left no room for treachery and deceit.
Externally, he set up a hundredfold profit,
collected taxes from mountains and lakes,
made the country rich and the people strong,
perfected weapons and armor,
and accumulated reserves.
Therefore, when attacking enemies and conquering countries,
seizing territory and expanding borders,
he did not tax the people, and the army was well-supplied.
Thus, the benefits were inexhaustible, and the people were unaware,
and the land stretched to the west of the Yellow River, and the people did not suffer.
The profits from salt and iron
were used to help the urgent needs of the people
and to cover the expenses of the military,
striving to accumulate reserves to prepare for shortages and emergencies.
The supplies provided were abundant,
benefiting the country
and causing no harm to the people.
What suffering do the people have,
and what worries do the scholars have?"
The *Wénxué* said:
"During the time of Emperor *Wén*,
there were no profits from salt and iron, yet the people were rich.
Now that we have them, the people are impoverished and needy.
I have not seen the benefit of these benefits,
but I have seen their harm.
Moreover, profit does not come from the sky
or emerge from the earth.
It is all taken from the people,
calling it a hundredfold return.
This is a miscalculation.
It is no different from a fool wearing his fur coat inside out to carry firewood,
cherishing the fur
but not realizing that the skin will be exhausted.
When plums and apricots bear abundant fruit,
they will decline in the following year.
When new grain ripens, the old grain diminishes.
Even heaven and earth cannot both be full at the same time,
let alone human affairs.
Therefore, what benefits one side must deplete the other,
just as the *yīn* and *yáng* cannot both shine at the same time,
and day and night have varying lengths.
*Shāng Yāng*'s harsh laws brought temporary gains,
but the people of Qin could not live in peace
and mourned *Xiàogōng* together.
*Wú Qǐ*'s aggressive military conquests
stirred up the people of Chu,
who wept and lamented *Dàowáng* together.
After that, Chu became increasingly precarious,
and Qin became increasingly weak.
Therefore, wealth accumulates, and resentment builds up;
land expands, and disasters are constructed.
Where is the inexhaustible benefit and the people's lack of suffering?
Where is the land stretching to the west of the Yellow River, and the people not suffering?
Now, *Shāng Yāng*'s policies are implemented internally,
and *Wú Qǐ*'s military strategies are used externally.
Travelers toil on the roads,
and residents are destitute in their homes.
Old mothers weep and wail,
and unmarried women sigh.
Even if I, a scholar, wished to have no worries,
how could I?"
The *Dàfū* said:
"When Qin employed *Shāng Yāng*,
the state became rich and strong.
Eventually, it annexed the six states and established the imperial enterprise.
By the time of the Second Emperor,
wicked ministers held power,
public justice was not practiced,
the feudal lords rebelled and defected,
and the ancestral temples collapsed and were destroyed.
The *Chūnqiū* says:
'To speak last is to say that [when] *Jì Zhòng* disappears, [the state is] lost.'
One who sings well makes others continue his song,
and one who creates well makes others carry on his work.
The cicada's capture of the wheel of a cart
is the teaching of the *Fùzǐ* insect.
The success of the Zhou dynasty
was due to the efforts of the *Zhōu Gōng*.
Even with *Bì Chén*'s initial drafts,
without *Zǐchǎn*'s refinement,
and with the standards of *Wén* and *Wǔ*,
but without the mortise and tenon of *Zhōu* and *Lǚ*,
the great work would not have been completed.
To blame *Shāng Yāng* for the downfall of Qin due to *Zhào Gāo*
is like blaming *Yī Yǐn* for the chaos of Yin due to *Chóng Hǔ*."
The Literary Man said:
"A good excavator builds a secure surrounding wall that cannot be breached,
and a good foundation builder reaches great heights without
collapsing.
Yī Yǐn used the ways of Yáo and Shùn as the foundation for the Yīn state,
and his descendants inherited the throne,
with the line unbroken for a hundred generations.
Shāng Yāng used harsh punishments and severe laws as the foundation for the Qín state,
so it was seized after two generations.
Not only were the punishments harsh and severe,
but he also created the law of mutual implication,
fabricated slanders,
and increased corporal punishments,
causing the people to tremble in fear,
not knowing what to do.
Not only were the taxes and levies burdensome and frequent,
but he also externally prohibited access to the resources of the mountains and marshes,
and internally established hundredfold profits,
leaving the people with no means to express their grievances or voice their opinions.
He valued profit and slighted righteousness,
exalted force and esteemed achievement.
It was not that he did not expand the territory and advance the land,
but it was like a person suffering from dropsy,
where adding water only deepens the illness.
He knew that he was opening up an imperial enterprise for Qín,
but he did not know that he was leading Qín down the road to ruin.
A fox-thorn tenon,
even Gōngshū Zǐ cannot make its mortise well.
A foundation of tamped earth,
even a skilled artisan cannot complete its height.
It is like autumn weeds covered with frost,
which fall and scatter when they encounter the wind.
Even if there were ten Zǐchǎn,
what could be done?
Therefore, Biǎn Què cannot restore flesh to bare bones,
and Wēi Zǐ and Jī Zǐ cannot save a collapsing state."
The Grandee said:
"Speaking is not difficult,
but acting is difficult.
Therefore, a virtuous person deals with reality and achieves results,
not merely reciting empty words.
In the past, Shāng Jūn was astute in the art of opening up and blocking,
seizing the power of the time,
and brought profit and achievement to Qín.
Therefore, he won battles and seized territory,
annexed nearby states and destroyed distant ones,
seized Yān and Zhào,
and subjugated Qí and Chǔ.
The feudal lords tucked in their robes,
faced west, and submitted to his influence.
Later,
Méng Tián campaigned against the Xiongnu,
expanding the territory by a thousand *lǐ*,
crossing north of the Hé River,
as if breaking rotten wood and snapping decayed branches.
Why?
Because of Shāng Jūn's plans,
well-prepared and thoroughly cultivated.
Therefore, every undertaking was profitable,
and every action was successful.
Accumulating plans and strategies
is how a state becomes strong.
To relax these efforts and return them to the people
is to fail to see the grand scheme and tread the great path."
The Literary Man said:
"Shāng Yāng's opening up and blocking
was not ineffective;
Méng Tián's driving back the Xiongnu by a thousand *lǐ*
was not without merit;
his power shaking the world
was not weakness;
the feudal lords following the wind and facing west
was not disobedience.
Yet all these things were the reasons for Qín's downfall.
Shāng Yāng endangered the Qín state with his schemes,
and Méng Tián destroyed the Qín state with his gaining a thousand *lǐ*.
These two men
knew profit but did not know harm,
knew advance but did not know retreat,
so ultimately they died and their achievements were defeated.
This is what is called the wisdom of a mole cricket
and the plans of a fool.
What great path is there in this?
Therefore, it is said:
'Small men agree at first but later disagree;
though they may initially ride in carriages,
in the end they will weep blood.'
This is what it means."
The Grandee said:
"People of virtue and excellence
are envied by the ugly and deformed;
men of wisdom and knowledge
are hated by the ignorant and foolish.
Therefore, Shàngguān Dàfū slandered Qū Yuán to Qǐng Xiāng,
and Gōngbó Liáo accused Zǐlù to Jì Sūn.
Shāng Jūn rose from humble origins,
entered Qín from Wèi,
and within a year became its chancellor,
reforming the laws and clarifying the teachings,
and the people of Qín achieved great order.
Therefore, when the army moved, land was seized,
and when the army rested, the country became rich.
Xiào Gōng was greatly pleased
and enfeoffed him in the land of Shāng, five hundred *lǐ* in area.
His achievements were like mountains,
and his name will be passed down to later generations.
People of the world cannot do what he did,
so they envy his ability and find fault with his achievements."
The Literary Man said:
"A virtuous person advances only through the proper way,
and retreats without losing righteousness,
is eminent but not arrogant,
works hard but does not boast,
is high in position but acts respectfully,
and has great achievements but governs smoothly.
Therefore, the common people do not begrudge their abilities,
and the world does not envy their accomplishments.
Now, Shāng Yāng abandoned the proper way and used schemes,
discarded virtue and relied on force,
imposed harsh laws and severe punishments,
making cruelty and violence the custom,
deceived old acquaintances to achieve success,
punished the imperial clan to establish his authority,
had no kindness towards the common people,
and no trustworthiness among the feudal lords.
People harbored resentment against him,
and families made him their enemy.
Although he gained merit and was enfeoffed,
it was like eating poisoned meat, enjoying the fullness but suffering the consequences.
Sū Qín united the states in horizontal and vertical alliances,
and governed the six states,
his achievements were not small;
Jié and Zhòu are mentioned in the same breath as Yáo and Shùn,
and their names have not perished to this day,
their fame is not short-lived;
yet those who are wrong are not worth esteeming.
Therefore, actions are not valued merely for being many,
and names are not valued merely for being passed down."
The Grandee said:
"White silk cannot distinguish itself from black ink,
and the wise and virtuous cannot manage themselves in a chaotic world.
Therefore, Jī Zǐ was imprisoned,
and Bǐgān was executed.
Wǔ Yuán assisted Hélǘ to achieve hegemony,
but Fūchāi was unprincipled
and exiled and killed him.
Yuè Yì faithfully served Zhāo of Yān and achieved great merit,
but was doubted by Huì Wáng.
Loyal ministers exhaust their efforts to pursue fame,
only to encounter rulers who do not use them.
Dàfū Zhǒng assisted the King of Yuè,
devising deep plans for him,
and ultimately captured the powerful Wú,
seizing control of the eastern barbarians,
yet in the end he was given the shǔlòu sword and died.
An arrogant ruler turns his back on kindness and virtue,
listens to slanderous words,
and does not consider their merits;
how can it be their own fault?"
The Literary Man said:
"Bǐgān had his heart cut out,
and Zǐxū was thrown into the river in a leather bag.
They did not lightly offend their rulers to endanger themselves,
or forcefully remonstrate to gain fame.
Their sincere and earnest loyalty
moved them from within,
causing them to forget the disasters that might befall them from without.
Their will was to rectify the ruler and save the people,
so they died without complaint.
A virtuous person can act rightly but cannot prevent wrongdoing,
so even if they are subjected to punishment,
it is not their fault.
Therefore, when Bǐgān died, the people of Yīn resented it,
and when Zǐxū died, the people of Wú regretted it.
Now, the people of Qín resented and loathed Shāng Yāng's laws
even more than personal enemies,
so on the day Xiào Gōng died,
the entire country attacked him.
He could not flee east, west, south, or north,
and he looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
'Alas,
the evils of governance
have reached this extreme!'
In the end, he was torn apart by chariots and his clan was exterminated,
becoming a laughingstock to the world.
This man killed himself,
not others who killed him."
2.2 Eighth Discussion: Cháo Cuò
The Grandee said:
"The principle of the *Chūnqiū*
is that rulers and parents must not be attacked;
attacking them must be punished.
Therefore, no crime of a minister is greater than regicide,
and no crime of a son is greater than patricide.
In the past,
Liú Ān of Huáinán and the Prince of Héngshān cultivated learning,
and recruited itinerant scholars from all directions.
Confucianists and Mohists from Shāndōng all gathered between the Jiāng and Huái Rivers,
lecturing and debating,
and writing dozens of books.
However, they ultimately ended up betraying righteousness and being disloyal,
being used to plot rebellion,
and their entire families were exterminated.
Cháo Cuò changed the laws and altered the norms,
disregarded established systems,
oppressed the imperial relatives,
and encroached upon the feudal lords.
The vassal subjects did not support him,
and the members of the imperial family were not close to him.
The states of Wú and Chǔ accumulated resentment,
and Cháo Cuò was beheaded in the eastern market
to appease the soldiers and apologize to the feudal lords.
So who killed him?"
The Literatus said:
"Kǒngzǐ would not drink from the stream of Dàoquán,
and Zēngzǐ would not enter the neighborhood of Shèngmǔ.
They detested even the names,
let alone acting disloyal and unfilial?
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ bathed and went to court,
to inform Duke Āi.
Chén Wénzǐ had ten teams of horses,
but abandoned them and left.
The *Commentary* says:
'A gentleman can be honored or demeaned,
can be punished or killed,
but cannot be made to participate in disorder.'
As for those who outwardly adorn their appearance but lack inner substance,
who recite the texts but do not act according to the Way,
they are robbers,
and are firmly grouped with robbers and not tolerated in the realm of gentlemen.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* does not punish a minority that offends the majority;
the principle of extermination has its limits,
and does not combine grievances and resentments.
Therefore, when Shùn punished,
he punished Gǔn;
when he promoted,
he promoted Yǔ.
To discard jade because of a small flaw,
and abandon the uncut gem,
to punish the many because of one person's crime,
and implicate the masses,
then the world will have no beautiful treasures or trustworthy men.
Cháo shēng said that the feudal lords' lands were large,
and that if they were wealthy, they would become arrogant and extravagant,
and would quickly form alliances.
Therefore, because of Wú's transgression, his territory of Kuàijī was reduced;
because of Chǔ's crime, his territory of Dōnghǎi was taken away.
This was to equalize the power,
divide their authority,
and plan for the benefit of ten thousand generations.
Xián Gāo lied to Qín but was trusted by Zhèng;
Cháo shēng was loyal to Hàn but was hated by the feudal lords.
Ministers each die for their lord,
and are used by their state.
This is why Jiě Yáng was honored by Jìn and despised by Jīng."
2.3 *Chapter 9: Criticizing Power*
The Grandee said:
"Now, the Jùqū marsh of Yuè,
the Yúnmèng marsh of Chǔ,
the Jùyě marsh of Sòng,
the Mèngzhū marsh of Qí,
are the wealth of a state and the resources of a hegemon.
If the ruler controls and protects them, the state will be strong;
if he does not restrict them, the state will perish.
Qí gave its stomach and intestines to others,
the family grew strong and could not be controlled,
the branches grew large and broke the trunk,
monopolizing the wealth of the vast sea and dominating the profits of fish and salt.
Their power was sufficient to command the masses,
and their kindness was sufficient to care for their inferiors.
Therefore, Qí's internal power doubled and its external support increased.
Authority shifted to the ministers,
and the government fell into the hands of the families.
The public house became weak, and the Tián lineage became strong.
Those whose axles turned and traveled the sea numbered about three thousand chariots.
It was lost at the root, and the branches could not be saved.
Now, the sources of mountains, rivers, seas, and marshes
are not only Yúnmèng and Mèngzhū.
Smelting metal and boiling salt
will inevitably lead to them dwelling deep in secluded valleys,
where the people rarely go.
The treacherous and cunning communicate between the mountains and seas,
and there is fear that great treachery will arise.
Riding on profit, they become arrogant and excessive,
abandoning simplicity and fostering deceit,
so that few people value the fundamentals.
The Grand Agriculturalist, the Salt and Iron Commissioner, Xián Yáng, Kǒng Jǐn, and others requested the emperor:
'We wish to recruit people to provide their own expenses,
use government-owned equipment,
boil salt for use,
in order to block the path of extravagance and falsehood.'
From this we can see that:
the emperor's intentions to prohibit are subtle,
and the officials' concerns are far-reaching."
The Literatus said:
"The officials' concerns are far-reaching,
but the power families' profits are near.
The emperor's intentions to prohibit are subtle,
but the path to extravagance and excess is clear.
Since the establishment of profit and harm,
and the rise of the three industries,
the homes of powerful men
had clouds of carriages on the roads,
and the sound of axles striking each other.
They disregarded public laws
and promoted private interests,
straddling mountains and marshes,
monopolizing official markets,
not just the fish and salt of the vast sea.
They held the reins of the state
and roamed the country,
not just the power of Tián Cháng and the authority of a subordinate minister.
Their authority outweighed the six ministers,
and their wealth surpassed Táo Zhū and Wèi Wén, their carriages and clothing exceeded those of kings and dukes,
and their palaces exceeded the regulations.
They combined adjacent residences,
separating neighborhoods and alleys,
with interconnected covered walkways
sufficient for strolling and viewing,
and excavated ponds and winding paths
sufficient for racing horses.
They fished by the deep pools,
released hounds to chase rabbits,
displayed their power with elaborate cauldrons,
played kickball and fought chickens.
The maidens of Zhōngshān played flowing melodies on the zheng in the halls,
and the drummers of Bā and Yú performed below the halls.
Women wore silk and fine silk,
and maids dragged coarse linen.
Their sons and grandsons rode in a continuous line of carriages,
going out to hunt,
excelling in nets and arrows.
Therefore, farmers put down their plows and became lazy,
and the people became disillusioned and lax.
Why?
Because they work for it, but others take it.
Extravagance and excess are imitated by each other,
rising and never ceasing.
This is why the people become increasingly false and rarely return to the fundamentals."
The Grandee said:
"Those who hold high office receive generous salaries,
and those with strong roots have flourishing branches.
Therefore, King Wén had virtue, and his descendants were enfeoffed;
the Duke of Zhōu assisted, and Bó Qín became wealthy.
Where the water is wide, the fish are large;
where the father is honored, the son is noble.
The *Commentary* says:
'The Yellow River and the Sea nourish a thousand miles.'
Great virtue extends to the four seas,
let alone one's wife and children?
Therefore, the husband is ennobled at court,
and the wife is ennobled at home;
wealth is called good,
this is the ancient way.
*Mèngzǐ* said:
'Princes are the same as other men,
but they are like that
because of their position.'
To live among the common people
and expect to be like the sons and grandsons of ministers and chancellors
is like a lame man wanting to catch up with Lóu Jì,
or wanting the treasure of a thousand gold coins without any money;
is that not an empty hope?"
The Literatus said:
"Yǔ and Jì were commoners,
but they worried that there were those in the world who were not in their proper place,
as if they had pushed them into a ditch.
Therefore, they rose up to assist Yáo,
to regulate the waters and the land,
and to teach the people to sow and reap.
Their responsibility to the world was so heavy,
how could they only think of eating their salaries to support their wives and children?
Those who eat the strength of ten thousand men
bear their worries
and take on their labor.
If one person loses his job,
or one office is not well-governed,
it is all the burden of the dukes and ministers.
Therefore, a gentleman serves
to practice his righteousness,
not to enjoy his power.
He receives a salary to enrich the worthy,
not to privatize his benefits.
He does not hide the worthy when he sees them,
and he does not monopolize his salary.
This is why Gōngshū was refined
and Wèi Chéngzǐ was worthy.
Therefore, King Wén's virtue was complete before his descendants were enfeoffed,
and the world did not consider it partisanship.
The Duke of Zhōu's achievements were complete before he received his fief,
and the world did not consider it greed."
But it is not so now.
Relatives recommend each other,
factions promote each other,
fathers are honored in their positions,
sons are excessive in their homes,
husbands are ennobled at court,
wives make calls and travel abroad.
They have the wealth of Zhōu Gōng 周公 without his virtue,
the extravagance of Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 without his merit,
thus even a lame commoner hopes to walk swiftly."
2.4 "Criticizing the Overabundance"
The grand master, feigning color, but his heart was not joyful,
said:
"Those who merely reside do not know the toil of bearing burdens,
those who advise from the sidelines have different concerns than those in charge.
At present, this is a commandery situated in the belly of the empire,
the various lords are all arriving,
the central court and the outer regions are not yet settled,
my heart is restless as if crossing a great river,
encountering wind without being able to moor.
Therefore, I think day and night about the needs of the state,
lie down and forget to sleep,
become hungry and forget to eat,
calculations are never far from my mind,
myriad affairs are examined in my heart.
The assistant officials are small vessels,
insufficient to consult with,
I alone harbor great principles,
longing to see men of letters,
as if waiting for Zhōu 周 and Shào 邵 and hoping for Gāo Zǐ 高子.
The imperial censor investigates affairs in the commanderies and kingdoms,
observes integrity and recommends virtuous talents,
and each year is not lacking.
Now, the virtuous and talented, the men of letters, who have arrived number over sixty,
cherishing the arts of the *Liù Yì* 六藝,
giving full rein to their ideas and arguing to the utmost,
seemingly as if opening light and dispelling ignorance,
but believing in the past and deviating from the present,
advocating antiquity and not conforming to the affairs of the world.
Does it mean that I am not capable of recognizing gentlemen?
Or are there many who embellish their words and falsely claim abilities in order to disrupt the truth?
Why are virtuous gentlemen so difficult to find!
Ever since Qiānchéng 千乘 and Ní Kuān 倪寬 used their governance of the *Shàngshū* 尚書 to rise to the rank of the Nine Ministers,
and from what I have heard and seen of the gentlemen selected,
promoted and advanced, praised and enacted, were extremely distinguished,
yet I have not seen any of extraordinary caliber,
who could invigorate what is stagnant and establish merit for the local government."
The men of letters said:
"When Shū Zǐ 輸子 fashions timber,
he corrects its compass and square and makes the mortise and tenon fit.
When Shī Kuàng 師曠 harmonizes the five notes,
he corrects the six pitch-pipes and makes the *gōng* 宮 and *shāng* 商 notes fit.
If the artisans of the present age
cannot make the mortise and tenon fit,
then they alter the compass and square;
if they cannot harmonize the sounds,
then they change the old pitch-pipes.
Therefore, the mortise and tenon are contrary and do not join,
the sounds are overflowing and not harmonious.
To hold the compass and square and know what is suitable,
to blow the pitch-pipe and know the changes,
is the highest;
to follow the old ways without creating anew,
and wait for the right person,
is the next best.
Therefore, Chancellor Cáo 曹 drank pure wine every day,
and Grand Master Ní 倪 kept his mouth shut and did not speak.
Thus, those who govern large matters cannot be vexed,
for if they are vexed, they will be chaotic;
those who govern small matters cannot be negligent,
for if they are negligent, they will be abandoned.
The *Chūnqiū* 春秋 says:
'If the government is broad and outstanding,
broad and outstanding can be used as ministers and chancellors.
If the government is meticulous and detailed,
meticulous and detailed can be used as commoners.'
If the guiding principles are not upheld,
rites and propriety are not practiced,
this is the worry of the dukes and ministers.
The documents on the desk,
the scheduled meetings,
are the responsibility of the assistant officials.
The *Shàngshū* 尚書 says:
'When the outstanding and talented are in office,
the hundred officials are teachers,
the hundred artisans keep to their times,
and all the officials are harmonious.'
It means that when an official gets the right person,
and the person is entrusted with their task,
therefore the government is orderly and not chaotic,
affairs arise and are not abandoned,
the gentlemen guard their positions,
the grand masters manage their stations,
and the dukes and ministers grasp the essentials and manage the ordinary only.
Therefore, those who entrust to ability achieve success without labor,
those who entrust to themselves abandon affairs without accomplishment.
Duke Huán 桓 treated Guǎn Zhòng 管仲
as his ears and eyes.
Therefore, the virtuous strive to seek out the worthy,
and relax in using them,
how can they be considered remiss?
In the past, when Zhōu Gōng 周公 was the prime minister,
he was humble and not arrogant,
in order to labor for the gentlemen of the empire,
therefore, the outstanding and talented filled the court,
the virtuous and wise filled the gates.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 had no rank or position,
yet he followed the talented gentlemen in common clothes, over seventy people,
all of whom were men of lords, dukes, and ministers,
how much more so those who occupy the honor of the Three Dukes, in order to support the gentlemen of the empire?
Now, with the high positions of dukes and ministers,
and the excellence of rank and emolument,
yet you cannot attract gentlemen,
then there is no way to advance the worthy.
When Yáo 堯 recommended Shùn 舜,
he treated him as a guest and married his daughter to him.
When Duke Huán 桓 recommended Guǎn Zhòng 管仲,
he treated him as a guest and made him his teacher.
For the Son of Heaven to marry his daughter to a commoner,
can be called being intimate with the worthy.
For a lord to make a commoner his teacher,
can be called respecting guests.
Therefore, the worthy followed him like a stream,
and returned to him without hesitation.
Now those in office in the present age,
have neither the lowering of oneself to gentlemen by Yān Zhāo 燕昭,
nor the delighting in the worthy of the *Lù Míng* 鹿鳴,
but practice the intentions of Zāng Wén 臧文 and Zǐ Jiāo 子椒,
obscuring the worthy and being jealous of ability,
exalting their own wisdom,
criticizing the talents of others,
being content with themselves and not inquiring,
looking down on gentlemen and not befriending them,
valuing the worthy by rank,
and being arrogant to gentlemen with emolument,
yet seeking the use of gentlemen,
it is also difficult!"
The grand master was perplexed and did not speak,
and the worthy gentlemen sighed deeply.
The imperial censor stepped forward and said:
"Tàigōng 太公 assisted Wén 文 and Wǔ 武 to become kings of the empire,
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 assisted Duke Huán 桓 to become hegemon of the feudal lords.
Therefore, when the worthy obtain positions,
it is like dragons obtaining water,
or soaring serpents traveling through the mist.
Chancellor Gōngsūn 公孫 used the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 to explain to the former emperor,
and immediately reached the Three Dukes,
occupying the ranks of Zhōu 周 and Shào 召,
holding the power of ten thousand *lǐ* 里,
becoming the standard for the empire,
not wearing doubled colors,
not eating doubled flavors,
in order to lead the empire,
but he was of no benefit to governance.
The erudite scholars Chǔ Tài 褚泰, Xú Yǎn 徐偃, and others,
received clear orders,
erected their staffs and rode in carriages,
touring and inspecting the commanderies and kingdoms,
recommending the filial and incorrupt,
and encouraging the common people,
but the current customs did not change.
Recruiting and recommending the virtuous, upright, and literary gentlemen,
promoting them beyond their ranks and titles,
some even reaching the rank of duke and grand master,
is this not the recommending of gentlemen by Yān Zhāo 燕昭,
and the broadening of the worthy by King Wén 文?
However, I have not seen any accomplishments achieved.
It is likely that they are not the talents of dragons and serpents,
and they are not the worthy that the *Lù Míng* 鹿鳴 delights in."
The men of letters said:
"Ice and charcoal cannot be put in the same vessel,
the sun and moon cannot shine together,
during the time of Gōngsūn Hóng 公孫弘,
the ruler was setting his mind and intentions on the four barbarians,
therefore, the schemes of deception were advanced,
and the gentlemen of Jīng 荊 and Chǔ 楚 were employed,
and generals and commanders even reached the point of being enfeoffed as lords and eating from the territory,
and those who conquered and captured all received generous rewards,
therefore, the warriors who fought fiercely arose from this.
Afterwards,
the fighting did not cease,
and military expeditions were constantly in sight,
the armored soldiers were exhausted and depleted,
and the government's resources were insufficient,
therefore, ministers who established dangers and raised profits arose,
and the gentlemen of Pánxī 磻溪, those like bears and grizzlies, hid themselves.
The Jīng 涇 and Wèi 渭 rivers were dredged to facilitate transport by water,
Dōngguō Xiányáng 東郭咸陽 and Kǒng Jǐn 孔僅 established the salt and iron monopolies,
and planned various profits,
the rich bought ranks and trafficked in official positions,
avoiding punishment and eliminating crimes,
public expenses increased all the more, while those who did so pursued private gain,
and both those above and below sought after them,
The common people could not bear it.
They wore themselves out trying to stop corruption and follow the law.
Therefore, ministers of harsh severity advanced,
and methods of showing knowledge and abolishing restrictions arose.
People like Dù Zhōu 杜周 and Xián Xuān 咸宣
were valued for settling matters with strict legalism,
and men like Wáng Wēnshū 王溫舒 became prominent through fierce attacks and killings.
Few desired to rely on benevolence and righteousness to guide their service to the ruler;
many sought to steal favor and gain acceptance.
Considering Gōngsūn Hóng 公孫弘 alone,
what can be said?"
2.5 Chapter Eleven: On Confucianism
The Imperial Secretary said:
"The Literati take Zhòngní 仲尼 as their ancestor
and praise his virtue,
claiming that from ancient times to the present,
there has never been anyone like him.
However, Kǒngzǐ 孔子 cultivated the Way between Lǔ 魯 and Wèi 衛,
teaching and transforming above the Zhū 洙 and Sì 泗 rivers.
His disciples did not change,
and his era did not achieve good governance;
the decline of the state of Lǔ 魯 only intensified.
Qí Xuānwáng 齊宣王 praised Confucianism and honored learning.
Mèng Kē 孟軻 and the like of Chún Yúkūn 淳于髡
received the salaries of high officials,
not holding office but discussing state affairs.
There were over a thousand scholars at the Jíxià 稷下 academy in Qí 齊 at that time.
At this time,
it was not just one Gōngsūn Hóng 公孫弘.
Weak Yān 燕 attacked Qí 齊,
advancing all the way to Línzī 臨淄.
Mǐnwáng 湣王 fled,
dying in Jǔ 莒 without being rescued.
Wáng Jiàn 王建 was captured by Qín 秦,
taken as a prisoner, and could not preserve his state.
If this is the case,
the Confucian scholars' ability to secure the state and honor the ruler
has never been effective."
The Literati said:
"Without a whip,
even Zàofù 造父 cannot train four horses.
Without power and position,
