even Shùn 舜 and Yǔ 禹 cannot govern the myriad people.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
'If the phoenix does not arrive,
and the river does not produce a map,
then I am finished!'
Therefore, a light carriage and fine horses
have no way to be driven;
sagely virtue, benevolence, and righteousness
have no place to be applied.
During the reigns of Qí Wēi 齊威 and Xuān 宣,
they made prominent the worthy and advanced scholars,
and the state became wealthy and powerful,
with its might extending to enemy states.
When it came to Mǐnwáng 湣王,
he roused the remaining strength of two generations,
southward seizing Chǔ 楚 and the Huái 淮 region,
northward annexing the large Sòng 宋 state,
encompassing twelve states,
westward crushing the Three Jìn 三晉 states,
repelling the strong Qín 秦,
and five states became his vassals.
The rulers of Zōu 鄒 and Lǔ 魯,
and the various lords on the Sì 泗 River, all became his subjects.
He boasted of his accomplishments without resting,
and the common people could not bear it.
The scholars advised him but he did not listen,
so they all scattered.
Shèn Dào 慎到 and Jié Zi 捷子 fled,
Tián Piān 田駢 went to Xuē 薛,
and Sūn Qīng 孫卿 went to Chǔ 楚.
With no good ministers within,
the feudal lords combined and attacked him.
Wáng Jiàn 王建 listened to rumors,
believed spies,
used Hòushèng's 后勝 schemes,
and did not maintain friendly relations with the feudal lords,
leading to the destruction of his state.
He was captured by Qín 秦.
Was this not appropriate?"
The Imperial Secretary said:
"Yī Yǐn 伊尹 served Tāng 湯 by cooking,
and Bǎilǐ 百里 sought an audience with Mùgōng 穆公 by feeding oxen.
They started by seeking temporary approval,
but were entrusted with achieving hegemony and kingship.
If this is the case,
why say that advice was not followed?
Why say that the Way was not practiced?
Therefore, Shāng Jūn 商君 tried to persuade Xiàogōng 孝公 with the Way of Kings,
but he did not use it.
Instead, he used the way to strengthen the state,
and eventually achieved success.
Zōu Zǐ 鄒子 tried to influence the rulers of the world with Confucian arts,
but he was not used.
Instead, he used theories of transformation from beginning to end,
and eventually became famous.
Therefore, a horse valued for traveling a thousand *lǐ* need not be from Hú 胡 or Dài 代;
a scholar values success,
not necessarily literary talent.
Mèng Kē 孟軻 clung to old arts
and did not understand worldly affairs,
so he was trapped in Liáng 梁 and Sòng 宋.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 could be square but not round,
so he went hungry in Líqiū 黎丘.
If modern scholars diligently practice virtue,
and sometimes face hardship and scarcity,
and their words are considered wrong,
then they cannot succeed.
Since the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
for over a thousand years,
only Wén 文, Wǔ 武, Chéng 成, and Kāng 康
can be said to have always followed advice.
To take what they cannot reach and praise it
is like a cripple who can speak of distant places but cannot travel there.
Sages take different paths but arrive at the same destination;
some advance and some stop,
but their purpose is the same.
Although Shāng Jūn 商君 reformed laws and changed teachings,
his intention was to strengthen the state and benefit the people.
The works of Zōu Zǐ 鄒子,
the arts of transformation,
also returned to benevolence and righteousness.
Jì Zhòng 祭仲 humbled himself to exercise power,
because of the circumstances.
Therefore, a small injustice for a great good
is what a gentleman does.
To stubbornly cling to one way,
invoking the intention of Wěishēng 尾生,
is to say that Jìn Wén 晉文 deceiving the feudal lords to honor the Zhōu 周 dynasty is not worth mentioning,
and that Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 enduring shame to preserve the state is not worth praising."
The Literati said:
"Yī Yǐn's 伊尹 service to Tāng 湯
was because he recognized a sagely ruler.
Bǎilǐ's 百里 return to Qín 秦
was because he recognized an enlightened ruler.
These two rulers were able to recognize a hegemon
because the criteria were clear to them;
it was not a matter of making decisions blindly in the dark.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
'If names are not correct, then words are not in accordance.
If words are not in accordance, then affairs cannot be accomplished.'
How could they seek temporary approval to achieve hegemony and kingship?
A gentleman holds virtue and adheres to righteousness in his actions,
so he will surely be like this in haste
and in distress.
Mèngzǐ 孟子 said:
'Living in today's court,
if one does not change the customs
and achieves the power of a thousand chariots,
one cannot live there for even a single morning.'
Would he rather be poor and hungry in a humble alley?
How could he change himself and follow the customs?
Hélǘ 闔閭 killed Liáo 僚,
and Gōngzǐ Zā 公子札 left and went to Yánlíng 延陵,
never entering the state of Wú 吳 again in his life.
The Duke of Lǔ 魯 killed Zǐchì 子赤,
and Shū Miǎn 叔眄 retreated and lived in seclusion,
not eating its salary.
Gaining honor by sacrificing righteousness,
or seeking acceptance by distorting the Way,
I would ☆ not do even if it meant dying.
Hearing that the correct way is not practiced,
they relinquish their positions and retire.
I have never heard of distorting the Way to seek acceptance."
The Imperial Secretary said:
"The *Lúnyǔ* 《論語》 says:
'A gentleman does not enter into a place where those close to the ruler do evil.'
There are such words, but actions do not follow.
The Jì 季 family acted without principle,
driving out their ruler,
seizing his government,
yet Rǎn Qiú 冉求 and Zhòng Yóu 仲由 served them.
The *Lǐ* 《禮》 says:
'Men and women do not give or receive directly,
nor do they exchange wine cups.'
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 went to Wèi 衛
and used the favorite minister Mí Zixia 彌子瑕 to be introduced to the wife of the ruler of Wèi 衛.
Zǐlù 子路 was displeased.
Zǐxia 彌子瑕
was a flattering minister;
the Master used him,
which was not proper.
Men and women do not interact directly,
yet Kǒngzǐ 孔子 met with Nánzi 南子,
which was against ritual propriety.
Ritual propriety originates from the Kǒng 孔 family,
yet he debased the Way to seek acceptance.
Where is the relinquishing of positions and retiring?"
The Literati said:
"If the world is not at peace,
the various states are not tranquil,
this is the worry of an enlightened king.
If there is no Son of Heaven above,
and no regional hegemon below,
the world will be in turmoil,
this is the worry of the virtuous and sages."
Therefore, Yáo 堯 worried about the great flood,
Yī Yǐn 伊尹 worried about the people,
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 was bound and shackled,
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 traveled around,
worrying about the disasters of the common people and wanting to secure them from danger.
Therefore, they carried cauldrons and chopping boards, were imprisoned, and crawled on the ground to save them.
Thus, those who pursue the fleeing run quickly,
and those who rescue the drowning get wet.
Now the people are trapped in ditches,
even if one does not want to get wet,
how can one avoid it?"
The Imperial Secretary remained silent.
2.6 Chapter 12: *Worrying About the Border*
The Grandee said:
The Worthy and Learned say:
"When the world is not at peace,
the various states are not tranquil;
this is the worry of a wise king.
Therefore, the relationship of the king to the world
is like that within a single room;
if even one person does not get what they deserve,
then it is said that there is no joy.
Therefore, to let the people drown and not rescue them
is not the mark of a benevolent ruler.
For a state to be in difficulty and not to worry
is not the mark of a loyal minister.
To uphold one's integrity and die in the face of difficulty
is the duty of a minister;
to provide food and clothing to those who are hungry and cold
is the way of a loving father.
Now that the sons and younger brothers toil far away from home,
the ruler is restless day and night because of it,
and the ministers exhaust their efforts and give their full advice,
so that the budget of the state grows.
Therefore, the Vice Director of the Lesser Treasury petitions to establish a liquor monopoly
in order to supply the border,
provide for the soldiers,
and rescue the people from hardship.
For those who are fathers and elder brothers,
how can this be stopped!
Internally examining our food and clothing to provide for those who are outside,
even that is still not enough;
now you want to abolish these measures
and reduce the expenses for supporting the border;
this cannot be described as being a loving father or a virtuous elder brother."
The Worthy and Learned said:
"At the end of the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
the Son of Heaven was weak
and the feudal lords used force to govern;
therefore the rulers of the states were uneasy,
and scheming ministers hurried about.
Why?
Because enemy states were numerous and the state was in danger.
Now that the nine provinces share one territory,
and the world is united under one rule,
Your Majesty leisurely enjoys the palace,
listens to the ministers' extreme words and ultimate arguments,
internally chants the *Odes* (*Yǎ* 雅) and *Hymns* (*Sòng* 頌),
and externally sounds the harmonious bells.
Your pure virtue shines brightly,
equaling Táng 唐 and Yú 虞,
and your meritorious achievements will flow to your descendants.
As for those Mán 蠻 and Mò 貊 peoples,
lands that produce no food,
why is there enough to trouble you,
and have the worries of the Warring States period?
If Your Majesty does not abandon them,
but adds to them with virtue,
and bestows upon them with kindness,
then the northern barbarians will surely turn inward,
come to the border and submit of their own accord,
and then use them as a restraint on the foreign ministers;
then even the Xiongnu 匈奴 will never again in their lives partake of what they are now using."
The Grandee said:
"The sage ruler is concerned about the unsettled state of the Central Kingdom
and the lack of peace on the northern border,
and has sent the former Court Counselor Píng 平 and others to ask about the sufferings of the people.
Rescuing and providing for the poor and lowly,
providing for the deficient is still not enough.
The ministers' proclamations of the Ming 明 kings' virtue
to pacify the world
have not yet grasped the essentials;
therefore, questions are put to you scholars.
The scholars' discussions do not reach to Heaven, so they sink into the depths;
they only want to govern by the means of the neighborhoods.
How much more is this true of the great affairs of the state!
It is not even close!
Coming from the fields,
emerging from poor alleys,
not knowing the cold of ice and water,
like being drunk and newly awakened,
they are utterly insufficient to discuss these matters with."
The Worthy and Learned said:
"The way to secure the people and enrich the state
lies in returning to the root;
when the root is established, the Way comes into being.
Following the principles of Heaven
and taking advantage of the benefits of the land
means that success is achieved without labor.
To not cultivate the source and instead attend to the stream,
to lack a root to govern things,
even if one exhausts one's spirit
and uses up one's thoughts,
it will not benefit governance.
To want to secure them will only make them more insecure;
to want to save them will only lead to their ruin.
The beginning of order and chaos
lies only in the root and the branch;
without exhausting one's mind, the Way can be attained.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
'Those who do not understand theory find it difficult to discuss governance;
those who do not share the same Way
do not consult with each other.'
Now the high officials have their minds set on something,
so the words of the Worthy and Learned
cannot be used."
The Grandee said:
"I have heard that those who are ministers should exhaust their loyalty to carry out their duties,
and those who are sons should exert their filial piety to continue their family's business.
If the ruler has faults,
then the ministers should cover them up.
If the father has faults,
then the sons should hide them and flee from them.
Therefore, when the ruler dies,
the ministers do not change the ruler's policies;
when the father dies,
the sons do not change the father's Way.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* (*Chūnqiū* 春秋) criticized the destruction of the spirit tower,
because it destroyed what the ancestors had done
and publicized the evils of the ruler and father.
Now salt, iron, and equal transport
have been around for a long time,
and if you want to abolish them,
wouldn't that harm the achievements of the late emperor
and obstruct the virtue of the sage ruler?
The officials rely on the path of loyalty and filial piety;
this path is different and does not agree with the plans of the Worthy and Learned."
The Worthy and Learned said:
"The wise change with the times,
and the intelligent make rules according to the era.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
'A hemp cap
is proper according to the rites.
Now it is made of pure silk,
which is simpler.
I follow the majority.'
Therefore, the sage values the worthy and does not depart from antiquity,
following customs without being biased.
Lǔ Dìnggōng 魯定公 ordered the ancestral tablets according to their order in the temple,
following the ancestors,
and Zhāo Gōng 昭公 dismissed the ministers
in order to simplify affairs and economize,
but it cannot be said that he changed what the ancestor had done
and altered the way of the father.
Èr Shì 二世 filled the Āpáng 阿房 Palace in order to continue the lineage,
and Zhào Gāo 趙高 increased the burdens of the Qín 秦 laws in order to expand his power,
but they cannot be called loyal ministers or filial sons."
3.1 Chapter 13: *Parks and Ponds*
The Grandee said:
"The feudal lords take their states as their families;
their worries are internal.
The Son of Heaven takes the eight directions as his boundary;
his concerns are external.
Therefore, those with small territories use little,
while those with great achievements use much.
Therefore, the state opens parks and ponds,
controls the mountains and seas,
and obtains profit to assist the tribute and taxes,
repairs canals,
establishes farming settlements,
expands fields and pastures,
and increases the number of parks and gardens.
The Master of Horses, the Superintendent of Parks, the Lesser Treasury, and the Grand Minister of Agriculture
annually assess the profits from fields and pastures,
the rents from the ponds and gardens,
and the placement of agricultural officials on the northern border
in order to supply the various expenses,
and yet it is still not enough.
Now you want to abolish these,
cut off their source,
block their flow,
so that both above and below are exhausted;
this is the response to difficulty and poverty.
Even if you like to simplify affairs and economize,
how can this be done?"
The Worthy and Learned said:
"In ancient times,
the land was sufficient to nourish the people,
and the people were sufficient to support their superiors.
A state with a thousand chariots
had a hundred *lǐ* 里 of land;
the dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons
each fulfilled their needs and satisfied their desires.
Qín 秦 annexed the lands of ten thousand states
and possessed the wealth of the four seas,
yet its desires were not satisfied.
This was not because the territory was small and the use was little,
but because the desires were many and the people could not bear their demands."
It is said:
"In the kitchen there is rotten meat,
in the state there are starving people,
in the stable there are fat horses,
on the road there are people dying of hunger."
Now the feeding of dogs and horses,
and the food for insects and beasts,
is surely not limited to the expense of rotten meat and fat horses!
Useless officials,
non-urgent projects,
extravagant and excessive clothing changes,
and many who receive clothing and food from the government without merit,
are the reasons why those above do not have enough and those below are impoverished.
Now, without reducing the root cause, you want to provide for the branches,
establish machinery for profit,
build fields and raise livestock,
competing with the common people for grazing land,
and competing with merchants for market profits.
This is not the way to manifest the virtue of a wise ruler and assist the state.
Husband plows and wife weaves,
this is the great enterprise of the world.
Therefore, in ancient times, land was distributed and people settled on it,
fields and acreage were regulated and people worked on them.
Thus, there was no unproductive land,
and the state had no people who did not work.
Now, the government excessively expands parks, hunting grounds, public fields, and ponds,
the state has the name of ownership,
but the benefits return to powerful families.
The Sān Fǔ (三輔) region is close to mountains and rivers,
the land is narrow and the population is large,
people from all directions gather,
and grain, rice, firewood, and vegetables
are not sufficient to support each other.
Public fields are repeatedly rented out,
mulberry and elm trees and vegetable gardens are not planted,
and the land's potential is not fully utilized.
I foolishly believe this is wrong.
The former emperor's opening of parks, hunting grounds,
and ponds
should be taxed and returned to the people,
and the government should only collect rent and taxes.
Different names for taxes, but the reality is the same.
If this were the case,
the strength of a common man
would be fully utilized in the southern fields,
and the strength of a common woman
would be fully utilized in hemp and flax.
If the fields are cultivated
and hemp and flax are processed,
then both those above and those below will be prosperous,
so how could there be poverty?"
The dàfū (大夫) remained silent,
looking at his chancellor and censor.
3.2 《Qīng Zhòng Dì Shísì (輕重第十四)》
The censor stepped forward and said:
"In the past, Tài Gōng (太公) was enfeoffed in Yíngqiū (營丘),
cleared the wilderness and settled there.
The land was poor and the population was small,
so he facilitated the ways of commerce and trade,
and maximized the skill of women's work.
Therefore, neighboring states associated with Qí (齊),
wealth and goods were accumulated,
and for generations it was a strong state.
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) served as chancellor to Duke Huán (桓公),
continued the work of his predecessors,
implemented changes in monetary policy,
pacified the powerful Chǔ (楚) in the south and became the hegemon among the feudal lords.
Now, Your Excellency follows the techniques of Tài Gōng (太公), Duke Huán (桓), and Guǎn Zhòng (管仲),
monopolizing salt and iron,
facilitating the benefits of mountains and rivers, and all things flourish.
Therefore, the government's resources are abundant,
the people are not impoverished,
both agriculture and commerce benefit,
and both those above and those below are sufficient.
This is the result of careful planning,
not solely relying on farming and sericulture."
The scholar said:
"Propriety and righteousness are
the foundation of the state,
while expediency and profit are
the ruin of governance.
Confucius said:
'If one can govern the state with propriety and yielding, what difficulty is there?'
Yǐ Yǐn (伊尹) and Tài Gōng (太公) made their lords rise from a hundred *lǐ*,
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) devoted himself to Duke Huán (桓),
but with Qí (齊), a state with a thousand chariots,
he could not reach the status of king,
because his efforts were misguided.
Therefore, his achievements and reputation were destroyed, and his way did not succeed.
At that time,
none of the feudal lords could use virtue,
and they competed for public gain,
so they used expediency to undermine each other.
Now that the world has been united as one family,
what evil desires are there to pursue commercial profit?
What evil schemes are there to implement?
Your Excellency uses cunning plans to manage the state's finances,
scheming against the feudal lords,
and involving them in the wine monopoly.
Xiányáng (咸陽) and Kǒng Jǐn (孔僅) increased salt and iron taxes,
and Jiāng Chōng (江充), Yáng Kě (楊可), and others,
each with their sharp skills,
spoke of trivial matters of commercial profit, dissecting every hair,
which can be said to be without flaw.
This is not merely Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) establishment of the Nine Offices
to control the mountains and seas.
However, the state has declined and wasted away,
and the cities and towns are empty.
Therefore, without valuing benevolence and righteousness, there is no way to transform the people, and without emphasizing agriculture, there is no way to enrich the state."
The censor said:
"When there are otters in the water, the pond fish suffer,
and when there are powerful oppressors in the state, the common people decline.
Therefore, under a dense forest there is no abundant grass,
and among large boulders there are no beautiful seedlings.
The way to govern a state
is to remove filth and eliminate the powerful,
then the common people will be equal and peaceful,
and each will live securely in his home.
Zhāng Tíngwèi (張廷尉) discusses and establishes laws and regulations,
clarifying the law to control the world,
punishing the treacherous and cunning,
and eliminating those who engage in annexation,
so that the strong do not bully the weak,
and the many do not oppress the few.
Your Excellency plans and strategizes,
establishes state finances,
controls the profits of salt and iron throughout the world,
to suppress wealthy merchants and large traders,
allowing people to buy official positions to redeem their crimes,
reducing the surplus
and supplementing the insufficient,
to equalize the common people.
Therefore, when soldiers and weapons are sent east and west for expeditions,
taxes are not increased, yet there are sufficient resources.
The matter of reducing the surplus and supplementing the insufficient
is something seen by the wise,
not something known by the common people."
The scholar said:
"Biǎn Què (扁鵲) feels the pulse and knows the cause of the illness,
when the *yáng* energy is excessive,
he reduces it to harmonize the *yīn*,
and when the cold energy is excessive,
he reduces it to harmonize the *yáng*,
so that the energy and pulse are harmonized,
and evil energy has no place to stay.
But a clumsy doctor does not know the subtleties of the pulse,
the division of blood and energy,
and recklessly punctures without benefiting the illness,
only harming the skin and flesh.
Now, wanting to reduce the surplus
and supplement the insufficient,
the rich become richer,
and the poor become poorer.
Strict laws and harsh punishments,
intended to prohibit violence and stop treachery,
but treachery still does not stop,
perhaps it is because they are not using Biǎn Què's (扁鵲) acupuncture and moxibustion,
so the people have not been able to fulfill their duties."
The censor said:
"When the Zhōu (周) dynasty established the state,
there were approximately eighteen hundred feudal lords.
Afterward,
the strong swallowed the weak,
the large annexed the small,
and they merged into the Six States.
The Six States allied and fought against each other for hundreds of years,
internally resisting enemy states,
and externally repelling the four barbarians.
From this perspective,
weapons and armor never ceased,
battles and wars were never lacking,
the military was supported externally,
and the warehouses were full internally.
Now, with the wealth of the world,
the resources within the seas,
and the tributes from hundreds of commanderies,
it is not just the accumulation of Qí (齊) and Chǔ (楚),
or the treasuries of Zhào (趙) and Wèi (魏).
Considering expenditure and measuring income,
even with urgent use,
there should be no time of shortage or exhaustion.
If the Senior Minister of Agriculture and others were to personally engage in farming with skill,
like the accomplishments of Hòu Jì (后稷),
and the army goes out in all directions but supplies are not sustained,
is it not that heaven's resources are few?
Using acupuncture and moxibustion,
harmonizing *yīn* and *yáng*,
equalizing the rich and poor,
supplementing the insufficient,
is it also not correct?
Your Excellency and the Chief Commandant of Grain manage the affairs of the Senior Minister of Agriculture,
unblocking blockages,
opening the hundred channels of profit,
so that all things flow,
and the government is wealthy and substantial."
At this time,
the four directions were engaged in suppressing violent rebellions.
The expenses for chariots and armor,
and the rewards for capturing enemies,
amounted to hundreds of millions,
all supplied by the dà Sìnóng (大司農, Grand Minister of Agriculture).
This was all due to the power of Biǎn Què (扁鵲),
and the benefits of salt and iron."
The Literary Man said:
"The border commanderies are located in mountains and valleys,
where the *yīnyáng* (陰陽) is not harmonious,
the cold freezes and cracks the earth,
violent winds blow away the salt,
and sand and stones accumulate,
making the land unsuitable for anything.
The Central States
are the center of the earth,
the intersection of *yīnyáng* (陰陽),
where the sun and moon pass through the south,
and the Dipper extends to the north,
containing harmonious qi (氣),
and producing all kinds of things.
Now, abandoning this and invading the borders,
mostly claiming barren and bitterly cold lands,
is like abandoning the banks of the Jiāng (江) and Hé (河),
and farming on mountain slopes and weedy marshes.
Transferring the reserves of the granaries,
and flying the wealth of the treasuries,
to supply the border people,
the people of the Central States are burdened with taxes and levies,
and the border people suffer from garrison duty.
Farming is inconvenient for planting grains,
there is no benefit of mulberry and hemp,
they rely on the silk floss of the Central States to clothe themselves,
and wearing fur coats,
is not even enough to cover their bodies.
In summer, they do not escape the heat,
and in winter, they do not leave their caves.
Fathers, sons, husbands, and wives hide within enclosed chambers of earth.
The interior and exterior are empty,
what power does Biǎn Què (扁鵲) have?
And what benefits are there from salt and iron?"
3.3 Section 15: "The Uninformed"
The Imperial Secretary said:
"The inner commanderies have a large population,
and the springs and grasses are plentiful,
but they cannot support each other.
The terrain is warm and humid,
unsuitable for cattle and horses;
the people tread on plows to cultivate,
and carry burdens on shoulder poles,
working hard but with little success.
Therefore, the common people are poor and miserable,
and their clothing and food are insufficient.
The old and weak carry carts on the roads,
while the high ministers and great officers
sometimes ride in ox-carts.
Xiào Wǔ (孝武) Emperor pacified the Bǎi Yuè (百越) to make gardens,
and drove back the Qiāng (羗) and Hú (胡) to make parks,
so that rare and strange objects
filled the rear palace,
and *táotú* (騊駼) and *kuaití* (駃騠) horses
filled the outer stables,
so that commoners all rode in strong carriages,
and the common people were tired of oranges and pomelos.
From this, we can see:
the benefits of the border commanderies are also abundant!
But you say, 'What benefits are there?'
You are uninformed about the calculations."
The Literary Man said:
"Yǔ (禹) regulated the waters and the land,
and established the nine provinces.
The four directions each contributed what their land produced,
enough to fill the palaces,
and satisfy the ruler's desires.
The fertile soil stretches for thousands of miles,
and the benefits of the mountains and rivers
are enough to enrich the common people,
without relying on the lands of the Mán (蠻) and Mò (貊),
or distant objects to meet our needs.
I have heard that before we attacked the Hú (胡) and Yuè (越),
the taxes and levies were light, and the people were rich and content,
warmly clothed and well-fed,
storing new grain and eating old grain,
with plenty of cloth and silk,
and herds of cattle and horses.
Farmers used horses to plow and carry,
and everyone rode horses;
at that time,
they even kicked away horses to use their dung.
Later,
when armies were frequently dispatched,
warhorses were insufficient,
and female animals entered the battle lines,
so that foals were born on the battlefield.
Livestock did not thrive at home,
and the five grains did not grow in the fields,
the people lacked even dregs and husks,
so how could they be tired of oranges and pomelos?
The *Chuán* (傳, Commentary) says:
'After a great army,
it takes generations to recover.'
Today, in the commanderies and states,
the fields have ridges but are not cultivated,
and the cities have houses but are not populated.
What abundance is there in the border commanderies?"
The Imperial Secretary said:
"In ancient times,
fields were measured with a hundred paces as a *mǔ* (畝),
and the people cultivated using the well-field system,
paying one-tenth as tax.
Putting public duty before personal gain
was the duty of the people as subjects.
The late emperor sympathized with the suffering of the people,
whose clothing and food were insufficient,
and set fields at two hundred and forty paces per *mǔ* (畝),
taxing at a rate of one-thirtieth.
If lazy people do not engage in farming,
and suffer hunger and cold,
it is only reasonable.
If they do not plow but want to sow,
and do not plant but want to harvest,
what fault is there in salt and iron?"
The Literary Man said:
"Taxing at one-tenth
is based on the people's strength.
Abundance or scarcity, good or bad,
should be shared with the people.
When the people are diligent,
the ruler should not be wealthy alone;
when the people are wealthy,
the ruler should not be diligent alone.
Therefore, it is said:
'One-tenth
is the proper middle ground for the empire.'
Although the field is taxed at one-thirtieth,
taxes are still levied based on the *qǐng* (頃) and *mǔ* (畝),
and in good years, even scattered grains are sparingly taken,
while in years of famine, the full amount is demanded.
Adding to this the poll tax and corvée labor,
the labor of one person
is equally divided.
The farmer gives all that he earns,
and may even borrow to add to it.
Therefore, the common people diligently cultivate and labor,
yet hunger and cold still befall them.
Those building a city first make the foundation thick and then seek its height,
and those nurturing the people first enrich their livelihoods and then seek their sustenance.
The *Lúnyǔ* (論語, Analects) says:
'When the people are sufficient,
with whom would the ruler be insufficient?'"
The Imperial Secretary said:
"In ancient times,
the feudal lords fought for power,
and the warring states rose up together.
Weapons and armor never rested,
and the people neglected their fields.
Although taxed at one-tenth,
they did not neglect their duties.
Now, thanks to Your Majesty's divine power,
weapons and armor have been idle for a long time,
yet the people do not all emerge from the southern fields.
Being taxed according to population and cultivated land is not enough,
so the granaries are emptied to provide for the poor and needy,
and the encroachments increase daily,
causing them to become even lazier and rely on the benefits of the government.
It is also a disease for those who govern,
as they labor to help the people;
the people still turn their backs on kindness and abandon righteousness to flee far away,
avoiding and concealing matters of public duty.
The people imitate each other, and the fields become increasingly barren,
and rents and taxes are not paid,
resisting the government.
Even if the ruler wishes to be sufficient,
with whom can he be sufficient?"
The Literary Man said:
"Trees that are frequently transplanted wither,
and insects and beasts that move their dwellings are ruined.
Therefore, 'the *dài* (代) horse leans towards the north wind,
and the flying bird soars to its old nest,'
and none do not grieve for their livelihood.
From this, we can see that
the people do not gladly avoid matters of public duty and enjoy fleeing far away.
In the past,
military campaigns frequently arose,
and expenses were insufficient,
so property was assessed and taxes were levied,
always taking from the visible wealth of the people,
and farming families were especially burdened by this labor,
so they did not all emerge from the southern fields.
For the most part, those who flee and wander
are all in large families,
and the officials fear and dread them,
and dare not strictly demand payment,
so they are harsh and urgent with the small people,
and the small people cannot bear it,
and flee far away;
the middle-class families are completely wiped out by this,
and those who flee later serve those who fled earlier;
The registering of the population began with wicked officials,
so they imitated each other.
Many went to the extreme of removing (people from the rolls), and then ameliorated it by adding a few back.
The *Zhuan* says:
“If the government is lenient, the people will die;
if the government is strict, fathers and sons will be separated.”
Therefore, fields and lands become desolate day by day,
and city walls and moats become empty.
The way to govern the people
is to remove what they dislike,
and adapt to what they are comfortable with.
If they are comfortable without being disturbed,
and employed without being burdened,
then the common people will be encouraged to work and be happy to pay public taxes.
If this is the case,
then the ruler will not need to provide relief to the people,
and the people will not seek favors from above.
Superiors and subordinates will communicate harmoniously, and songs of praise will arise.
Therefore, taking from them will not make the people resentful,
and employing them will not make the people bitter.
The poem *Língtái*
was not made because someone ordered it;
the people made it themselves.
If it is like this,
then what lack could the ruler have?"
The Yùshǐ said:
"In ancient times,
at fifteen, one entered the *tàixué*
and performed minor labor;
at twenty, one donned the cap and became an adult,
and engaged in military affairs;
above fifty,
when the blood vessels were full and the strength was firm,
one was called *ài zhuàng*.
The *Shī* says:
'Fāng Shū, the original elder,
was able to strengthen his plans.'
Therefore, the Shāng army was like *wū*,
and the Zhōu army was like *tú*.
Now, Your Majesty pities the common people,
and has relaxed the policies on labor service,
beginning taxation at twenty-three,
and exempting it at fifty-six.
This is to assist the strong and give rest to the elderly.
Those of working age cultivate their fields,
and the elderly repair their ponds and gardens,
being frugal in their efforts and diligent in their timing,
without the worries of hunger and cold.
To not manage one's household and instead sue the county government
is also perverse."
The Wénxué said:
"Those under nineteen are considered *shāng*,
not yet adults;
one dons the cap at twenty;
one marries at thirty,
and can then engage in military affairs;
those above fifty are called *ài lǎo*,
using a cane at home,
and are not subjected to labor service.
This is to support the inadequate and give rest to the aged.
In the rites of village drinking,
the elders have different dishes,
in order to favor the aged and make clear the importance of supporting the elderly.
Therefore, the elderly will not be full without meat,
will not be warm without silk,
and will not walk without a cane.
Now, those from fifty up to sixty
are made to pull carts and transport goods with their children and grandchildren,
and are given labor service in addition,
which is not the intent of supporting the elderly.
In ancient times, for those who had a major bereavement,
the ruler would not call at their door for three years,
extending their filial piety
and fulfilling their sorrowful hearts.
What the gentleman values and devotes himself to
is only the loss of his parents!
Now, some corpses are still unburied,
and people are abandoning mourning clothes to engage in military affairs,
which is not the way to treat the people as children
and accord with the heart of filial piety and brotherly love.
The Duke of Zhōu embraced King Chéng and listened to all under Heaven,
his kindness filling the seas,
his beneficence covering the four quarters;
how much more so with human faces,
embracing benevolence and preserving virtue,
none failed to obtain their proper place.
The *Shī* says:
'Early and late, lay the foundation of the mandate with care.'
Your Majesty is rich in years,
entrusting responsibilities to the great ministers,
with dukes and ministers assisting in government.
However, the policies and teachings are not yet balanced,
and therefore the common people are critical."
The Yùshǐ remained silent and did not reply.
4.1 Chapter 16: Expanding Territory
The Dàfū said:
"The king embraces and covers all,
loving universally without partiality,
not favoring those near him with heavy benefits,
nor neglecting those far away with forgotten kindness.
Now, all are the people,
all are the subjects.
Should we not adjust the fact that their safety, danger, toil, and ease are not equal?
Is it not right to regulate this?
To not think of them and only consider this,
is also fond of criticism, isn't it?
The people on the borders
live in a cold and bitter land,
facing the difficulties of the powerful Hú,
and with the movement of a single beacon,
they face the trouble of losing their lives.
Therefore, the border people fight hundreds of battles,
while the people of the central states rest peacefully,
because the border commanderies serve as a barrier.
The *Shī* says:
'Nothing is not a royal matter,
but I alone toil.'
It criticizes inequality.
Therefore, the sage kings were concerned about the unique suffering in the four directions,
raising armies to push back the Hú and Yuè,
keeping away enemies and settling disasters,
distributing the surplus wealth of the central states
to regulate the borders.
When the borders are strong,
then the central states are safe;
when the central states are safe, then there is peace and tranquility.
Why seek and not be silent?"
The Wénxué said:
"In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven stood in the center of all under Heaven,
and the area within his domain was no more than a thousand *lǐ*.
The feudal lords were ranked in their states,
and there was no land that was not subject to taxation.
The *Yǔ Gòng* reaches to five thousand *lǐ*;
the people each supplied their lord,
and the feudal lords each protected their states.
Therefore, the people were equally regulated,
and the labor service was not burdensome.
Now, the territory extends to the Hú and Yuè, thousands of *lǐ* away,
with roads winding and long,
and soldiers exhausted.
Therefore, the border people face the danger of having their throats cut,
and the people of the central states face the worry of death.
This is why the people are clamorous and not silent.
The way to govern a state
is to proceed from the center to the outside,
starting from what is near.
When those near are attached,
then the distant ones will come;
when the people within are sufficient,
then we can care for those outside.
Therefore, the officials discussed wanting to cultivate the Lúntái,
but the enlightened ruler did not permit it,
thinking that it was first necessary to relieve the urgent tasks and focus on fundamental occupations.
Therefore, he issued a decree saying:
'The task of the present is
to prohibit harshness and violence,
stop unauthorized taxation,
and strive for agriculture.'
The dukes and ministers should understand his intention,
and request to reduce and eliminate what is unbearable,
in order to assist the urgent needs of the people.
Now, we do not worry about the decline of the central states,
but focus on the borders.
Is it that the land is vast but not cultivated,
much is planted but not weeded,
wasting effort without success?
The *Shī* says:
'Do not field the wide fields,
for the weeds grow luxuriantly.'
Is it not referring to this?"
The Dàfū said:
"Tāng and Wǔ's campaigns
were not because they liked to use soldiers;
King Xuān of Zhōu expanded the state by a thousand *lǐ*,
not because he was greedy for invasion;
it was to eliminate bandits and secure the people.
Therefore, a gentleman does not undertake a fruitless army;
the sage king does not covet useless land.
The late Emperor raised the armies of Tāng and Wǔ,
settled the difficulties of the three frontiers,
controlled the enemy on one side,
and the Xiōngnú fled.
Therefore, he used the river and mountains as defenses,
abandoning the salty, alkaline, and barren lands,
thus ceding the counties of Dòubì,
abandoning the land of Zàoyáng to give to the Hú,
reducing the winding fortresses,
relying on the river's dangers,
and guarding the key points,
in order to ease the labor services
and protect the soldiers and people.
From this perspective,
the sage ruler's intentions
were not merely to expand territory and exhaust the masses."
The Literary Scholar said:
"Qín's use of military force can be said to have reached its extreme
, and Méng Tián's expansion of the territory can be said to have been far-reaching.
Now, going beyond the borders established by Méng Tián
, establishing commanderies and counties in the lands of the Xiongnu,
the territory becomes ever more distant, and the people increasingly weary.
West of Shuòfāng
, and north of Cháng'ān,
the efforts put into establishing new commanderies,
and the expenses for constructing outer walls
, are beyond calculation.
It is not only this,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú and Táng Méng opened up routes to the southwest Yi tribes,
causing Bà and Shǔ to suffer from the tribes of Qióng and Zuò;
campaigns across the sea to subdue the southern Yi,
and the garrisoning of the eastern Yuè with war ships
, exhausted Jīng and Chǔ due to the Ōu and Luò tribes.
The General of the Left attacked Cháoxiǎn
, opening up Líntún,
causing Yān and Qí to be troubled by the Huì Mò.
Zhāng Qiān traveled to distant lands,
bringing back useless things,
and the treasures of the imperial storehouses
flowed out to foreign countries;
it was not just the expenses of Dòu Bì and the
construction of Zàoyáng.
Judging from this,
it was not the ruler's careful planning,
but the excessive calculations of ministers eager to gain favor for the imperial court."
The Grandee said:
"One who possesses the wisdom of Guǎn Zhòng
should not be employed as a mere servant.
One who possesses the foresight of Táo Zhūgōng
would not remain in poverty-stricken places.
The Literary Scholar can speak but cannot act,
criticizes those above while being in a lower position,
dislikes wealth while living in poverty,
speaks grandly but is not followed,
makes loud pronouncements but acts in a base manner,
engages in slander, praise, and criticism,
in order to gain fame and acquire a reputation for goodness in the present age.
One whose salary is no more than what can be held in the hand
is not fit to speak of governance,
and one whose household wealth is not enough to fill a roof
is not fit to discuss important matters.
Scholars are all poor and weak,
and their clothes and hats are incomplete,
how can they know about the affairs of the state
and the matters of the imperial court?
What do they know of Dòu Bì and the construction of Zàoyáng!"
The Literary Scholar said:
"Low social status does not hinder wisdom,
and poverty does not prevent good conduct.
Yán Yuān was often empty-handed
but was not considered unworthy.
Kǒngzǐ was not accepted
but was not considered unholy.
If people must be judged by their appearance
and scholars advanced by their talents,
then Tài Gōng would have spent his whole life wielding a butcher's knife
and Níng Qī would never have left his job of feeding cattle.
The ancient gentlemen
upheld the Way to establish their name,
cultivated themselves to await the right time,
did not change their principles due to poverty,
and did not alter their ambitions due to low status,
adhering only to benevolence
and practicing only righteousness.
To hastily seek gain when facing wealth,
to turn against righteousness when seeing profit,
to become wealthy through unrighteous means,
and to become noble without merit
are things that the benevolent do not do.
Therefore, Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Zǐqiān
would not exchange their benevolence for the wealth of Jìn and Chǔ.
Bó Yí would not exchange his conduct for the position of a feudal lord.
This is why Qí Jǐnggōng, although he had a thousand teams of horses,
could not compete with them for fame.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'How virtuous is Huí!
A single basket of food,
a single gourd of water,
living in a poor alley,
others cannot bear such hardship,
but Huí does not change his joy.'
Therefore, only the benevolent can find joy in living frugally
and endure poverty. Petty people become tyrannical when rich
and excessive when poor.
Yáng Zǐ said:
'Being benevolent does not bring wealth,
and being wealthy does not bring benevolence.'
If one puts profit before righteousness,
one will never be satisfied with taking and seizing.
Ministers accumulate hundreds of millions,
Grandees accumulate thousands of gold,
and scholars accumulate hundreds of gold,
selfishly gathering wealth to amass it;
while the common people suffer from cold and hardship,
wandering homelessly on the roads,
how can scholars alone maintain their proper attire?"
4.2 《Poverty and Wealth, Chapter Seventeen》
The Grandee said:
"Since I bound my hair in ritual fashion at the age of thirteen
, I was fortunate enough to serve as a palace guard,
attending to matters at the emperor's side
, eventually rising to the position of Grandee.
I have received salaries and rewards
for more than sixty years.
I carefully managed expenses for carriages, horses, clothing,
the cost of my wife, children, and servants,
living frugally within my means.
I have carefully planned my salaries and rewards,
calculating one or two steps ahead,
gradually accumulating wealth and establishing my enterprise.
Therefore, if land is divided equally,
the wise can preserve it;
if wealth is divided equally,
the intelligent can manage it.
The gains and losses of Bái Guī,
and Zǐ Gòng's three instances of accumulating a thousand gold,
did they necessarily rely on exploiting the people?
They managed things within a few inches,
turning things around by adjusting to small gains and losses,
profiting from the fluctuations of prices!"
The Literary Scholar said:
"In ancient times,
one's career and business were kept separate,
and profit and position were not combined.
Only then could different occupations not be too far apart
and the gap between rich and poor not be too wide.
Those who use their rank and salary to act modestly
are too numerous to mention;
those who use their power and influence to seek profit
earn immeasurable income.
Those who live off lakes and ponds
and control mountains and seas
leave gleaners with no place to compete for resources,
and merchants with no opportunity to contend for profit.
Zǐ Gòng achieved it as a commoner
, and Kǒngzǐ criticized him for it,
how much more so should one criticize those who seek it through power and position?
Therefore, in ancient times, Grandees thought about their benevolence and righteousness to fulfill their positions,
not about using their power and advantage to enrich themselves."
The Grandee said:
"If mountains have abundance,
then the people are well-provided for.
If rivers and seas have moisture,
then the people have enough to take.
A small puddle
cannot irrigate a large marsh,
and trees on small hills
cannot build palaces.
The small cannot contain the large,
and the few cannot provide for the many.
There has never been someone who could not provide for themselves but could provide for others.
There has never been someone who could not govern themselves but could govern others.
Therefore, one who is good at benefiting others
is one who is good at benefiting themselves;
one who is good at governing others
is one who is good at governing themselves.
If the Literary Scholar cannot manage his own household,
how can he manage external affairs?"
The Literary Scholar said:
"One who travels a long distance relies on a carriage,
and one who crosses rivers and seas relies on a boat.
Therefore, the establishment of merit and fame by virtuous scholars
depends on leveraging resources and borrowing from external means.
Gōngshū Bān could use the ruler's timber
to build palaces and terraces
, but could not build a simple hut for himself
, because he lacked the necessary materials.
Ōuyě Zǐ could use the ruler's bronze and iron
to make large bells and tripods
, but could not make pots, tripods, plates, and basins for himself
, because he lacked the necessary use.
A gentleman can use the ruler's proper court
to harmonize the people
and benefit the masses
, but cannot enrich his own family
, because the circumstances are not suitable.
Therefore, when Shùn farmed at Mount Lì,
his favor did not extend beyond the village;
when Tài Gōng butchered cows at Zhāogē,
his benefit did not reach his wife and children.
But when they were employed,
their favor flowed to the eight regions
and their virtue overflowed the four seas.
Therefore, Shùn was indebted to Yáo,
and Tài Gōng relied on Zhōu.
A gentleman can cultivate himself to take advantage of the Way,
but cannot pervert the Way to take advantage of wealth."
Grandee said:
"The Dao is suspended in Heaven,
things are spread out on Earth,
the wise expand with it,
the foolish are trapped by it.
Zǐ Gòng 子貢 distinguished himself among the feudal lords by his evident accumulation of wealth,
Táo Zhūgōng 陶朱公 was honored in his time by dealing in goods.
The rich associated with him,
the poor were helped by him.
Therefore, from the ruler of men
down to the commoners,
none did not bear his virtue
and praise his benevolence.
Yuán Xiàn 原憲 and Kǒng Jí 孔伋
suffered from hunger and cold in their time,
Yán Huí 顏回 was often impoverished in poor alleys.
At such times,
constrained in caves,
confined in hemp robes,
even if they wanted to use wealth to gain the trust of treacherous people,
they could not."
The Scholar said:
"Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
'If wealth can be obtained by seeking it,
even the job of holding a whip,
I would do it;
if it cannot be obtained by seeking it,
I will follow what I love.'
A *jūnzǐ* 君子 seeks righteousness,
not wealth for its own sake.
Therefore, he criticized Zǐ Gòng 子貢 for not accepting his fate and engaging in trade.
A *jūnzǐ* 君子 becomes wealthy and noble when he meets the right time,
if not,
he retreats and enjoys the Dao.
He does not let profit burden himself.
Therefore, he does not violate righteousness to take things recklessly.
He lives in seclusion and cultivates his integrity,
not wanting to hinder his conduct,
so he does not ruin his reputation to pursue power.
Even if he were given the estates of the Hán 韓 and Wèi 魏 families,
if it is not his ambition,
then he would not accept it.
Wealth and nobility cannot glorify him,
slander and defamation cannot harm him.
Therefore, Yuán Xiàn's 原憲 hemp robe
is superior to the fox furs of Jìsūn 季孫,
Zhào Xuānmèng's 趙宣孟 fish meals
are sweeter than the livestock of Zhì Bó 智伯,
Zǐ Sī's 子思 silver pendant
is more beautiful than the *chuíjí* 垂棘 jade of Lord Yú 虞.
Wèi Wénhóu 魏文侯 bowed to the lane of Dùan Gānmù 段干木,
not because he had power;
Jìn Wéngōng 晉文公 got out of his carriage and hurried to meet Hán Qìng 韓慶,
not because he had much wealth,
but because he was rich in benevolence
and full of virtue.
Therefore, why must nobility be wealth?
It is simply benevolence and righteousness!"
4.3 《Dǐ Huì Xué Dì Shíbā》毀學第十八 (Refuting Learning, Section Eighteen)
Grandee said:
"To harbor wrong and speak of right,
to pretend to be without desires but not really follow them,
is this not the true nature of a *shì* 士?
Formerly, Lǐ Sī 李斯 and Bāo Qiūzi 包丘子 both served Xún Qīng 荀卿.
Later, Lǐ Sī 李斯 entered Qín 秦,
and eventually took the Three Ducal Ministers’ positions,
holding the power of ten thousand chariots to control the realm,
his accomplishments were comparable to Yī Yǐn 伊尹 and Lǚ Wàng 呂望,
his name was as great as Mount Tài 泰山;
but Bāo Qiūzi 包丘子 could not escape living in a humble house with a small window,
like a frog in a year of floods,
his mouth was not lacking words,
but he eventually died in a ditch.
Now, if you have nothing to nourish yourself inwardly,
and nothing to commend yourself outwardly,
being poor and lowly yet loving righteousness,
even if you speak of benevolence and righteousness,
it is not worth praising!"
The Scholar said:
"When Lǐ Sī 李斯 was the prime minister of Qín 秦,
Shǐ Huáng 始皇 trusted him,
and no other ministers could compare,
yet Xún Qīng 荀卿 refused to eat because of it,
anticipating his impending disaster.
Bāo Qiūzi 包丘子 ate hemp and goosefoot,
cultivating the Dao under a humble roof,
rejoicing in his aspirations,
and finding contentment in it, rather than in grand mansions and livestock.
He had no prominent power,
nor did he have anxious worries.
The *chuíjí* 垂棘 jade of Duke Xiàn of Jìn 晉獻,
was not lacking in beauty,
but Gōng Zhīqí 宮之奇 sighed when he saw it,
knowing that Xún Xī 荀息 was plotting with it.
Zhì Bó 智伯 was wealthy and possessed the three Jìn 晉 states,
he was not lacking in splendor,
but he did not know that Xiàngzi 襄子 was plotting against him.
The fox furs of Jìsūn 季孫
were not lacking in beauty,
but he did not know that the Lord of Lǔ 魯 was troubled by them.
Therefore, Duke Xiàn of Jìn 晉獻 used treasure horses to entice Yú 虞 and Guó 虢,
Xiàngzi 襄子 used ruined cities to lure Zhì Bó 智伯.
Thus, Zhì Bó 智伯 was captured alive by Zhào 趙,
and Yú 虞 and Guó 虢 were eventually annexed by Jìn 晉,
because they were focused on obtaining benefits without considering the consequences,
being greedy for land and coveting treasure horses.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
'A man who does not think far ahead
will surely have troubles near at hand.'
Those in positions of power today,
see profit but do not anticipate harm,
are greedy for gain without considering shame,
trading their lives for profit,
and exchanging their deaths for wealth.
Lacking the virtue of benevolence and righteousness,
yet having the emoluments of wealth and nobility,
is like stepping into a pit,
eating under a hanging gate,
this is why Lǐ Sī 李斯 was subjected to the five punishments.
In the south there is a bird called *yuānchú* 鵷鶵,
it does not eat anything but bamboo seeds,
and does not drink anything but sweet spring water.
Flying over Mount Tài 泰山,
the owl of Mount Tài 泰山,
bowing its head to peck at rotten rats,
looks up and sees the *yuānchú* 鵷雛 and screeches at it.
Now, if high officials laugh at scholars because of their wealth and nobility, considering it a normal practice,
wouldn't that be like the owl of Mount Tài 泰山 screeching at the *yuānchú* 鵷鶵?"
Grandee said:
"Learning is for guarding against frivolous speech,
rites are for adorning vulgar behavior.
Therefore, learning assists virtue,
and rites embellish substance.
Speech should be thoughtful and reasonable,
and actions should be thoughtful and pleasing.
Evil words should not come out of the mouth,
and evil deeds should not reach oneself.
Actions should conform to rites,
and composure should be in accordance with the Dao.
Therefore, rites are used to practice them,
and humility is used to express them.
Thus, speaking all day long,
one will have no verbal faults;
acting throughout one's life,
one will have no grievances.
Now, people advocate establishing officials in court to govern the people,
and distributing ranks and emoluments to reward the worthy,
yet you say 'hanging gate' and 'rotten rats,'
how can such vulgar and contradictory words be in accordance with what is heard?"
The Scholar said:
"Sage rulers establish officials to assign responsibilities,
and those who are capable take the positions;
they distribute emoluments to employ the worthy,
and those who are capable receive them.
Righteousness values having none too high,
and righteousness takes none too many.
Therefore, Shùn 舜 received the realm of Yáo 堯,
and Tài Gōng 太公 did not avoid being one of the Three Dukes of Zhōu 周;
if it is not the right person,
even a bamboo basket of food and a bean soup are still a burden on the people.
Therefore, if virtue is thin but the position is high,
and strength is little but the responsibility is heavy,
few escape disaster.
The owl of Mount Tài 泰山 pecking at rotten rats in a remote marsh and secluded valley
is not harmful to anyone.
The officials of today,
steal the ruler's wealth and consume it near the prisons and laws,
not knowing that the crisis is about to erupt,
and still use it to intimidate people,
how can their harm be like that of the owl of Mount Tài 泰山?"
Grandee said:
"Sīmǎ Zǐ 司馬子 said:
'The world is bustling,
everyone goes for profit.'
The women of Zhào 趙 do not choose between ugly and handsome men,
the old women of Zhèng 鄭 do not choose between near and far places,
merchants are not ashamed of disgrace,
soldiers do not hesitate to use deadly force,
the *shì* 士 do not insist on kinship,
serving the ruler without avoiding difficulties,
all is for profit and emolument.
The Ru 儒 and Mò 墨, inwardly greedy but outwardly pretentious,
travel back and forth to persuade others,
are also restless and have not yet achieved anything.
Therefore, honor and glory are the desire of the *shì* 士,
wealth and nobility are the expectation of the *shì* 士.
When Lǐ Sī 李斯 was at the gate of Xún Qīng 荀卿,
he was on par with mediocre people,
but when he spread his wings and soared high,
like a dragon ascending and a fine horse galloping,
surpassing nine generations and doubling that,
soaring ten thousand *rèn* 仞 high,
even swans and beautiful steeds would be his companions,
how much more so the lame sheep and sparrows!"
Occupying the power of the world,
governing the masses within the universe,
with a hundred carriages following behind,
and enjoying ten thousand *zhōng* of salary.
Yet the confined Confucian scholars with their incomplete coarse clothes,
not getting enough even of bran and dregs,
not preferring beans and greens while slighting large houses,
are also unable to help themselves.
Even if they want to frighten people,
how could they stop themselves!"
The Literary Man said:
"The *jūnzǐ* cherishes virtue,
the petty person cherishes land.
The worthy man pursues fame,
the greedy man dies for profit.
*Lǐ Sī* 李斯, greedy for what he desired,
brought about what he hated.
*Sūn Shū'áo* 孫叔敖 saw things early before they sprouted,
and did not regret resigning from his position as chancellor three times,
not because he enjoyed being humble and despised great emoluments,
but because he worried about trouble from afar and cautiously avoided harm.
The ox for the suburban sacrifice,
nourished and fed for a full year,
clothed in embroidered garments,
to be brought into the ancestral temple,
the Grand Chef holding his bell-adorned knife
to open its hide;
at such a time,
wishing to take on heavy responsibilities and climb steep slopes,
it is impossible.
*Shāng Yāng* 商鞅 trapped in *Péngchí*,
*Wú Qǐ's* 吳起 corpse lying prostrate,
wishing to wear coarse clothes and live in a poor, remote, thatched hut,
it is impossible.
*Lǐ Sī* 李斯, as Chancellor of *Qín* 秦,
occupied the power of the world,
and considered the myriad chariots as trivial;
but when he was imprisoned in jail,
and dismembered by chariots in the market of *Yúnyáng*,
he also wished to carry firewood and enter the east gate,
walking the winding paths of *Shàngcài*,
it was impossible.
*Sū Qín* 蘇秦 and *Wú Qǐ* 吳起 killed themselves with power and influence,
*Shāng Yāng* 商鞅 and *Lǐ Sī* 李斯 destroyed themselves with respect and importance,
all of them greedily sought emoluments and admired glory, thereby losing their lives.
The hundred chariots following behind
were not even enough to carry their misfortune!"
4.4 Chapter 19: Praising the Worthy
The Grandee said:
"*Bó Yí* 伯夷 starved because of his integrity,
*Wěi Shēng* 尾生 died because of his trustworthiness.
They impaired the greater good because of small matters,
which is the trustworthiness of common men and women.
They are drowned in ditches and nobody knows about it.
What meritorious fame do they have?
*Sū Qín* 蘇秦 and *Zhāng Yí* 張儀,
their wisdom was enough to strengthen states,
their courage was enough to awe enemies,
one outburst and the feudal lords were afraid,
peaceful dwelling and the world rested.
The lords of ten thousand chariots
all humbled themselves, used humble words,
and requested alliance with heavy gifts.
These are what are called famous scholars of the world.
If wisdom is not enough to make plans,
and power cannot uplift the present age,
the people consider that inferior.
Nowadays, they hold up vanishing as existing,
emptiness as fullness,
commoners wearing shoes,
thinking deeply and walking slowly,
as if something were lost,
they are not men who establish merit and achieve fame,
but are also unable to avoid being common."
The Literary Man said:
"*Sū Qín* 蘇秦 became prominent in *Zhào* 趙 through alliance,
*Zhāng Yí* 張儀 was entrusted in *Qín* 秦 through vertical alliance.
At that time,
they were not not honored and noble,
but wise men followed them with worry,
knowing that those who do not advance through the Way will certainly not retreat through the Way;
those who do not gain through righteousness will certainly not lose through righteousness.
The power of the *Jì* 季 family and *Mèng* 孟 family,
the wealth of the Three *Huán* 桓,
could not be matched,
yet *Kǒngzǐ* 孔子 said of them, "How diminished!".
Being a minister,
if one's power equals the ruler's,
and one's wealth matches the state's,
one will perish.
Therefore, the higher the position, the heavier the crime,
the thicker the emolument, the more the crimes.
One who acts first perfects himself and then seeks fame;
one who serves first avoids harm and then seeks emolument.
Therefore, the fragrant bait is not not delicious,
but turtles and dragons hear of it and hide deep,
and phoenixes see it and fly high,
knowing that it harms their bodies.
Being crows, magpies, fish, and turtles,
they wildly fly and run after eating the fragrant bait,
lowering their heads and bending their necks,
which is of no benefit in death.
Now, the officers steal and wield the laws of the state,
advancing without regard for their crimes.
Suddenly there is an emergency,
and then carriages rush and people run,
which is of no benefit in death.
What they stole is not enough to repay the servants,
their wives and children flee and have nowhere to go,
their bodies are in deep prisons,
and nobody knows to take care of them.
At such a time,
how can they have time to laugh?"
The Grandee said:
"The Literary Man's high conduct
is upright and seems impossible to bend;
his abundant integrity and pure words
are bright and seem impossible to sully.
Yet the garrison soldier *Chén Shèng* 陳勝 abandoned his cart,
and took the lead in rebellion,
establishing himself as *Zhāng Chǔ* 張楚.
He originally did not have the conduct of the recluse *Huí* 回 or *Yóu* 由,
or the position of the chancellor and listed ministers.
Rising up in the great swamp,
it was no more than ten months,
and the Confucian and *Mò* 墨 scholars and gentlemen of *Qí* 齊 and *Lǔ* 魯,
displayed their long robes,
long robes being ceremonial robes. Carrying the ritual vessels, the *Shī* 詩 (Classic of Poetry), and the *Shū* 書 (Classic of Documents) of the *Kǒng* 孔 clan,
they entrusted themselves as ministers.
*Kǒng Jiǎ* 孔甲 became a lecturing academician,
and in the end all died in *Chén* 陳,
becoming a great laughingstock for the world.
Is deeply hiding and flying high really like this?"
The Literary Man said:
"The *Zhōu* 周 Dynasty declined,
ritual and righteousness were ruined,
unable to govern,
the feudal lords of the world fought each other,
destroying each other,
merging into six states,
with weapons and armor not ceasing,
and the people not able to rest in peace.
*Qín* 秦, with the heart of a tiger and wolf,
nibbled away at the feudal lords,
merging and swallowing the warring states into commanderies and counties,
attacking and boasting of its achievements,
considering itself superior to *Yáo* 堯 and *Shùn* 舜 and ashamed to be in the same league with them.
It abandoned benevolence and righteousness and valued punishments,
thinking that the present age should not model itself on culture but decide through military force.
*Zhào Gāo* 趙高 managed the prisons within,
*Méng Tián* 蒙恬 used troops without,
the common people were distressed and bitter,
and unanimously hated *Qín* 秦.
King *Chén* 陳 fiercely bared his claws and teeth to be the first to take action in the world.
Although the path was dangerous, the Confucian and *Mò* scholars assisted him,
thinking that there had been no king for a long time,
and the Way was blocked and could not be practiced.
From *Kǒngzǐ* 孔子 to this day,
*Qín* 秦 again heavily prohibited it,
hence they vented their anger with King *Chén* 陳.
*Kǒngzǐ* 孔子 said:
"If there were one who would employ me,
I would create an eastern *Zhōu* 周!"
Hoping to achieve the accomplishments of *Chéng Tāng* 成湯, *Wén* 文, and *Wǔ* 武,
and eliminate the cruel and remove the bandits for the common people,
how could they be greedily seeking emolument and enjoying position?"
The Grandee said:
"Although the Literary Man's words and actions have the integrity of *Bó Yí* 伯夷,
they do not have the constancy of *Liǔxià Huì* 柳下惠,
but are no more than looking down from a high place,
with pure words and sullied actions,
delaying in yielding the cup of wine and the dish of meat,
feigning deference,
relinquishing the small to take the big,
like a chicken's integrity with a wolf's greed.
*Zhào Wǎn* 趙綰 and *Wáng Zāng* 王臧 and the like
were promoted to high ministers through Confucian arts,
but had treacherous, greedy, and cruel hearts.
*Zhǔfù Yǎn* 主父偃 obtained high office through his glib tongue,
and stole weighty power,
deceiving the imperial clan,
receiving bribes from the feudal lords,
and in the end were all executed.
*Dōngfāng Shuò* 東方朔 called himself eloquent and resourceful,
melting the hard and releasing the solid,
unmatched in his time;
yet examining his private conduct,
even a madman would not bear to do it.
Moreover, lacking *Dōngfāng Shuò's* 東方朔 tongue,
the rest is nothing worth looking at?"
The Literary Man said:
"One with good intentions forgets the bad,
one careful in small matters achieves the great.
Rituals can be observed between the sacrificial vessels,
and conduct can be discussed within the inner chambers.
To wear the clothes of the ancients,
and recite the Way of the ancients,
and abandon this to do what is wrong
is rare.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* speaks when the time is right,
takes only what is just,
and does not dwell in what is not obtained through proper means.
Being full but not overflowing,
prosperous but not arrogant.
Thus, Yuán Āng was intimate with Emperor Jǐng,
but his horses never exceeded one team of four;
Gōngsūn Hóng reached the position of one of the Three Dukes,
but his household never exceeded ten chariots;
Dōngfāng Xiānshēng's words were listened to and his actions followed by Emperor Wǔ,
yet he was not arrogant or excessive;
Zhǔfù saw the days of hardship were long ago,
and resented that those in positions of power did not love the Way but were rich and noble,
and no one knew to care for scholars.
Therefore, he took the leftovers from abundance to relieve the urgent needs of poor scholars,
not for the sake of personal gain.
The world is noisy,
not worried about the petty frugality of scholars,
but worried about the ravenous gluttony of those in power,
who leave nothing behind in their search for profit."
5.1 《Xiāng Cì Dì Èrshí》 (Chapter 20: Mutual Criticism)
The Grandee said:
"In ancient times,
they managed the *jǐngtián* system,
and regulated market districts.
Men cultivated their fields,
and women worked with hemp and ramie.
There was no uncultivated land,
and no idle people.
Therefore, those who were not merchants or artisans could not eat from petty profits,
those who were not good farmers could not eat from harvests,
and those who were not in government could not eat from official rank.
Now, scholars abandon plows and hoes to learn impractical words,
wasting time day after day,
without benefiting governance.
They wander around idly,
eating without cultivating,
and dressing without weaving.
They cleverly deceive the good people,
taking away from farmers and hindering governance.
This is also what the world worries about."
The Literary Man said:
"*Yǔ* grieved over the floods,
personally undertaking the labor,
traveling by foot and sleeping on the road,
passing by his own door without entering.
At that time,
he dropped his hairpin without picking it up,
and his hat fell off without him noticing.
Did he have time to farm?
Confucius said:
'Poets resent not being able to remain silent;
I, Qiū, resent not being able to be still.'
Therefore, he presented seventy different theories in all directions without being adopted,
then he withdrew and cultivated the Way of Kings,
composing the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
leaving it for ten thousand generations to come.
The world finds its standard therein.
How can this be the same as common men and women farming and weaving?
The *Zhuàn* (Commentary) says:
'If the *jūnzǐ* does not act at the proper time,
the people will have nothing to watch and emulate.'
Therefore, without the *jūnzǐ*, the common people cannot be governed,
and without the common people, the *jūnzǐ* cannot be supported.
It is not proper for the *jūnzǐ* to only farm and weave like common men and women.
If the *jūnzǐ* farms but does not learn,
this is the way to chaos."
The Grandee said:
"The Literary Man's words about governance esteem Táng and
Yú, and his words about righteousness are higher than the heavens.
There are flowery words,
but I have not seen their substance.
In the past, during the time of Duke Mù of Lǔ,
Gōngyí was the prime minister,
Zǐsī
and Zǐliǔ were his ministers.
Yet, in the north, they were weakened by Qí,
with the Sì River as the border;
in the south, they feared the people of Chǔ;
in the west, they treated the state of Qín as a guest.
Mèng Kē resided in Liáng,
but their army was defeated by Qí,
the supreme general died, and the heir apparent was captured;
in the west, they were defeated by Qín,
their land was seized and their borders were chipped away,
losing Hénèi
and Héwài.
The disciples of Zhòngní,
the followers of the seventy disciples,
leaving their parents,
abandoning their homes,
carrying their burdens and following Confucius,
learning without farming,
only increased the chaos.
Therefore, having jade dust fill a chest
does not mean one possesses treasure;
reciting poetry and carrying books
does not mean one possesses the Way.
What matters is to secure the state
and benefit the people,
not merely to engage in elaborate rhetoric and numerous words."
The Literary Man said:
"Yú did not use Bǎilǐ Xī's plans and was destroyed,
while Duke Mù of Qín used them to achieve hegemony.
If one does not use the worthy, he will perish.
How can one avoid being weakened?
Mèngzǐ went to Liáng,
and King Huì asked about profit,
but he answered with benevolence and righteousness.
Their inclinations did not align,
so he was not used and left,
holding his treasure but without speaking.
Therefore, having grain but not eating does not alleviate hunger;
seeing the worthy but not using them does not prevent weakening.
During the time of Zhòu,
internally there were the two sons Wēi
and Jī,
and externally there were Jiāo Gé
and Jí Zǐ,
yet he could not survive.
If one speaks but is not used,
and advises but is not listened to,
even if one is worthy,
how can he benefit governance?"
The Grandee said:
"Oranges and pomelos grow in Jiāngnán,
and the people all find them sweet to the taste;
the taste is the same.
Beautiful music originates in Zhèng
and Wèi, and people all enjoy it in their ears;
the sound is the same.
The Yùe person Zǐ Zāng
and the Róng person Yóu Yú
needed interpreters to communicate,
but both became prominent in Qí
and Qín.
People's hearts are the same when it comes to good and evil.
Therefore, Zēngzǐ leaned against a mountain and chanted,
and mountain birds descended and soared;
Shī Kuàng played the zither,
and all the beasts danced.
There has never been good that does not resonate,
or sincerity that does not receive a response.
Is it that your intentions are not sincere?
Why is it that when you speak, you are not followed,
and when you act, you do not align?"
The Literary Man said:
"Biǎn Què cannot cure a disease that does not accept acupuncture and medicine,
and sages cannot correct a ruler who does not accept admonishment.
Therefore, Jié had Guān Lóngféng and Xià perished,
Zhòu had the Three Worthies and Shāng was destroyed.
Thus, the worry is not the lack of Yóu Yú's
and Zǐ Zāng's arguments,
but the lack of Duke Huán's
and Duke Mù's listening.
That is why Confucius had nowhere suitable to go in the east or west,
and Qū Yuán was exiled in the state of Chǔ.
Therefore, it is said:
'Serving a ruler with integrity,
where can one go without being dismissed three times?
Serving a ruler with dishonesty,
why necessarily leave one's parents' state?'
Ultimately, it is not because of this that your words are not followed,
and your actions do not align."
The Grandee said:
"A singer does not aim for sharp sounds,
but values being in tune;
a speaker does not aim for beautiful words,
but focuses on facts.
Being good at sound but not knowing how to modulate
cannot be considered a skilled singer;
being good at words but not knowing how to adapt
cannot be considered a skilled speaker.
Holding a compass but not a square,
holding a level but not a plumb line,
understanding one aspect,
knowing one principle,
but not understanding how to weigh and measure,
using what one does not see to distrust others,
like a cicada not knowing snow,
firmly adhering to ancient texts to respond to the current world,
is like the positions of the stars Chén and Shēn being reversed,
gluing the bridge to tune a zither—
rigid and difficult to reconcile.
That is why Confucius was not used by the world,
and Mèng Kē was despised by the feudal lords."
The Literary Scholar said:
"The light of the sun and moon,
the blind cannot see;
the sound of thunder and lightning,
the deaf cannot hear.
To speak to one who does not understand music,
is like talking to the mute and deaf.
Why single out the cicada for not knowing about heavy snow?
Even with the wisdom of Yī Yǐn
and the virtue of Tài Gōng,
they could not persuade Jié
and Zhòu. It's not that the persuaders were wrong,
but the listeners were at fault.
Therefore, Biān Hé wept blood while holding his uncut jade,
saying:
'Where can I find a skilled craftsman to cut it open!'
Qū Yuán walked and chanted by the marsh,
saying:
'Where can I find Gāo Yáo to discern me!'
The lords of men all desire to seek out the worthy to assist them,
and appoint the capable to govern the state.
Yet, they are swayed by popular opinion,
and deluded by flattering words.
Thus, the worthy and sage are obscured,
while the slanderous and sycophantic are employed.
Because of this, states are destroyed and families ruined,
and worthy men starve in caves.
In the past, Zhào Gāo had no extraordinary ambitions,
yet he occupied a position above ten thousand people.
Thus, he overturned the Qín state and brought disaster to his clan.
They lost all their *sè* zithers;
what tuning with a fixed bridge could there be?"
The Grandee said:
"Those so-called high-ranking literary scholars
possess the wisdom and strategic ability to understand the methods of the former kings,
and the talent to put their principles into practice.
Therefore, when at home, they are teachers;
when employed, they are models for the world.
Now, the literary scholars speak of Yáo
and Shùn when discussing governance, and speak of Kǒng
and Mò when discussing the practice of virtue.
But when given political office, they fail to achieve anything. They cherish ancient ways but cannot implement them.
Their words are upright, but their actions are crooked;
what they deem right is not what they feel.
Their clothing and hats distinguish them from the common folk,
but in reality, they are no different from ordinary people.
Those so-called upright scholars
meet with fortune and enjoy luck,
merely filling a position by chance.
They are probably not those clearly chosen for their abilities,
so they definitely cannot be discussed with about matters of governance."
The Literary Scholar said:
"Heaven established the three luminaries to shine and record,
the Son of Heaven establishes dukes and ministers to clarify governance.
Therefore, it is said:
Dukes and ministers
are the exemplary models for the whole world,
the divine transformations depicted in paintings.
Above, they have the responsibility to assist an enlightened ruler;
below, they have the task of carrying out the sagely transformations.
They harmonize *yīn* and *yáng*,
regulate the four seasons,
bring peace to the masses,
nurture all living things,
making the people harmonious and friendly,
with no expressions of resentment or complaint.
The four barbarians submit to virtue,
with no worries of rebellion or treachery.
This is the duty of dukes and ministers,
and the task of the worthy.
If Ī Yǐn,
and the Dukes of Zhōu and Shào, had the talent of the three highest ministers,
and Tài Diān
and Hóng Yāo the abilities of the nine ministers,
then the literary scholars would not be unworthy of the sage ruler's clear selection.
Today's officials
cannot be called possessors of flourishing virtue."
The Grandee was displeased
and changed color, not responding.
The Literary Scholar said:
"A court without loyal ministers indicates a dark government;
a grandee without upright officials indicates a precarious position.
Rèn Zuò spoke directly about the ruler's faults,
and Marquis Wén changed his words and actions,
and was called a wise ruler.
Yuán Àng openly criticized the arrogance of Marquis Jiàng,
and ultimately received blessings.
Therefore, those who risk death to point out the ruler's faults
are loyal ministers;
those who offend strict countenances to correct the errors of dukes and ministers
are upright officials.
I, a humble person, cannot speak differently in private than in public.
The present decrees regarding encouraging grain contributions
are proclaimed but not implemented;
many who receive stipends are unworthy of them,
hindering farmers, merchants, and artisans,
and the benefits of the marketplace
have not returned to the people.
The people's hopes are not fulfilled.
Moreover, the ways of emperors and kings
are often neglected and not repaired.
The *Shī* says:
'Abundant are the officers.'
It is intended to truly appoint and employ their plans,
not merely put on a display of empty words."
5.2 《Shū Lù Dì Èr Shí Yī》
The Grandee said:
"The seventy disciples personally received the teachings of the sage,
their names listed at the gate of Kǒngzǐ,
all were men of the ability of princes and ministers,
several could sit facing south as rulers.
Those skilled in governance were Rǎn Yǒu
and Jì Lù;
those skilled in speech were Zǎi Wǒ
and Zǐ Gòng.
Zǎi Wǒ held office
and was favored in Qí.
Tián Cháng created trouble,
his way could not be practiced.
He died in the courtyard,
and Duke Jiǎn was killed at the Tán Terrace.
Zǐ Lù served in Wèi.
Kǒng Kuī rebelled.
He could not save his lord from fleeing into exile
and was minced in Wèi;
Zǐ Gòng
and Zǐ Gāo escaped and fled,
unable to die in that calamity.
They ate the heavy stipends of others but could not change the situation;
they occupied the honorable positions of others but could not preserve them.
How self-serving, and how indifferent to their lord!
Sharing the same gate and studying the same profession,
they thought they understood the meaning of past and present,
and understood the rites of ruler and subject.
Some died, some fled.
The ways of these two or three men diverged.
How perverse their way is!"
The Literary Scholar said:
"Duke Shāng of Sòng knew the worthiness of Kǒng Fù but did not appoint him early,
so he died.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ knew the worthiness of Jì Yǒu,
but gave him political office too late, and the state was in chaos.
The ruler of Wèi was close to flatterers and distant from the worthy.
Zǐ Lù resided in Pú,
Kǒng Kuī was in charge of the government.
