Duke Jiǎn did not listen to Zǎi Wǒ and leaked his plans.
Therefore, the two lords were killed and exiled,
and disaster befell the loyal ministers.
These two men had affairs but were not involved in their planning,
so they could die
or live,
leave or stay;
their righteousness was the same.
Yàn Yīng did not die in the disaster of Cuī
and Qìng,
and cannot be called unrighteous.
Wēi Zǐ left the chaos of Yīn;
can he be called unbenevolent?"
The Grandee said:
"Utmost beauty is unadorned jade;
nothing can embellish it.
Utmost virtue preserves its true nature;
false artifice cannot enhance it.
Therefore, gold and jade are not carved,
beautiful pearls are not painted.
Now, Zhòng Yóu
and Rǎn Qiú do not have the material of sandalwood or catalpa,
or the uncut jade of Suí and Hé,
yet you force artifice upon them.
It's like carving rotten wood and sharpening a leaden knife,
adorning Mómǔ and painting a clay figure.
Covered with five colors,
beautifully patterned,
when encountering a flood or flowing wave,
they will be destroyed.
Those who heavily cherish ancient ways,
and are steeped in the *Shī*
and the *Shū*,
cannot bring peace in times of danger
or order in times of chaos.
Chasing chickens in the village,
do the chickens have factions?"
Scholar:
“Without learning, one cannot cultivate oneself;
without propriety, one cannot assist virtue.
The jade of Hé Shì,
the most beautiful treasure in the world,
must await the craftsman Gǎnzhū before its brilliance is revealed.
Máo Qiáng,
the most beautiful woman in the world,
must await fragrant oils and powders before her beauty is complete.
The Dān Zhōu Duke,
the most sagely person in the world,
must await a wise teacher and learning before he is thoroughly enlightened.
Now, the mediocre people of this generation,
dislike learning,
and rely solely on their own foolishness to shoulder great responsibilities.
They are like lacking oars and rudder,
crossing rivers and seas and encountering great winds,
being swept away into the abyss of a hundred *rèn*,
flowing eastward in a river without banks.
How can they be stopped?”
Grandee:
“Nature has its strengths and weaknesses,
form has its beauty and ugliness.
The sage can follow them but cannot change them.
Kǒngzǐ externally changed the clothing of his disciples,
but could not transform their hearts.
Thus, Zǐlù relinquished his long sword,
removed his towering cap,
and humbled himself at the Master's gate,
yet when managing the affairs of fellow students,
he would still act impetuously,
his crude nature remaining.
Zǎiyǔ slept during the day
and wished to shorten the three-year mourning period.
Kǒngzǐ said,
‘A wall of dung,
cannot be plastered,’
‘As if Yóu will not die a violent death.’
Therefore, if one lacks the inner substance but only learns the external form,
even with wise teachers and good friends,
it is like painting on fat or carving on ice,
wasting time and diminishing effort.
Thus, a good teacher cannot beautify Qīshī,
and fragrant oils cannot transform Mómǔ.”
Scholar:
“Xī Shī, covered in filth,
would cause even base men to hold their noses;
but an ugly person, splendidly adorned,
can be worthy of ancestral sacrifices to the Diety Above.
If these two were not to enter the gate of the sages,
they would inevitably remain poor people.
How could they obtain the names of ministers and grandees?
Therefore, a whetstone is used to sharpen a blade,
and learning is used to fully realize one's talents.
Kǒngzǐ said,
‘If a *gū* is not a *gū*,
is it still a *gū*,
is it still a *gū*!’
Thus, with the addition of human effort, something can become a vessel for the ancestral temple;
otherwise, it is merely firewood to be burned.
The metal of a dry or yuè sword, if not sharpened,
is despised by commoners;
but when a craftsman applies his skill,
the ruler wears it to court.
An ugly person thinks himself beautiful,
so he does not adorn himself;
a foolish person thinks himself wise,
so he does not learn.
To see others laughing at oneself and not realize it,
to dislike employing others,
this is the fault of self-conceit.”
5.3 《Sòng Xián Dì Èrshí'èr》 (Commending the Worthy, Section Twenty-Two)
Grandee:
“The rigid breaks,
the pliable bends.
Thus, Jì Yóu died from his stubbornness,
and Zǎi Wǒ was killed for his weakness.
If these two had not learned,
they might not have met such ends.
Why?
Because they were arrogant and boastful,
possessed petty wisdom but held great power,
wished others to follow them,
but could not follow others,
saw themselves without being seen,
and valued themselves without being valued by others.
This is why their bodies were killed and ultimately pickled.
I have not seen them become vessels for the ancestral temple,
but have witnessed them become examples for the world to punish.
At such a time,
where can one find peace?”
Scholar:
“A fine steed pulling a salt cart,
hangs its head on the slopes of Mount Tài Háng,
while a butcher, knife in hand, glares at it.
Tài Gōng, in his poverty,
sold goods in the market of Zhāogē,
where disheveled people gathered and laughed at him.
At such times,
it is not that there is a lack of horses with great speed and talent,
but that King Wén and
Bólè have not recognized their value.
Zǐlù and
Zǎi Wǒ were born without encountering the promotion of Bólè,
but instead met a mad butcher,
so gentlemen lament them.
If
‘Yóu will not die a violent death,’
‘Heaven will surely bless me.’
Kǒng Fù suffered the troubles of Huá Dū,
which cannot be said to be unjust.
Chóu Mù faced the disaster of Sòng Wàn,
which cannot be said to be unwise.”
Grandee:
“Today's scholars
lack the abilities of Tài Gōng,
and the talents of fine steeds,
but possess the venom of bees and scorpions, harming themselves.
For example, Chéng Yóng of the East Sea and
Hú Jiàn of Hédōng.
These two, through trickery, secured recommendation,
rose from the ranks of common soldiers,
and became county magistrates.
They alone were self-righteous
and did not agree with others.
They could not be drawn near
and could not be pushed forward;
they were arrogant and disrespectful,
envious and disobedient,
harshly criticizing princesses
and insulting great ministers.
Knowing it was impossible, they stubbornly pursued their course,
seeking fame.
Their actions were improper,
and they ultimately destroyed themselves.
Before seeing the achievement of their endeavors, they met with disaster in the East Pavilion,
suffered severe punishments,
and could not live out their natural lifespan.
They were cunning and thought it wisdom,
critical and thought it uprightness,
disrespectful and thought it courage.
Their encountering misfortune
was therefore fitting.”
Scholar:
“These two officials held pure and honest hearts,
followed the path of loyalty and righteousness,
were upright in serving their superiors,
and exerted themselves for the public good.
They upheld the law and reasoned with others,
not avoiding the powerful and tyrannical,
not favoring their relatives,
not valuing the comfort of their wives and children,
and not caring for their private affairs.
Yet, in the end, they could not escape the jealousy of others
and were rejected by the masses.
This is why they suffered unexpected punishments and their merits were not fulfilled.
If the royal clan is not upright, then the laws will not be enforced;
if the trusted officials are not upright, then treachery will arise.
Zhào Shē carried it out in Píngyuán,
and Fàn Jū carried it out with Rǎng Hóu;
the two states were well-governed, and the two families were preserved.
Therefore, if the ruler errs and the ministers correct him,
if the superiors are wrong and the subordinates criticize them,
if the great ministers are upright,
what can the county magistrates do?
To not reflect on oneself but find fault with others
is a great mistake in governance.
Qū Yuán drowned himself in the river
because he suffered the slander of Zǐjiāo;
Guǎn Zhòng was able to carry out his way
because of the strength of Bào Shū.
Now, not seeing the strength of Bào Shū,
but seeing the disaster of the Mìluó River,
even if one wishes to live out one's natural lifespan,
how can one achieve it?”
5.4 《Zūn Dào Dì Èrshísān》 (Following the Way, Section Twenty-Three)
Grandee:
“Imperial Secretary!”
The Imperial Secretary did not respond.
Said to the Chancellor's Secretary:
"Scholars from the time they bind their hair and learn to speak,
embrace learning and do not abandon it,
their words flow like a cycle,
turning like a potter's wheel.
Their writing is as profuse as the flowers of spring,
but as ineffective as grasping at wind.
They adorn empty words to confuse reality,
and talk about the past to harm the present.
If we follow them,
then the official business of the government will be wasted,
for empty words cannot be made real and put into practice;
if we do not follow them,
the scholars will think it wrong,
and the clamor of the multitude will be
too much to bear.
You gentlemen have been in the Dà Fǔ for a long time,
understanding the ancient past
and being clear about the present age,
what should we follow to be right?"
The Chancellor's Secretary replied:
"Jìn Wéngōng was cunning but not upright,
Qí Huángōng was upright but not cunning;
their methods differed,
but both achieved hegemony.
To insist on following the past without change,
and adhering to old ways without alteration,
is to leave the substance unchanged,
and the blunt carriage still in use.
Therefore, some create and
others narrate,
and then laws and ordinances are adjusted to the people,
and tools and implements become convenient for use.
Kǒngzǐ responded to three rulers with different intentions,
and Yàn Zǐ served three rulers with different approaches;
this was not merely to be contrary,
but because the demands of the time were different.
Since you, gentlemen, have established the path to great achievements
and laid a foundation that will never be exhausted,
I hope you will not be concerned with minor details,
or be swayed by the arguments of the Rú and
Mò schools."
The Scholar said:
"Shī Kuàng's tuning of the five notes
did not depart from the Gōng and Shāng tones.
The sage kings' governance of the world
did not depart from benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, there was the name of changing institutions,
but not the reality of altering the Way.
From the time of the Huángdì
down to the Three Kings,
none failed to emphasize virtuous teachings,
to pay close attention to the xiáng and xù schools,
to exalt benevolence and righteousness,
and to establish education.
This is the way that will not change for a hundred generations.
The Yīn and Zhōu dynasties prospered by following these ways,
while the King of Qín perished by changing the laws.
The *Shī* says:
'Though there are no experienced elders,
there are still models to follow.'
This speaks of laws and teachings,
therefore, what is lost should be preserved,
and what is raised should be carried through,
carried through and practiced;
why change anything further?"
The Chancellor's Secretary said:
"Speaking of Xī Shī's beauty does not improve one's appearance,
and speaking of Yáo and
Shùn's virtue does not improve governance.
Now, the scholars do not speak of how to govern,
but say that there is no merit in governing,
like not speaking of methods of farming,
but praising the granaries of the rich.
Those who desire grain must be mindful of the seasons,
and those who desire governance must adapt to the times.
Therefore, Shāng Jūn clearly saw that survival and destruction cannot be the same as the customs of the world,
because they obstruct achievement and are often near at hand.
Mediocre people are comfortable with their old ways,
and foolish people believe what they have heard.
Therefore, the administration of boats and carriages
causes the people to feel at ease only after three years.
When the laws of Shāng Jūn were established,
then the people trusted them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'One may share learning with someone,
but not necessarily weigh the circumstances with them.'
Scholars can be instructed to hold the rope and follow the markings,
but they are not the ones to discuss matters beyond the realm of the Way."
The Scholar said:
"A gentleman hears much and questions what he doubts,
narrates but does not create,
a sage understands and plans greatly,
is wise and has few affairs.
Therefore, his achievements are completed and not ruined,
and his name is established and not overturned.
A petty person has shallow wisdom but great plans,
is weak but carries heavy burdens,
therefore, they fail midway;
Sū Qín and
Shāng Yāng are examples of this.
Without the laws of the former kings,
and not following the Way of the sages,
but relying on oneself,
is why they perished.
The *Yì* says:
'When a petty person is in a high position,
even if high, they will surely collapse.
Not fulfilling their path,
nor making their virtue constant,
and being able to end their lives well,
has never happened.
Therefore, they initially ascend to heaven,
and later enter the earth.'
When Yǔ controlled the floods,
the people knew its benefit,
and none did not encourage his work.
When Shāng Yāng established the laws,
the people knew its harm,
and none did not fear his punishments.
Therefore, the Xià ruler established his merit and became king,
while Shāng Yāng's laws were implemented and he perished.
Shāng Yāng had the foresight of unique wisdom,
but the world lacked proof of his unique vision.
I, a scholar, am not enough to weigh the circumstances of the present age,
nor will I bear the burden of misfortune."
5. 5 On Criticisms
The Chancellor's Secretary said:
"Yàn Zǐ has said:
'The Rú are flowery in words but meager in substance,
elaborate in music but neglectful of the people,
prolonging mourning to harm life,
and engaging in extravagant burials to injure livelihood,
their rituals are cumbersome and difficult to practice,
their ways are circuitous and difficult to follow,
they praise the past and criticize the present,
they despise what they see and value what they hear.'
These people are fundamentally twisted,
and take themselves as the model.
This is why Yán Yì was punished and dismissed,
and Dí Shān died among the Xióngnú.
Living in a position but not supporting its court,
living in the world but slandering their superiors,
ultimately being executed and losing their lives,
who else is responsible for bearing their burdens and misfortunes?"
The Scholar said:
"Rituals are for preventing excess,
and music is for transforming customs;
when rituals flourish and music is correct, then punishments are just.
Therefore, when dikes are built, the people have no water disasters,
and when ritual and righteousness are established, the people have no disorders or calamities.
Therefore, when ritual and righteousness are destroyed,
and dikes are breached,
there is no way to govern.
There has never been such a way.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'In ritual,
rather than extravagance,
prefer frugality;
in mourning, rather than ease,
prefer sorrow.'
Therefore, the purpose of rituals
is not to harm life or injure livelihood,
and the purpose of dignified ceremonies and regulated patterns
is not to disrupt customs or injure morality.
Govern a state with careful observance of ritual,
and defend a state in danger with careful observance of law.
In the past, Qín swallowed the world with military might,
but Sī and
Gāo accumulated disasters with their evil deeds,
abandoning ancient practices,
destroying old rituals,
and exclusively relying on penal law,
so that the Rú and
Mò schools were lost.
Blocking the path of scholars
and silencing the mouths of the people,
the path of flattery advanced daily, and the ruler did not hear his faults;
this is why Qín lost the world and its state collapsed.
Therefore, when a sage governs,
he must first punish those
who use clever words to assist in wrong and overthrow the state.
Now, why do you take the words of a ruined state and bring them here?
You gentlemen, occupying your positions,
do not correct the Way,
but instead, with your intentions, agree and conform to the trend,
hating petty people who superficially comply,
and thereby compounding the faults of others.
Therefore, those who know the truth die
because they cannot bear to follow those who blindly agree,
and thus they cannot avoid imprisonment.
Alas!"
The Prime Minister's Secretary said:
"The tánzhè tree has its village,
the *Pharagmites australis* has its thicket,
speaking of how things of the same kind follow each other.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Virtue is never solitary;
it is sure to have neighbors.'
Therefore, Tāng rose and Yī Yǐn arrived;
the unkind are far away.
There has never been a bright ruler above with rebellious ministers below.
Now, the late emperor personally practiced the way of benevolence and sagacity
to govern within the seas,
recruiting outstanding talents and virtuous scholars,
using only the benevolent,
executing and expelling rebellious ministers,
not avoiding those close to him,
striving to seek the virtuous and dismiss the unworthy,
just like Yáo's promotion of Shùn,
Yǔ's elimination of the Gǔn clan,
and the banishment of Huāndōu.
And to say
'followers who merely agree'
means that the ruler is wrong and the ministers flatter,
doesn't it?"
The Literary Man said:
"Gāoyáo said to Shùn:
'Knowing men is difficult;
only the Emperor finds it hard.'
During the flood disaster,
Yáo alone was worried and unable to control it,
but with Shùn
and Yǔ, the nine provinces were pacified.
Therefore, even with a bright ruler like Yáo,
without the assistance of Shùn
and Yǔ,
pure virtue would not flow.
The *Chūnqiū* criticizes having a ruler without ministers.
During the time of the late emperor,
good ministers were not fully prepared,
so evil ministers found gaps.
Yáo got Shùn
and Yǔ, and Gǔn was executed and Huāndōu punished;
Zhào Jiǎnzi got Shū Xiàng, and Shèng Qīngjiān yielded.
The saying goes:
'Without seeing a gentleman,
one does not know a false minister.'
The *Shī* says:
'Before seeing my lord,
my heart was full of sorrow.
Now that I have seen my lord,
my heart is at peace.'
This is what it means."
The Prime Minister's Secretary said:
"Yáo appointed Gǔn
and Huāndōu,
but when he got Shùn
and Yǔ, he banished and executed them for their crimes,
and the world was content,
punishing the unkind.
The ruler used the common people,
but Yán Yì,
the head of the Jǐnán pavilion,
was promoted by the late emperor and given a high position,
rising to the rank of senior minister.
Dí Shān, starting as a commoner,
became a minister in the Hàn court,
occupying the positions of Shùn
and Yǔ,
holding the balance of the world,
but unable to govern,
and instead being accused of slandering the emperor;
therefore, the punishment of Huāndōu was added and the execution arrived.
The virtuous are rewarded, and the unworthy are punished;
this is naturally the case.
What does the Literary Man find strange about it?"
The Literary Man said:
"Debaters assist each other with righteousness,
enlighten each other with the Way,
follow good without seeking victory,
and accept righteousness without being ashamed of poverty.
If they mislead each other with falsehoods,
confuse each other with words,
boast about stopping last,
and aim for temporary victory,
they are not to be valued.
Sū Qín
and Zhāng Yí
deceived the feudal lords,
overthrew ten-thousand-chariot states,
and caused rulers to lose what they held;
it was not that they were not eloquent,
but it was the way of chaos.
A gentleman dislikes a mean person's inability to serve a ruler
and worries that his compliance will go to any length.
Now, you do not listen to righteous arguments to assist the ministers,
but instead follow and agree with them,
favoring momentary arguments
and not considering the consequences.
If you were to be an official,
you should receive imperial punishment.
You should be quiet!"
The Prime Minister's Secretary said:
"I have heard that when a scholar lives in the world,
clothes should be enough to cover the body,
food and drink should be enough to provide for parents,
enough internally to provide for each other,
and not seek anything from others externally.
Therefore, one can manage the family only after cultivating oneself,
and one can govern as an official only after managing the family.
Therefore, those who eat coarse rice cannot speak of filial piety,
those whose wives and children are hungry and cold cannot speak of kindness,
and those who do not cultivate their ancestral business cannot speak of management.
Living in this world,
conducting oneself in this way,
and having these three burdens,
is enough to remain silent."
5.6 *Chapter Twenty-Fifth: Filial Piety and Nurturing*
The Literary Man said:
"Good nurturing does not necessarily require delicacies;
good clothing does not necessarily require silk.
To do one's best to serve one's parents with what one has
is the height of filial piety.
Therefore, even a commoner can be diligent enough to follow propriety,
drinking bean soup and water is enough to show respect.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Nowadays, filial piety is merely being able to provide sustenance.
Without reverence,
how does it differ?'
Therefore, the highest filial piety is to nurture the will,
the next is to nurture the appearance,
and the next is to nurture the body.
Value the ritual,
do not be greedy for the nourishment.
If the ritual is followed, the heart is harmonious,
and even if the nourishment is not complete,
it is acceptable.
The *Yì* says:
'The east neighbor's sacrifice of an ox
is not as good as the west neighbor's simple sacrifice.'
Therefore, wealth and nobility without ritual
are not as good as poverty and lowliness with filial piety and fraternal respect.
Within the inner chambers, practice filial piety to the fullest;
outside the inner chambers, practice fraternal respect to the fullest;
in the way of friends, practice trustworthiness to the fullest.
These three
are the height of filial piety.
Managing the household well does not mean accumulating wealth;
serving one's parents filially does not mean providing fresh delicacies;
it is also about having a gentle expression,
following their intentions, and fulfilling ritual and righteousness."
The Prime Minister's Secretary said:
"Eighty is called 'dié,'
seventy is called 'mào.'
Those who are 'mào' are not satisfied with food unless it is meat,
and are not warm unless they wear silk.
Therefore, a filial son provides sweet and soft things to nourish the mouth
and light and warm things to nourish the body.
Zēngzǐ, in nurturing Zēngxī,
always had wine and meat.
Without a proper cap,
even Gōngxī Chì could not find it acceptable.
Without delicacies,
even Mǐn
and Zēng could not complete the nurturing.
Ritual has no empty additions,
so there must be reality before there can be embellishment.
Rather than having excessive ritual and insufficient nourishment,
it is better to have excessive nourishment and insufficient ritual.
To wash the cup to hold water,
to rise and fall to offer coarse rice,
even if the ritual is complete,
it is not what is valued."
The Literary Man said:
"The mother of Zhōu Xiāng Wáng was not lacking in wine and meat,
nor were her clothes and food inferior to those of Zēng Xī;
however, she was labeled as unfilial,
because she could not serve her parents well.
The noble man values propriety,
while the petty man is greedy for sustenance.
If one calls out with a 'Hey, you!' and beckons,
or throws something and gives it,
even a beggar would not accept it.
If a noble man lacks proper ceremony,
he will not eat even if the food is delicious.
Therefore, if the host does not personally offer food,
the guest will not make a food sacrifice.
This shows that the food is light, but propriety is heavy."
The Prime Minister's Secretary said:
"The greatest filial piety is to support one's parents with the resources of the whole country,
next is to support them with official salary,
and the lowest is to support them with physical labor.
Therefore, kings, dukes, and rulers
are at the top,
and ministers and grand officers
are next.
Speaking in terms of a family,
if there is a capable son who is successful in the world,
his parents will live in tall buildings and deep houses,
ride in comfortable carriages and large horses,
wear light and warm clothes,
and eat delicious and soft foods.
If not,
they will wear coarse clothes and leather caps,
live in poor and narrow alleys,
have no certainty for the next day,
eat only vegetables and coarse grains,
and only see meat after the year-end sacrifice.
The stomachs of old parents are not like the gardens of Táng,
which are only filled with vegetables.
Vegetables and coarse grains
are what even beggars would not take,
yet the son uses them to support his parents;
even if he wants to follow the proper ceremonies,
it is not considered honorable."
The Literary Man said:
"To steal a position without the ability,
to receive a salary without merit,
even if one has wealth and honor,
it is like the support provided by Zhí
and Qiāo.
Living in high towers with extreme views,
and having tables that are one square *zhàng* in size
cannot be called filial piety.
The stomachs of old parents are not like the bags of thieves;
why are they constantly filled with things obtained through immoral means?
Taking what is not rightfully yours or your duty,
wealth enters but trouble follows;
one's own body will die in disaster,
how can one have meat to eat at the year-end sacrifice?
Zēng Shēn
and Mǐn Zǐ lacked the support of a high-ranking official,
but had the reputation of filial sons;
Zhōu Xiāng Wáng was wealthy and possessed the world,
but had the burden of not being able to serve his parents.
Therefore, meager ceremony with abundant support
is not filial piety.
Plundering granaries to provide support
is not filial piety."
The Prime Minister's Secretary said:
"The highest filial piety is to please one's parents with one's countenance,
the next is to keep one's parents at ease,
and the next is to preserve one's own life.
In the past,
Chén Yú turned his back on Hàn,
and was beheaded at the Zhī River;
Wǔ Bèi was rebellious and perverse,
and his three clans were exterminated.
In recent times,
Zhǔfù Yǎn acted improperly and was executed,
Lǚ Bùshū used clever words and was killed;
not being careful in conducting oneself,
execution extended to innocent relatives.
From this perspective,
empty propriety is of no benefit to oneself.
Matching words with actions,
and practicing both propriety and support,
then one can speak of filial piety.
Filial piety lies in substance,
not in outward appearance;
preserving oneself lies in caution,
not in reckless speech."
The Literary Man said:
"Speaking without sincerity,
making promises without keeping them,
lacking courage in times of difficulty,
and being disloyal in serving the ruler are
the greatest forms of unfilial piety.
Mèngzǐ said:
'The officials of today,
the grand officers of today,
are all criminals.
They all cater to the ruler's desires to indulge his evils.'
Now you are disloyal and untrustworthy,
using clever words to disrupt the government,
and leading with flattery to seek agreement.
Those like you
are not tolerated in the world.
The *Chūnqiū* says:
'An official holds to one principle without wavering,
follows reason without seeking external support,
and fulfills his duty alone.'
Therefore, for a low-ranking person to speak about high matters
is a crime,
and to speak when not asked
is arrogance.
There is an imperial decree for dukes and ministers to discuss this,
and are you just fighting with words in vain?"
5.7 *Cìyì Dì Èrshíliù* (Insinuations and Criticisms, Section Twenty-Six)
The Prime Minister's Secretary said:
"Mountains and hills do not reject a single handful of soil,
in order to achieve their great height;
the noble man does not refuse the words of a firewood gatherer,
in order to broaden his reputation.
Therefore, those who see much are broad-minded,
those who hear much are knowledgeable,
those who reject advice are obstructed,
and those who are self-centered are isolated.
Therefore, plans that involve those below will not fail,
and actions that involve the masses will not be delayed.
The *Shī* says:
'Consult with the grass cutters and firewood gatherers.'
Therefore, even commoners can express their opinions,
let alone the Prime Minister's Secretary?
The *Chūnqiū* does not record the writings of ordinary officials,
but it does record Xuān,
considering him to be a scribe.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Even if I am not employed,
I will still participate in the discussions.'
Although I am not talented,
I have always lent an ear and listened respectfully,
adjusted my robes and pointed my fingers,
and received instruction directly on the path of the noble man.
If what the Literary Man says is correct,
what harm is there in my words?
If what the Literary Man says is wrong,
even if I am a humble Prime Minister's Secretary,
who would not disagree?"
The Literary Man said:
"To assist people with righteousness is called loyalty,
to guide people with evil is called flattery.
Those who reject faults and accept goodness
are loyal ministers of the ruler,
and upright officials of the grand officer.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'If a grand officer has three remonstrating ministers,
even if he is without principle,
he will not lose his family.'
Now you hold the position of a scribe,
but you have no heart of loyalty and righteousness;
you cannot correct what is crooked,
you cannot rectify what is evil,
you follow the current to accommodate yourself,
and follow the wind to please your superiors.
You listen carelessly to what your superiors say,
and follow crookedly what your superiors do,
like a shadow following a form,
or an echo responding to a sound,
never distinguishing right from wrong.
You wear the clothes of a scholar,
and the hat of a scholar,
but you cannot practice their Way;
you are not a true scholar.
It is like an earthen dragon,
with all the markings of a dragon but not a real dragon.
*Tínglì* resembles vegetables but tastes different,
jade and stones look alike but are different in kind.
You are not a scholar of the Kǒng family who holds to the classics and guards the Way,
but a scholar who complies with dukes and ministers;
you are not one of my kind.
Rǎn Yǒu, as the steward of the Jì family, increased its wealth,
and Kǒngzǐ said:
'Young men, beat the drums and attack him,
it is permissible.'
Therefore, one who assists Jié is not wise,
and one who collects wealth for Jié is not benevolent."
The Prime Minister's Secretary was silent and did not reply.
5.8 *Lìyì Dì Èrshíqī* (Debates on Profit, Section Twenty-Seven)
The Dàfū said:
"The wise ruler who creates a prosperous world
worries about and labors for the myriad people,
thinking about the unpeacefulness of the northern border.
Therefore, he sends envoys to recommend worthy and virtuous men,
and outstanding literary scholars.
He respectfully invites men of Dao,
intending to observe their unique opinions and different strategies,
humbly listening with an open mind,
hoping to gain something from them.
If you scholars cannot produce extraordinary plans or far-reaching strategies
for attacking the Xiōngnú and securing the borders,
clinging to dried bamboo slips,
adhering to empty words,
ignorant of what to adopt and what to discard,
and the changes of the times,
your discussions lack substance,
like scratching the back when the knee itches.
Arguing and debating in public,
the clamor is unbearable to hear,
like judging taste by mouth to accomplish a task.
Is this what a wise ruler wants to hear?"
The Literary Scholar said:
"The scholars' responses,
though different in approach, converge on the same goal,
which is to emphasize ritual propriety and righteousness,
reject wealth and profit,
restore the ways of the past,
and correct the errors of the present age,
all speaking of great peace.
Even if not all of it is completely reliable,
there should be something that can be implemented.
You, sir, are ignorant of understanding propriety,
but comprehend the pursuit of trivial gains,
obstructing affairs and destroying proposals,
scheming and plotting.
Therefore, nothing has been decided until now.
Without Confucian scholars, nothing can be accomplished;
the ministers and high officials only seek to profit."
The Dàfū said:
"Fierce in appearance but weak inside,
you are those who confuse the genuine.
Eloquence on the surface but hemp within,
you are those who confuse reality.
The literary scholars wear coarse gowns and wide belts,
stealing the attire of Duke Zhōu,
bowing and shuffling,
stealing the appearance of Zhòng Ní.
Their arguments and praises,
steal the words of Shāng
and Cì;
their criticisms and discussions of governance,
steal the talents of Guǎn
and Yàn.
Their hearts are inferior to ministers and chancellors,
their ambitions are smaller than a ruler's.
When given power,
they become confused and unable to govern.
Therefore, selecting people based on their words
is like judging horses by their fur.
This is why so many do not live up to their recommendations.
The imperial decree says:
'I appreciate the talents within the realm,
therefore, I respectfully invite distinguished men from all directions, learned literary scholars, and those with extensive knowledge,
and promote them to higher ranks and salaries.'
Those who speak well do not necessarily have virtue.
Why?
Because speaking is easy, but acting is difficult.
There are those who abandon their carriage but recognize their ox,
valuing those who accomplish much without speaking much.
Wú Tuó destroyed himself with his tongue,
and Zhǔfù Yǎn committed suicide with his tongue.
The crow-pheasant cries at night,
but it is of no help for the dawn;
Zhǔfù's hooting owl,
is of no help to the dead.
It is not that the officials seek to profit,
but that the literary scholars are shackled by old techniques,
and misled by slanderous words."
The Literary Scholar said:
"Those who can speak and can act are
Tāng and Wǔ.
Those who can speak but cannot act
are the officials.
The literary scholars steal the attire of Duke Zhōu,
and the officials steal the positions of Duke Zhōu.
The literary scholars are shackled by old techniques,
and the officials are shackled by wealth and profit.
Zhǔfù Yǎn committed suicide with his tongue,
and the officials are trapped by their own greed.
The talent of a Jì horse is for a thousand *lǐ*,
but without Zào Fù, it cannot be used;
Yǔ's knowledge extends to ten thousand people,
but without Shùn as his assistant, he could not use it.
Therefore, when Jì Huánzǐ was in power,
Liǔxià Huì suddenly disappeared.
When Kǒngzǐ became Minister of Justice,
then the disobedient ones flourished.
The Jì horse is recognized by Bólè,
but its accomplishment lies with Zào Fù.
When Zào Fù takes the reins,
there is no distinction between good and bad horses;
all can be used on the road.
In the time of Duke Zhōu,
there was no distinction between worthy and unworthy men;
all could discuss perfect governance.
Therefore, a good driver is skilled at training horses,
and a wise minister is skilled at employing men.
Now, to recommend extraordinary talents and have Zāng Zōu drive them
is like burdening a Jì horse with a salt cart and demanding speed from it.
This is why the worthy and virtuous men
and literary scholars often do not live up to their recommendations."
The Dàfū said:
"Alas!
You scholars are base and without integrity,
speaking much but accomplishing nothing,
your outward appearance does not match your inner self.
Like burglars who tunnel through walls,
they have been a problem since ancient times.
Kǒng Qiū was expelled by the Lord of Lǔ,
and was never used by the world.
Why?
Because he concerned himself with too many details,
being out of touch with the times and missing the essentials.
Therefore, the King of Qín burned his teachings and did not implement them,
and buried them in the Wèi River and did not use them.
How can you wag your tongues,
stretch your faces and eyebrows,
and participate in preliminary discussions,
about the affairs of the state?"
5.9 Chapter 28: The Nation's Ills
The Literary Scholar said:
"If a state has worthy men but does not use them,
it is not the fault of the men,
but the shame of those who govern the state.
Kǒngzǐ was
a great sage,
but none of the feudal lords could use him.
Holding a minor position in Lǔ,
in three months,
things were done without orders,
and stopped without prohibitions,
like timely rain watering all things,
causing everything to flourish.
How much more so for the fundamental court that governs the world,
if it were to implement the virtuous words and teachings of a sage ruler?
Now, you ministers and high officials hold esteemed positions,
and control the essentials of the world,
for more than ten years,
yet your merits and virtues are not extended to the world,
but your hard labor is imposed on the people.
The people are poor and impoverished,
while your private families accumulate tens of thousands in gold.
This is what gentlemen are ashamed of,
and what the 'Cutting the Sandalwood' poem satirizes.
In the past,
when Shāng Yāng was the Prime Minister of Qín,
he disregarded propriety and yielded,
prioritized greed and baseness,
valued military achievements,
strove for advancement,
without bestowing virtue and kindness upon the people,
but imposed strict laws and punishments on the state.
Customs deteriorated day by day, and the people's resentment grew.
Therefore, King Huì had his body minced into pickle,
to apologize to the world.
At that time,
he could not discuss matters either.
Now, the ruling officials worry that the Confucian scholars are poor, lowly, and talkative,
and the Confucian scholars also worry that the ruling officials are rich, powerful, and have many worries."
The Dàfū looked at the literary scholar,
feeling dejected and without words.
The Chancellor's aide said:
"When discussing national affairs and
debating the merits and demerits of governance,
why not slowly explain and persuade each other?
Why be so intense and insistent?
The Senior Official finds it difficult to abolish the salt and
iron monopolies,
not for any personal gain,
but out of concern for the nation's expenditures
and the expenses of the border regions.
The scholars heatedly debate the salt and
iron, also not for themselves,
but wishing to return to the ways of the ancients and assist in establishing benevolence and righteousness.
Both sides have their principles.
Times and circumstances change,
so how can one stubbornly cling to ancient practices and reject the principles of the present?
Moreover, even minor flaws are criticized,
so there must be something to change.
If the scholars can pacify the nation,
bring distant lands to submit,
prevent disasters from bandits and invaders on the borders,
and have all taxes remitted,
what then of salt,
iron, and equitable transport?
The reason we value Confucian scholars
is their humility, deference,
and dedication to serving others with virtue.
Now your debates are shockingly loud,
lacking the eloquence of Chì (赤) and
Cì (賜),
and revealing expressions of disdain and opposition,
which is unheard of.
The Senior Official's words were excessive,
and the scholars are the same.
The scholars should apologize to the Senior Official."
The Worthies and
Literati all rose from their seats and said:
"We are ignorant and narrow-minded,
rarely attending court,
and our rash words are often inappropriate,
thus contradicting those in charge.
But medicine is bitter to the taste yet beneficial to the illness,
and honest advice is grating to the ear yet beneficial to conduct.
Therefore, speaking frankly is a blessing,
while flattering words are a curse.
The forest is full of strong winds,
and wealth and status are full of flattery.
In the court of ten thousand *lǐ*,
all that is heard daily is 'yes, yes,'
and only now do we hear the bluntness of the scholars,
which is truly good medicine and acupuncture for the ministers."
The Senior Official's expression softened slightly,
and he turned to the Literati and addressed the Worthies, saying:
"Secluded alleys are full of twisted arguments,
and those with limited views are difficult to persuade.
The Literati stubbornly cling to obscure and vague sayings,
and will never change.
Past events
and ancient sayings
can already be seen clearly.
Now, looking at recent times,
relying on what we have seen with our own eyes
and heard with our own ears,
times have changed, and circumstances are different.
During the reigns of Emperor Wén (文) and Emperor Jǐng (景),
and at the beginning of the Yuán (元) era,
the people were simple and returned to fundamentals,
officials were honest and respected themselves,
diligently and earnestly toiling,
people prospered and families became wealthy.
Now, it is not that policies have not been changed or teachings not been altered,
so why is the world becoming increasingly corrupt and customs increasingly decadent?
Officials are becoming less honest,
the people are losing their sense of shame,
punishments do not eradicate evil,
and wickedness still does not stop.
People say:
'A petty Confucian is not as good as a metropolitan official.'
The Literati all come from Shāndōng (山東)
and rarely participate in major discussions.
Senior Officials have debated matters in the capital for a long time,
and wish to clearly distinguish the merits and demerits of governance,
and this is why things are the way they are."
The *Xiánliáng* said:
"Shāndōng
is the heartland of all under Heaven
and the battlefield of worthy men.
Emperor Gāo soared like a dragon and rose like a phoenix between Sòng and
Chǔ,
with Shāndōng children Xiāo,
Cáo, Fán,
Lì, Téng,
Guàn and others as his assistants.
Even though they lived in a different era,
they were merely comparable to Hóng Yāo and
Tài Diān.
Yǔ emerged from the Western Qiāng,
King Wén was born among the Northern Yí,
yet their sage-like virtues towered above the world.
They possessed the talent of ten thousand men
and bore the responsibility of surpassing the masses.
They moved in and out of cities,
but once they failed to return,
they eventually ended up as common servants.
Although I was not born and raised in the capital
and am foolish and of low talent,
unworthy of participating in great discussions,
I have secretly heard the words of the elders of my village.
In the past,
the clothing of common people was warm but not extravagant,
and their utensils were simple, sturdy, and practical.
Clothing was sufficient to cover the body,
utensils were sufficient to facilitate work,
horses were sufficient for riding,
carriages were sufficient for self-transport,
wine was sufficient for celebration without excess,
music was sufficient to regulate the heart without indulgence.
There was no sound of banquets and revelry indoors,
and no sight of leisurely outings outdoors.
When traveling, they carried burdens on their backs;
when resting, they worked at plowing and weeding.
Their consumption was frugal, and their wealth was abundant;
their foundations were solid, and their people were prosperous.
Funerals were mournful but not elaborate,
and living was comfortable but not extravagant.
High officials were upright and without desires,
and the government was lenient and not harsh.
Therefore, the common people lived in peace with their nature,
and the officials maintained their positions.
At the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
when literature was esteemed and virtue was cultivated,
all under Heaven was in good order.
Afterward,
wicked ministers each used their skills
to disrupt the well-ordered government,
creating barriers beyond the mountains and seas
and initiating various forms of profiteering.
Yáng Kě reported wealth,
Jiāng Chōng restricted clothing,
Grand Master Zhāng changed decrees,
and Dù Zhōu administered prisons.
Fines, redemptions, levies, and taxes
were all implemented on even the smallest matters,
beyond what could be recorded.
Xià Lán and his ilk falsely accused,
Wáng Wēnshū and his gang wantonly killed,
and cruel officials sprang up everywhere,
disturbing the good people.
At that time,
the common people could not protect their heads,
and the wealthy could not be sure of their family names.
The sage ruler became aware of this
and executed Chōng and others,
exterminating the cruel and treacherous,
using their deaths to appease the grievances
and fulfill the responsibilities of all under Heaven,
so the people once again lived freely and in peace.
However, the harm caused by those events persists to this day,
and the wounds have not yet healed.
Therefore, the officials still practice remnants of cruel policies,
and powerful magistrates still have greedy hearts.
High officials abuse their power and make arbitrary decisions,
and powerful and cunning people form cliques and oppress others.
The rich are extravagant and wasteful,
while the poor engage in usurpation and murder.
Women's work is difficult to complete but easily ruined,
and carriages and utensils are difficult to make but easily broken.
Carriages do not last a full year,
and utensils do not last the whole year.
A single carriage costs a thousand *shí*,
and a single garment costs ten *zhōng*.
Common people use painted cups and tables,
and their mats and seats are embroidered with silk.
Maidservants and concubines wear silk and silk shoes,
and commoners eat polished rice and meat.
Villages have their customs,
and communities have their gatherings.
People race each other on broad roads
and play football in narrow alleys.
Few hold plows and carry hoes,
personally farming and weaving.
Many gather to show off,
applying white powder and dark eye shadow.
They pretend to have what they do not,
and the poor boast even though they are impoverished.
The exterior is elaborate, but the interior is empty.
The sons of the wealthy wear silk clothes, but their luggage is made of hemp.
They do not support the living
but lavishly provide for the dead.
Funerals exhaust the family's wealth,
and daughters are sent off with carriages full of goods.
The rich want to exceed others,
and the poor want to catch up.
The rich hoard their wealth,
and the poor borrow money.
Therefore, the people's years pass quickly,
and the poor are shameless.
When they are lacking, they have little integrity.
This is why punishments fail to eliminate evil, and crimes still do not cease.
Therefore, if a state imposes strict levies,
it will inevitably suffer from a lack of resources."
6.1 *Sàn Bùzú Di Ershíjiǔ* (Extravagance and Insufficiency, Part 29)
The Grand Master said:
"I thought the *xiánliáng* would be somewhat better,
but they have revealed both the obscure and the obvious,
like the sounds of a barbarian carriage following and echoing.
Have you gentlemen not seen the cicadas of late summer?
Their sounds enter the ear,
but when the autumn winds arrive, their sounds disappear.
Those who are born should not speak carelessly,
disregarding the consequences.
When trouble arrives and they then fall silent,
it is too late."
The *Xiánliáng* said:
"Confucius read the *Shǐjì*
and sighed deeply,
lamenting the decline of upright virtue
and the peril of rulers and ministers.
Worthy men and gentlemen
take all under Heaven as their responsibility.
Those who bear great responsibilities think far ahead,
and those who think far ahead forget what is near.
With sincere hearts, they mourn and grieve,
and their compassion increases.
Therefore, their loyalty is pure and without encumbrances.
This is why poets lament and create,
and Bǐgān and
Zǐxū sacrificed themselves and forgot the danger.
Since they detested the exploitation of the people with such urgency,
how could they remain silent?
The *Book of Poetry* says:
'My heart is consumed with grief,
and I dare not jest.'
Confucius was restless,
distressed by the state of affairs.
Mòzǐ was anxious,
lamenting the state of the world."
The Grand Master was silent.
The Prime Minister said:
"I wish to hear about extravagance and insufficiency."
The *Xiánliáng* said:
"Palaces, carriages, horses,
clothing, utensils,
funerals, sacrifices, food, drink,
music, colors, and playthings
are all things that human nature cannot do without.
Therefore, the sages established rules and regulations to prevent excess.
Recently,
the officials have focused on power and profit
and neglected etiquette and righteousness.
Therefore, the common people imitate them,
often exceeding the prescribed limits.
Now, I will present the facts:
it is said:
"In ancient times,
grains, vegetables, and fruits
were not eaten out of season,
and birds, beasts, fish, and turtles
were not eaten unless they were killed at the proper time.
Therefore, nets were not allowed in the marshes,
and mixed-breed animals were not taken.
Now, the wealthy pursue, chase, and exterminate with nets and traps,
capturing fawns and fledglings,
indulging in wine, and covering hundreds of rivers.
They eat tender lamb and suckling pigs,
embryos with heads on their shoulders,
yellow-skinned and open-mouthed.
They eat spring geese and autumn chicks,
winter mallows and warm chives,
dredged *zǐ* and *liáo* and fragrant *sū*,
mushrooms, *ěrcài* vegetables,
hairy fruits, insects, and badgers."
"In ancient times,
the rafters were of unplaned wood, the roofs of thatch,
pottery pots were used as floats in humble homes,
sufficient to ward off cold and heat,
and to shelter from wind and rain.
As generations passed,
the rafters were not planed,
the thatch was not trimmed,
there was no planing and chiseling,
nor the labor of polishing and grinding.
The dàfū (大夫) had square pillars,
the shì (士) had pointed rafters,
and commoners merely used hewn wood for their structures.
Now, the wealthy use stacked beams and layered rafters,
carved railings and balustrades,
and walls adorned with jewels and jade."
"In ancient times,
clothing that did not conform to regulations,
and tools that were not fit for purpose,
were not sold in the market.
Now, commoners carve and sculpt useless objects,
and engrave and paint frivolous, impractical items.
With black and yellow mixed with blue,
and five-colored embroidered garments,
they stage puppet shows of men and women,
and various animal acts, horse plays, and tiger fights,
with figurines of Táng (唐) officials chasing after people,
and strange insects and foreign concubines."
"In ancient times,
the zhūhóu (諸侯) did not feed their horses with grain,
but by order of the Tiānzǐ (天子),
they would bring their chariots to pasture.
Those commoners who rode horses
did so only to relieve their labor.
Thus, when traveling, they wore the yoke,
and when resting, they worked the plow.
Now, the wealthy travel in continuous carriages and lined-up riders,
with accompanying riders and curtained wagons.
Those of moderate means have small carriages with short axles,
adorned with elaborate manes and hoof coverings.
A single horse stabled and fed
consumes the food of six members of a middling family,
and requires the labor of a full grown male."
"In ancient times,
commoners only wore silk in their old age,
the rest of the time they wore hemp and ramie,
hence they were called 'clothed in cloth'.
Later,
they wore silk linings with hemp exteriors,
straight collars without overlap,
and robes sewn together without hems.
Silk damask and embroidered fabrics
were garments for the rulers and their consorts.
Coarse and fine silks and plain silk
were for auspicious adornments in marriage.
Therefore, patterned thin silks and fine weaves
were not sold in the market.
Now, the wealthy wear intricately embroidered silk damask,
and those of moderate means wear plain fine silk and brocade.
Commoners now wear the garments of empresses and consorts,
and lowly people wear the adornments of marriage.
The price of fine white silk is double that of plain silk,
and the use of plain silk is double that of fine white silk."
"In ancient times,
the plain carts had no cushions,
and the rough litters had no padding.
Later,
the wooden carriage frames were not covered,
with long axles and numerous spokes,
rush mats and woven canopies,
and the canopies had no lacquer or silk adornments.
The dàfū (大夫) and shì (士) used simple and double wooden implements,
with coiled reins and soft leather.
Commoners used lacquered carriages with large frames and Shǔ (蜀) wheels.
Now, the wealthy commoners use silver and yellow ornamented scrapers,
and tied tassels and covered shafts.
Those of moderate means have inlaid bits with painted decorations,
adorned bridles and flying carriages."
"In ancient times,
commoners wore deer hides and leather caps,
with the hooves and feet not removed.
Later,
the dàfū (大夫) and shì (士) wore fox and badger furs sewn at the armpits,
and lamb and fawn furs with leopard trim.
Commoners wore trousers of coarse hair with red patches,
sheepskin coats and furred leggings.
Now, the wealthy wear marmot and sable,
and white fox and wild duck down.
Those of moderate means wear woolen garments with gold thread,
and swallowtail feathers instead of yellow."
"In ancient times,
commoners cheaply rode with rope reins,
and leather stirrups and hide mats only.
Later,
leather saddles were lined with yak hair,
and iron bits were not decorated.
Now, the wealthy have inlaid ears, silver tweezers,
golden jingles,
embroidered saddle blankets,
and bright, fresh reins.
Those of moderate means use lacquered leather with thin ties,
and colorful painted stirrups."
"In ancient times,
they drank from soiled vessels with cupped hands,
and there were no goblets, cups, or serving dishes.
Later,
commoners used utensils made of bamboo, willow, pottery, and gourds only.
Only the hú (瑚), lián (璉), shāng (觴), and dòu (豆) were carved and painted red.
Now, the wealthy have silver-rimmed and yellow-handled vessels,
and gold-inlaid bronze and jade cups.
Those of moderate means have Yěwáng (野王) hemp utensils,
and gold-inlaid Shǔ (蜀) cups.
One ornate cup is worth ten bronze cups,
but the cost is lower and the usage is no different.
Jīzǐ's (箕子) criticisms
began with the Tiānzǐ (天子),
but now extend to the commoners."
"In ancient times,
they roasted millet and ate wild grains,
and split pork to feast together.
Later,
when villagers drank wine,
the elders had layered dishes,
and the young stood and ate,
with one sauce and one meat dish,
merely a communal drink.
Later still,
when guests were invited to weddings,
they served bean soup and plain rice,
sliced fish and cooked meat.
Now, commoners' feasts,
have stacked dishes,
and roasted meats fill the tables,
with turtle stew and carp sashimi,
fawn eggs, quail, oranges, and Chinese raisins,
salted fish sauce, sweet wine, and pickled sauces,
a variety of ingredients and mixed flavors."
"In ancient times,
commoners plowed and sowed in spring and summer,
and harvested and stored in autumn and winter,
toiling from dawn to dusk,
and continuing into the night.
The *Shī* (詩) says:
'During the day, you gather thatch,
and at night, you twist ropes,
quickly ascend the roof,
and begin to sow all kinds of grains.'
They did not rest except during the *lólà* (膢臘) festivals,
and had no wine or meat except during sacrifices.
Now, wedding feasts
follow one after another,
dissipating half of the day's energy from hangovers,
abandoning work to follow the revelry,
without considering the days when they will be without."
"In ancient times,
commoners ate coarse grains and weeds,
and had no wine or meat except during village drinking ceremonies, *lólà* (膢臘) festivals, and sacrifices.
Therefore, the zhūhóu (諸侯) did not kill cattle or sheep without reason,
and the dàfū (大夫) and shì (士) did not kill dogs or pigs without reason.
Now, the people in neighborhoods and towns,
those who sell and slaughter,
kill and cook animals without cause,
gathering in the open fields.
They carry grain to these gatherings,
and return with meat.
The meat of one pig
equals the harvest of a middle-aged person,
and fifteen *dǒu* (斗) of grain
is half a month's food for a grown man."
"In ancient times,
commoners offered fish and beans as sacrifices,
and in spring and autumn, they maintained their ancestral shrines.
The shì (士) had one shrine,
and the dàfū (大夫) had three,
and they regularly performed the Five Sacrifices,
and there were no sacrifices outside the home.
Now, the wealthy pray at famous peaks,
and venerate mountains and rivers,
slaughtering cattle and beating drums,
with actors and dancers performing.
Those of moderate means build facing the road to the south,
with water features and elevated terraces,
slaughtering sheep and killing dogs,
playing the *sè* (瑟) and blowing the *shēng* (笙).
The poor offer chickens and pigs with five spices,
and make offerings to protect and ward off misfortune,
in public fields."
"In ancient times,
people sought happiness through virtue,
so their sacrifices were generous.
They sought good fortune through benevolence and righteousness,
so they rarely consulted divination.
Nowadays, common people are lax in their conduct but seek help from spirits,
negligent in ritual but devoted to sacrifices,
disrespectful to relatives but value power,
extremely superstitious and believe in lucky days,
listen to deceitful words and hope to gain,
offer real things in exchange for illusory blessings.
"In ancient times,
a *jūnzǐ* (君子) diligently pondered his virtue day and night;
a common person diligently pondered his strength from dawn till dusk.
Therefore, a *jūnzǐ* (君子) did not eat without working,
and a common person did not eat without laboring.
Nowadays, common people embellish false conduct and practice deceit,
acting as shamans and invocators for the people,
to obtain offerings and thank-you gifts,
with brazen faces and glib tongues,
some even making a career and becoming rich,
so those who are afraid of work
abandon their original professions to study such practices.
Thus, there are shamans in every street and lane,
and invocators in every neighborhood.
"In ancient times,
there were no beds with *gàngmán* (杠樠),
nor desks of *chuángyí* (床栘).
Later generations,
commoners would use branches for the bed frame,
and birch bark for the bed boards.
Scholars did not use finished materials,
and high officials only used reeds and rushes.
Now the rich have embroidered and painted curtains and screens,
with painted screens and inlaid legs.
Those of middling status have brocade and fine silk hung high,
with painted and lacquered surfaces.
"In ancient times,
people used animal skins and grass mats,
without adding fine mats or cushions,
or using fine *zhānrú* (旃蒻).
Later,
high officials and scholars added woven grass edges to their mats,
and used plain rush mats and simple rushes.
Commoners only used grass mats tied with cords,
and simple rush mats and coarse *qújú* (蘧蒢).
Now the rich have embroidered mats and *díróu* (翟柔),
with beds adorned with cattails.
Those of middling status use worn leather instead of *zhān* (旃),
and sit on worn rush mats.
"In ancient times,
people did not buy cooked food,
nor did they buy food from the market.
Later,
there were butchers and wine sellers,
selling only wine, dried meat, fish, and salt.
Now cooked food is displayed everywhere,
with delicacies arranged like a market,
work is neglected and people become lazy,
food must be in season,
with steamed piglet and leek omelets,
dog sausage and horse penis,
fried fish and sliced liver,
pickled lamb and cold chicken,
churned mare's milk and yeast wine,
preserved dried stomach and salted tripe,
boiled lamb and bean offerings,
fried chicken embryos and wild goose soup,
stinky abalone and sweet gourds,
cooked fine grains and barbarian roast.
"In ancient times,
people used earthen drums and clay-tipped drumsticks,
struck wood and rubbed stones,
to express their joy fully.
Later,
high officials had wind and percussion instruments,
and scholars had *qín* (琴) and *sè* (瑟).
In the past,
at folk wine gatherings,
each followed local customs,
playing zithers and earthen drums.
There were no sophisticated melodies,
or complex musical variations.
Now the rich have bells, drums, and complete orchestras,
with numerous troupes of singers.
Those of middling status play the *yú* (竽) and tune the *sè* (瑟),
performing *Zhèng* (鄭) dances and *Zhào* (趙) songs.
"In ancient times,
clay coffins held the corpse,
and wooden boards surrounded it,
enough to contain the body,
and store the hair and teeth.
Later,
paulownia coffins were not ornamented,
and painted outer coffins were not carved.
Now the rich have embroidered walls and mortise-and-tenon construction.
Those of middling status have *zǐ* (梓) coffins and *pián* (楩) outer coffins,
and the poor paint rough clothes,
and use silk bags and brocade pouches.
"In ancient times,
funerary objects had form but no substance,
to show the people they were not for practical use.
Later,
there were stores of pickled sauces,
paulownia horses and clay figures for offerings,
but the items were incomplete.
Now, large sums of money are buried,
and the objects are like those for the living.
The commandery and state conscript laborers,
using undressed mulberry and pliable wood to make model carts and oarlocks,
even the common person lacks a proper collar,
but the paulownia figures wear fine silk and brocade.
"In ancient times,
there was no burial mound or planting of trees,
the *fǎnyú* (反虞) sacrifice was performed in the bedchamber,
with no altar or dwelling,
or position in the ancestral hall.
Later,
there were burial mounds,
the commoner's grave was half a fathom,
and its height could be concealed.
Now the rich pile up earth to form mountains,
and plant trees to form forests,
with connected terraces and pavilions,
creating viewing platforms and adding towers.
Those of middling status have ancestral halls and private chambers,
with enclosing walls and screen walls.
"In ancient times,
when a neighbor had a funeral,
people did not pound grain together,
nor sing in the lanes.
When Kǒngzǐ (孔子) ate beside someone in mourning,
he never ate his fill,
and if he wept that day,
he did not sing.
Now, the common people use the occasion of someone's funeral to seek wine and meat,
hoping to sit for a short while and demand something,
singing, dancing, and acting,
engaging in continuous laughter and theatrical performances.
"In ancient times,
the relationship between men and women was highly valued,
but the clothing for weddings
was not recorded in detail.
After the Yú (虞) and
Xià (夏) dynasties,
the outer garment was plain cloth, the inner was silk,
with bone hairpins and ivory earrings,
and the wives of feudal lords added brocade and a simple outer garment.
Now the rich wear leather coats of red fox,
and elaborate jade pendants and belts.
Those of middling status wear long robes with crossed lapels,
jade ornaments and hairpins and earrings.
"In ancient times,
people devoted their love to the living,
and expressed their grief fully for the dead.
Therefore, the sages created regulations,
not adding them arbitrarily.
Now people fail to show love and respect in life,
but compete with extravagance in death;
even without feelings of sorrow,
those who have lavish burials and heavy offerings
are praised as filial,
their names made famous in the world,
and their glory is established in custom.
Thus, the common people emulate each other,
even to the point of demolishing houses and selling property.
"In ancient times,
marital harmony between husband and wife,
with one son and one daughter,
completed the way of the household.
Later,
a scholar had one concubine,
a high official had two,
and a feudal lord had nieces and younger sisters, no more than nine women.
Now feudal lords have hundreds,
high officials have dozens,
those of middling status have attendants,
and the rich have rooms full.
Therefore, women are sometimes left lonely and miss their prime,
and men sometimes die without a match.
“In ancient times,
years of famine were supplemented by
years of plenty,
maintaining the old customs without alteration.
Now, the craftsmen change their methods, and the officials have different intentions,
ruining successful works
to conceal their purposes.
Their intentions are focused on achievements,
and their efforts are aimed at appearances.
They accumulate achievements to buy praise,
not caring about the people's urgent needs.
The fields are not cultivated,
but they decorate pavilions;
the settlements are in ruins,
but they heighten their city walls.
“In ancient times,
human labor was not wasted on birds and beasts,
nor was the people’s wealth taken to feed dogs and horses;
therefore, wealth increased, and labor was sufficient.
Now, fierce beasts and strange insects cannot be used for plowing,
yet those who should be plowing are made to feed them.
The common people sometimes lack complete coarse clothing,
while dogs and horses wear embroidered garments;
the people sometimes have no grain to eat,
while birds and beasts eat fine rice and meat.
“In ancient times,
the rulers revered their duties and loved their inferiors,
employing the people at the proper times.
The Son of Heaven regarded the empire as his family,
and servants each supplied their public duties at their appointed times—
this is a common principle of ancient and modern times.
Now, the government offices raise many slaves,
who sit idle, receiving food and clothing,
privately engaging in business
for illicit profit.
Their labor is not fully utilized,
and the government loses revenue.
The common people may not have even a dù-shāo of savings,
while government slaves accumulate hundreds of gold coins;
the people work from dawn till dusk without rest,
while slaves idly stroll about.
“In ancient times,
the close were favored and the distant were kept at a distance,
those of the same kind were valued, and those of different kinds were despised.
There were no rewards without merit
and no support for the useless.
Now, the Mán and
Mò barbarians have no merit,
yet they live freely in government housing,
in spacious houses and large mansions,
receiving food and clothing without working.
The common people sometimes lack enough for morning and evening meals,
while the Mán and Yí barbarians are sated with wine and meat.
The people toil in sweat,
while the Mán and
Yí barbarians sit with legs crossed, sprawling.
“In ancient times,
commoners wore coarse hemp and grass sandals,
using thin silk and tanned leather only.
Later,
even the lowest could not borrow,
wearing leather shoes and boots.
Now, the wealthy wear leather from famous craftsmen,
light and delicate,
with silk lining and silk laces,
with elaborate trimming.
Those of middling status wear sandals made of kuǎi and jū reeds from Dèng-lǐ.
Even lowly servants and maids
wear leather sandals and silk shoes.
Those who walk wear hemp sandals with silk ties.
“The ancient sages exerted their bodies to nourish their spirits,
tempered their desires and suited their emotions,
honored Heaven and revered Earth,
practiced virtue and acted with benevolence.
Therefore, Heaven was pleased,
prolonging their reigns and enriching their years.
Thus, Yáo had beautiful eyebrows and high spirit,
reigning for a hundred years.
Qín Shǐhuáng, however, studied strange anomalies,
believed in omens,
and sent Lú Shēng to seek Xiànméngāo,
and Xú Shì and others to search the sea for the elixir of immortality.
At that time,
the scholars of Yān and Qí
abandoned their plows
and vied to speak of deities and immortals.
Magicians then flocked to Xiányáng by the thousands,
claiming that immortals ate gold and drank pearls,
and thus their lives would be as secure as Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, he frequently toured the Five Peaks
and the coastal palaces,
seeking deities and the like of Pénglái.
He frequently visited commanderies and counties,
the rich contributing with their wealth,
and the poor building roadsides.
Afterward,
the lesser ones fled and escaped,
while the greater ones hid;
the officials pursued and searched harshly,
without reason.
Beside the famous palaces,
huts and dwellings lay in ruins,
with no seedlings growing or trees standing;
the people lost heart,
and more than half resented and yearned.
The *Book of Documents* says:
‘Sacrifices have many rites;
rites that do not reach the objects are not sacrifices.’
Therefore, sages do not embrace in themselves what is not benevolent and righteous,
nor do they employ before them what is not the right way.
That is why the former emperors executed Wén Chéng and
Wǔ Lì,
and Xuān Dì established schools,
befriending the loyal and good,
intending to cut off the sources of strangeness and evil
and to illuminate the path to utmost virtue.
“Extravagance in palaces
is a detriment to forests and trees.
Elaborate carvings on utensils
are a detriment to finances.
Luxurious clothing
is a detriment to cloth.
Dogs and horses eating people's food
are a detriment to grain.
Self-indulgence
is a detriment to fish and meat.
Unrestrained spending
is a detriment to the treasury.
Unchecked waste
is a detriment to the fields.
Unrestrained funerals and sacrifices
are a detriment to life.
Destroying accomplishments and changing customs harms work,
and allowing merchants to rise above farming harms agriculture.
Thus, a single cup requires the labor of a hundred people,
and a single screen requires the work of ten thousand people;
the harm they cause is indeed great!
The eyes are indulged in five colors,
the ears are captivated by five tones,
the body seeks utmost comfort,
the mouth seeks utmost sweetness and crispness.
Efforts are expended on the useless,
and wealth is exhausted on the unnecessary.
The appetites of the mouth and stomach cannot be satisfied in excess.
Therefore, a state’s illness accumulates until insufficiency leads to governmental negligence,
and a person’s illness accumulates until insufficiency endangers the body.”
The Prime Minister said:
“What can be done to remedy accumulated insufficiency?”
6.2 *Saving from Want*
The Worthy and Good replied:
“To correct the crooked, one must go past straightness;
to remedy extravagance, one must use frugality.
In the past,
when Yàn Zǐ was the prime minister of Qí,
he wore a fox-fur coat for thirty years.
If the people are extravagant,
show them frugality;
if the people are frugal,
show them propriety.
If the ministers and high officials and their descendants
could truly reduce carriages,
moderate clothing,
personally practice frugality,
lead by simplicity,
abolish parks and ponds,
reduce fields and residences,
have nothing to do with the marketplaces within,
and have nothing to do with the mountains and lakes without,
so that farmers can apply their labor,
and women can devote themselves to their work;
if this is done,
then the qi and pulse will be harmonious,
and there will be no illness of accumulated insufficiency.”
The Daìfū said:
"An orphan speaks of filial piety;
a cripple speaks of a walking stick;
a poor man speaks of benevolence;
a lowly man speaks of governance.
It is easy to comment on matters that don't concern oneself;
it is easy to agree with opinions from the sidelines;
but when one is in charge, things become chaotic.
Thus, Gōngsūn Hóng wore a hemp cloth covering,
and Ní Kuān wore a plain robe,
dressing like servants;
eating like common laborers.
Huáinán rebelled internally,
the Mán and Yí were violent externally,
bandits and thieves were not suppressed,
luxury was not restrained;
they were like witches in a year of plague,
only able to flap their mouths and ears,
how could they remedy deficiencies and govern well?"
The Xiánliáng said:
"In the time of Emperor Gāo,
Xiāo Hé and Cáo Cān served as ministers,
and Téng Gōng and Guàn Yīng and others were high officials,
they were truly abundant in talent and wisdom.
During the reigns of Emperor Wén and Emperor Jǐng,
and at the beginning of the Jìanyuán era,
the high officials still contended to uphold righteousness.
Since then,
many catered to the emperor's will and desires,
few dared to speak frankly and directly criticize to his face,
using public office for private gain.
Thus, the Chancellor of Wǔ'ān contested over gardens and fields,
arguing right and wrong before the ruler;
if a nine-story tower collapses,
Gōngshū Zǐ cannot right it;
if the court is wicked,
Yī Yǐn and Wàng Zài cannot restore it.
Therefore, Chancellor Gōngsūn and
Daìfū Ní cultivated the Way with humility,
sharing their salaries to support the worthy,
humbling themselves to befriend scholars,
and their achievements were clearly established,
yet their strength was insufficient,
and there was no successor like Xíngrén Zǐchǎn.
And Gě Yì,
Péng Hóu, and others
ruined their accomplishments,
threw their principles into chaos,
destroyed their guesthouses and assembly halls,
turning them into horse stables and women's quarters,
lacking the proper etiquette for supporting scholars,
while still displaying an arrogant manner,
shame and integrity declined, and they contended for profit.
Therefore, fertile fields and spacious houses,
leave the people with nowhere to go;
those who are shameless in pursuing profit fill the court,
and those who arrange fields and livestock spread throughout the prefectures and states,
acting oppressively and violently,
next to large mansions and giant houses,
the roads are almost impassable,
this is certainly difficult to cure and cannot be remedied by artisans."
The Daìfū flushed with anger,
and remained silent.
6.3 "Probing Stone Thirty-First"
The Chéngxiàng said:
"I have heard Zhèng the Elder say:
'When a gentleman corrects his countenance,
he keeps violence and disrespect at a distance;
when he expresses his words and manner,
he keeps vulgarity and treachery at a distance.'
Therefore, words can be recounted,
and actions can be emulated.
This is what the officials have long desired to witness.
If debaters of swordsmanship
and arguers of board games,
with grand countenance assist each other,
establishing power so as not to yield to each other,
causing the officials to be unable to accept the Xiánliáng's advice,
and the Xiánliáng
and Wénxué are burdened with a reputation for insolence,
I privately believe that this is unacceptable for the scholars.
Gōngsūn Lóng had a saying:
'The Way of debate is to argue,
therefore one cannot but focus one's attention;
focusing one's attention leads to mutual leniency,
mutual leniency leads to contention,
contending without yielding,
then descends into vulgarity.'
Now the officials are inhumane,
and also bear the burden of eating without contributing,
they have no way to further demand vindication and wash away the shame.
The Imperial Court recruits and recommends Xiánliáng
and Wénxué,
and even those who are close to the people and hold great office,
but I have yet to see that they can use a probing stone to heal the illnesses of the people."
The Xiánliáng said:
"Jiǎ Yī had a saying:
'If one speaks earnestly, then one's words are shallow and do not penetrate,
if one speaks profoundly, then one's words are jarring and miss the point.'
Therefore, it is said:
'How easy is it to speak?'
Speaking is already not easy,
how much more so is it to act?
This is why Hú Jiàn did not die a natural death,
and Wú Déjǐ almost did not escape disaster.
A proverb says:
'Five robbers seize one good man,
crooked wood hates a straight measuring line.'
Now if one wishes to apply the probing stone,
to clear blockages,
then I fear the troubles of Shèng Gōng
and Hú Jiàn,
if one carries probing stones and mugwort bags,
then one receives a reputation for incompetence.
'The wolf stumbles on its dewlap,
and bruises its tail.'
The path of the gentleman,
the way of acting and resting is certainly narrow.
This is why Zǐ Shí sighed."
6.4 "Eliminating Narrowness Thirty-Second"
The Daìfū said:
"A wise man dwells in a great forest,
and does not get lost when encountering wind and thunder.
A fool, even if he dwells on a flat, wide road,
is still confused and bewildered.
Now the Shǒu and
Xiàng, having personally received the symbols of authority and appointment,
preside over the multitude of a commandery,
which is the ancient position of a regional overseer.
They receive orders to act with authority,
governing thousands of *lǐ*,
without interference from within;
good and evil depend on themselves,
it is only because they are incapable,
how can the Way be narrow?"
Xiánliáng said:
"In ancient times, to advance scholars,
the countryside selected and the neighborhood chose,
discussing their talents,
and then they were given official positions,
and only after being competent in their duties were they given titles and emoluments.
Therefore, scholars cultivated themselves in their hometowns,
ascended to the imperial court,
their actions were evident in both obscurity and prominence,
and their brightness was manifestly apparent.
No worthy men were overlooked from a distance,
and no meritorious deeds, small or great, were omitted.
Thus, the virtuous were promoted and employed,
while the unworthy were dismissed and rejected.
Now, the way of officialdom is mixed and unselective,
the wealthy buy offices with their wealth,
and the brave shoot for merit with their lives.
Performers of acrobatics and those who jump over cauldrons
all end up filling official positions,
accumulating merit day by day,
and some even reach the position of high ministers.
They wear the green cords
and carry the silver tortoise,
wielding the power of life and death,
and controlling the fate of the common people.
If they are weak,
it is like using sheep to lead wolves,
chaos is certain.
If they are strong,
it is like giving a madman a sharp sword,
they will surely kill wantonly.
Therefore, in the past,
the common people of commanderies and kingdoms could not be governed even when working together,
and some even saw their necks sawn off and innocent people killed without redress.
To grasp the key principles in a wrong way,
only makes the chaos even worse.
In ancient times,
fiefs were granted to the virtuous and stipends given to the capable,
but no more than a hundred *lǐ*;
and within the hundred *lǐ* was the capital,
with boundaries no more than fifty,
yet it was still thought that the body of one man
was not bright enough to illuminate,
nor perceptive enough to understand,
so they established *qīng*,
*dàfū*,
and *shì* to assist him,
and only then was the governance complete.
Now, commandery governors and
chancellors may not be as virtuous as the ancient feudal lords,
yet they oversee the governance of a thousand *lǐ*,
and rule over the multitude of an entire commandery,
implementing the virtue of a sage ruler,
and wielding the power of life and death,
which is extremely important.
Only a benevolent man can shoulder this responsibility,
and only the right man can carry it out.
The order or chaos of one man's body
lies within himself;
a thousand *lǐ* will transform with him,
so it is impossible not to choose carefully.
Therefore, the ruler should have personal connections based on wealth,
but not base official appointments on personal connections;
determine rewards based on merit,
rank titles according to virtue,
promoting the good as if it were insufficient,
and dismissing the wicked as if they were enemies;
this is to prevent them from being undeserving and harming the common people.
Assisting the ruler's virtue
and opening the path for ministers
lies in selecting the virtuous and employing them appropriately,
and choosing capable governors and
chancellors before entrusting them with responsibility."
6.5 *Jí Tān Dì Sānshísān* (Dislike of Greed, Chapter Thirty-three)
The *dàfū* said:
"Indeed.
To be a doctor and yet be unskilled,
is to demand excessive gratitude.
To be an official and yet be largely corrupt,
is to further encroach upon the people.
Senior officials oppress petty officials,
and petty officials oppress the people.
Therefore, the worry is not about the lack of careful selection,
but about the difference between what is sought and what is obtained;
the worry is not about insufficiency,
but about insatiable greed."
Xiánliáng said:
"The ancient system of titles and stipends
was such that *qīng* and *dàfū* had enough to enrich the virtuous and generous scholars,
and scholars had enough to provide for themselves and their clans;
the common people who served as officials
