had enough to replace their farming and eat from their stipends.
Now, the petty officials' stipends are meager,
and the corvée labor of the commanderies and kingdoms
extends as far as the Three Metropolises;
grain and rice are expensive,
and it is not enough to support them.
If they live in their usual places, they lack clothing and food,
and if there is an emergency, they sell their livestock and abandon their livelihoods.
It is not only that,
but the corvée officials are sent to each other,
and the official courts pursue and arrest people;
the petty accountants and legal officials
go around begging and borrowing,
and the senior officials encroach and extort;
the upper prefectures demand from the lower counties,
and the counties demand from the townships,
so where can the townships get it from?
As the saying goes,
'The flow of bribes is like water flowing downwards,
it will not stop until it is exhausted.'
Now, the great rivers drink from the vast sea,
and the vast sea receives them,
yet one expects the streams and valleys to yield their flowing water;
the integrity of the hundreds of officials
is unattainable.
If you want the shadow to be straight, straighten the object that casts it;
if you want those below to be honest, start with yourself.
Therefore, greed and baseness lie in the leaders, not in those below,
and teaching and guidance lie in the government, not in the people."
The *dàfū* said:
"Virtue and wickedness have substance,
and greed and baseness have nature;
a gentleman can purify himself internally but cannot completely teach others.
Therefore, Zhōu Gōng was not able to correct Guǎn and
Cài's wickedness,
and Zǐchǎn was not able to correct Dèng Xī's falsehood.
If internally they do not follow the teachings of their fathers and elder brothers,
and externally they do not fear the punishments of the law,
then Zhōu Gōng and
Zǐchǎn cannot transform them,
certainly.
Now, for each and every case, you blame the officers in charge;
how can the officers in charge bind their hands and feet and prevent them from doing wrong?"
Xiánliáng said:
"If a team of four horses is not well-trained, it is the fault of the driver.
If the people are not well-governed, it is the crime of the officers in charge.
The *Chūnqiū* criticizes and satirizes, but it does not reach the common people;
it blames their leaders.
Therefore, in ancient times, when a *dàfū* was about to face execution,
music and women were not enjoyed,
even if the punishment was justified,
they would still sigh and lament three times.
They were ashamed of their inability to transform them and grieved for their incompleteness.
If the government's teachings are obscure and unclear,
and the people stumble and fall without being helped,
it is like a baby approaching a well,
and one listens as it falls in.
If this is the case,
then what is the point of being the parents of the people?
Therefore, a gentleman is eager to teach,
and lenient in punishment.
Punish one to correct a hundred,
and kill one to warn ten thousand.
That is why Zhōu Gōng executed Guǎn and
Cài, and Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī.
Once punishment is applied,
the people will follow propriety and righteousness.
The influence of those above on those below
is like the wind bending the grass,
and none will fail to follow the teachings.
Why bind them one by one?"
6.6 *Hòu Xíng Dì Sānshísì* (Postponing Punishments, Chapter Thirty-four)
The *dàfū* said:
"The gentlemen of ancient times
cherished the good and hated the bad.
A ruler does not harbor wicked people,
and a farmer does not harbor useless seedlings.
Useless seedlings
are harmful to the seedlings;
useless people
are traitors to the people.
Uproot one harmful thing and many seedlings will thrive,
punish one wicked person and ten thousand people will be pleased.
Even Zhōu Gōng and
Kǒngzǐ could not release the punishments and use the wicked.
If a family has thieves,
the utensils will not stay in place,
how much more so with a thieving people!
The people are arrogant with love but listen to punishment.
Therefore, punishment
is for correcting the people,
and hoeing is for distinguishing the seedlings."
The Worthy and Good said:
"In ancient times,
they valued education to guide the people,
and enlightened rulers used laws to rectify punishments.
Punishment in governance
is like using a whip in driving a chariot.
A skilled charioteer cannot drive without a whip,
nor can he have a whip and not use it.
Sages use laws to perfect education,
and when education is complete, punishment is not needed.
Thus, authority is stern but not deadly,
and laws are established but not violated.
Now, if we abandon our guiding principles and fail to uphold them,
and destroy our propriety and righteousness without being able to prevent wrongdoing,
the people will fall into confusion,
and then we hunt them down with punishments.
This is like opening the pen,
and shooting poisonous arrows at them.
It will not stop until it is finished.
Zēng Zǐ said:
'When those above lose their way,
the people have long been scattered.
If you understand their situation,
you should pity and sympathize, not rejoice.'
Not lamenting the people's lack of order,
but boasting of one's ability to uncover wrongdoing,
is like a hunter rejoicing when he sees birds and beasts caught in his nets.
Today, those who are being punished under Heaven
do not necessarily have the wickedness of Guǎn,
and Cài,
or the deceit of Dèng Xī,
I fear that the grain will be exhausted without distinguishing between weeds,
and the people will deceive without being governed.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'If a man is not benevolent,
to hate him excessively
is disorder.'
Therefore, if the people are in disorder, reflect on the government;
if the government is in disorder, reflect on oneself;
if one is upright, the world will be at peace.
Thus, a virtuous person praises good and has compassion for those who are not capable,
extends grace to criminals,
enriches the poor with virtue,
grants favor with joy,
and does not delight in administering punishment."
6.7 《Shòu Shí Dì Sānshíwǔ》
The Grand Master said:
"Sharing the land,
living in this world,
if there are no natural disasters or epidemics,
and one is still poor,
it is due to laziness or extravagance;
if there are no extraordinary side incomes,
and one is still wealthy and sufficient,
it is due to frugality or hard work.
Now you say to grant favor with joy,
and not to delight in administering punishment;
this is to pity the worthless,
and to support the lazy and extravagant.
Therefore, giving recklessly is not benevolence,
and being kind to the wicked is not righteousness."
The Worthy and Good said:
"In the golden ages of the Three Dynasties, there was no sprout of disorder,
because of education;
in the degenerate times of the Xià and Shāng Dynasties, there were no obedient people,
because of the customs.
Therefore, the rulers established schools,
elucidated teachings,
to guide their people,
and when governance and education were in harmony,
they were inherently benevolent and understood goodness.
Thus, when propriety and righteousness are established,
the farmers yield in the fields;
when propriety and righteousness are destroyed,
gentlemen contend in court.
When people contend, there is disorder,
and when there is disorder, the world is unequal,
hence there are those who are poor and those who are rich.
When there is wealth, benevolence arises,
and when there is abundance, contention ceases.
Knocking on people's doors at dusk,
asking for water and fire,
the greedy do not begrudge,
why?
Because they have plenty.
If governing were to make grain as accessible as water and fire,
how could the people not be benevolent!"
The Grand Master said:
"Those who gamble and race
are all sons of wealthy families,
not those who are in need.
Therefore, when the people are affluent, they become presumptuous and extravagant,
when they are rich, they become proud and luxurious,
sitting lazily,
and rising to do wrong,
I have not seen them become benevolent.
If one does not work hard in their affairs,
and does not use their wealth frugally,
even if they have wealth like water and fire,
poverty can be waited for to stand.
If one does not care for the people,
even if the officials help them with plowing and weaving,
can they be sufficient?"
The Worthy and Good said:
"When the Duke of Zhōu assisted Chéng Wáng,
the people were affluent and happy,
and the country had no poor,
it was not by substituting their plowing and weaving.
Ease their fields,
lighten their taxes,
and the people will be rich.
Those above can provide for their lords and parents,
those below will have no worry of hunger and cold,
then education can be completed.
The *Analects* says:
'Since they are already rich,
what more should be added?'
It says: 'Teach them.'
Teach them with virtue,
regulate them with propriety,
then the people will move towards righteousness and follow goodness,
none will fail to be filial at home and fraternal abroad,
then how could there be extravagance or violence?"
Guǎnzi said:
'When the granaries are full, they know etiquette;
when the people are sufficient, they know honor and shame.'
Therefore, it is easy to lead a wealthy people to propriety,
but difficult to lead them to the Dao."
The Grand Master said:
"The government's relationship with the people
is like that of a loving father with his son:
how can they not be faithfully taught?
How can they be loved without being labored?
Therefore, in spring, they personally plow to encourage farming,
and provide relief loans to aid the insufficient,
dredging water,
granting lenient bonds,
to make the people focus on the seasons.
Receiving grace and being blessed,
yet still being poor and destitute,
how difficult it is to lead them to the Dao!"
The Worthy and Good said:
"In ancient times,
in spring, they inspected farming to supplement the insufficient,
in autumn, they inspected the harvest to aid those who were lacking.
If the people are diligent in managing their wealth, then contributions and taxes are light;
if the people are diligent in their labor, then construction projects are rare.
Caring for the people's labor,
not taking it for even a moment,
therefore, Shào Bó listened to cases beneath the sweet pear tree,
to avoid interfering with agricultural affairs.
Now, when timely rains bring moisture,
seeds are suspended and cannot be sown,
and autumn crops fall on the fields and cannot be harvested.
The fields are barren,
but abandoned land becomes a marketplace,
only after the spring equinox,
do they hang green banners and whip clay oxen,
this is hardly the intention of an enlightened ruler encouraging farming,
nor what the spring decrees are about."
6.8 《Shuǐ Hàn Dì Sānshíliù》
The Grand Master said:
"Yǔ and
Tāng were sage rulers,
Hòujì and
Yī Yǐn were virtuous ministers,
yet there were disasters of flood and drought.
Floods and droughts
are caused by Heaven,
famine and abundance
are the movements of Yin and Yang,
not by human effort.
Therefore, the number of the annual star,
when in the Yang, is drought,
when in the Yin, is flood.
There is a famine every six years,
and a major crop failure every twelve years.
This is the way of Heaven,
it is hardly the sole fault of the officials."
The Worthy and Good said:
"In ancient times,
if the government had virtue,
then the *yīn* and *yáng* were harmonious,
the stars and constellations were in order,
and wind and rain were timely.
Therefore, if one cultivates oneself internally,
one's reputation is heard externally,
if good deeds are done below,
blessings respond from above.
*Zhōu Gōng* recorded events and the world was at peace,
the country had no premature deaths,
and the years had no famines.
At that time,
the rain didn't break the soil clods,
the wind didn't rustle the branches,
it rained once every ten days,
and the rain always came at night.
Whether hills or lowlands, all were fertile.
The *Shī* says:
'Dense clouds gather,
bringing abundant rain.'
Now, without examining the reasons for this,
to say
'it is the operation of *yīn* and *yáng*,'
is something I have not heard.
*Mèng Zǐ* said:
'In the fields there are starving corpses,
and you do not know to gather them;
the dogs and pigs eat human food,
and you do not know to restrain them;
you act as parents of the people,
and the people die of hunger,
and you say,
'It is not I,
it is the year,'
how is this different from killing them with a knife,
and saying,
'It is not I,
it is the weapon?'
The present task
lies in eliminating the suffering from hunger and cold,
abolishing salt and iron monopolies, withdrawing special privileges,
distributing land,
encouraging fundamental occupations,
promoting the cultivation of mulberry and hemp,
and maximizing the land's productivity.
Reduce expenditures and economize on resources,
and the people will naturally become rich.
If you do so,
then you will not worry about floods and droughts,
and bad years will not be a burden."
The Grandee said:
"Those who offer counsel value concise language and clear points,
understandable to the common people,
avoiding elaborate and dense wording,
because verbose speech hinders the officials' plans to transform customs,
and it becomes like household chatter.
*Táo Zhū*'s business practices
had different approaches to fundamental and peripheral industries,
with numerous affairs within the family,
yet his ways of managing his livelihood were comprehensive.
Now, the central government casts farming tools,
making the people focus on fundamental occupations,
not engaging in peripheral ones,
so that there will be no suffering from hunger and cold.
What harm do salt and iron do that they must be abolished?"
The Worthy and Good said:
"Agriculture
is the great undertaking of the world,
and iron implements
are of great use to the people.
If implements are convenient,
then less effort is required and more work is accomplished,
and farmers happily engage in their work and are encouraged to contribute.
If implements are not sufficient,
then the fields become barren,
grains are not planted,
little effort is made,
and half the work is lost.
The difference between convenient and inconvenient implements
can result in a tenfold or double increase in work accomplished.
The central government forges iron implements,
but mostly makes large implements,
striving to meet the required quota,
without providing for the needs of the people.
The people's implements are dull and worn,
unable to cut grass effectively,
and therefore farmers work hard,
but harvest little,
and the common people suffer because of this."
The Grandee said:
"Soldiers and artisans
work on public affairs for the central government daily,
resources are abundant,
and implements are complete.
When families gather,
they are limited by time and diligent in use,
but the iron is not thoroughly smelted,
and hardness and flexibility are not harmonized.
Therefore, the officials request to monopolize salt and iron,
to unify its use,
and to equalize its price,
in order to benefit the people both publicly and privately.
Even the governance of *Yú* and *Xià*
cannot be better than this.
If the officials clarify their teachings,
and the artisans perfect their work,
then hardness and flexibility will be harmonized,
and implements will be convenient.
In this case, how can the people suffer?
And how can the farmers be in distress?"
The Worthy and Good said:
"Soldiers and artisans!
When the people were allowed to rent equipment to cast iron and boil salt,
the price of salt was the same as that of the five grains,
and the implements were harmonious, sharp, and useful.
Now, the central government makes iron implements,
mostly of poor quality,
spending without thrift,
the soldiers are troubled and their efforts are not fully utilized.
Families unite,
fathers and sons work together,
each striving to make good implements,
and poorly made implements are not collected.
When farming is urgent,
they transport them along the paths between the fields.
The people trade with each other,
exchanging wealth, goods, grains, and new currency;
sometimes they lend to the people,
not abandoning their work.
They acquire farming tools,
each getting what they desire.
The conscript labor is reduced and economized,
and the central government uses the soldiers for other tasks,
repairing roads and bridges,
making things convenient for the people.
Now, monopolizing the source,
and unifying the price,
the implements are mostly hard and rough,
and there is no choice between good and bad.
The officials are often not present,
and the implements are hard to obtain.
Families cannot store much,
and storing too much causes anxiety.
If they miss the season of fertile soil,
and travel far to buy farming tools,
they will be late for the good time.
When the prices of salt and iron are high,
the people are inconvenienced.
Poor people may plow with wood and weed with their hands,
using dirt clods for clod breakers and eating plain food.
The iron officials sell implements that are not sold or are partly given to the people as taxes.
The soldiers' work is not properly presented,
and they are sometimes ordered to help.
Requisitions are unlimited,
and the conscript labor is equally burdensome,
therefore the people suffer from it.
In ancient times,
in a town of a thousand households,
or a family with a hundred carriages,
potters, smelters, artisans, and merchants,
the needs of the four classes of people,
were sufficient to support each other.
Therefore, farmers do not leave their fields,
yet have enough farming tools,
artisans do not cut down trees, yet have enough timber,
potters and smelters do not till the fields, yet have enough millet,
the people each get what is convenient for them,
and the ruler has nothing to do.
Therefore, the king focuses on fundamentals and does not engage in peripherals,
removes extravagance,
eliminates carving and ornamentation,
immersing the people in ritual,
showing the people simplicity,
therefore the people focus on fundamentals and do not engage in peripherals."
7.1 *Chóng Lǐ* (Esteeming Ritual) 37
The Grandee said:
"To decorate tables and staffs,
to embellish wine vessels and stands,
is for guests,
not for the host.
To display strange and unusual things
is to present them to the four barbarian tribes,
not for the people.
When a family has a guest,
they still have the entertainment of performers and unusual transformations,
much more so for the government of a county!
Therefore, to array feathered banners
and display war horses
is to show power and might.
Rare insects and precious oddities
are to show embracing vast distances,
illuminating great virtue,
so that distant countries will all come."
The Worthy and Good said:
"A true king values rites and bestows virtue,
esteems benevolence and righteousness, and disparages strange forces;
therefore, the sage ignores and does not speak of them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Words of loyalty and trustworthiness,
conduct of sincerity and respect,
even in the lands of the Mán
and Mò barbarians,
cannot be abandoned.'
Now, the rulers of myriad distant countries who present tributes
cherish the magnificent virtue of the Son of Heaven
and wish to observe the rites and ceremonies of China.
Therefore, the Míngtáng hall and Bìyōng school are established to show them these,
the shields and axes are brandished,
and the *Yǎ*
and *Sòng*
are proclaimed to edify them.
Now, to display and boast of playthings and unused implements,
strange insects and un-raised beasts,
wrestling and other theatrical performances,
and dazzling objects
is quite different from how the Duke of Zhōu treated distant lands.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu conducted himself with humility to associate with humble men,
and upheld rites and virtue to condescend to the world.
Therefore, he declined the tribute of Yuèshāng,
showing the rites of respect and deference.
Afterwards, he brought them into the temple of King Wén,
showing the rites of great filial piety.
Their eyes witnessed the solemn appearance of shields and axes,
their ears heard the clear songs of the *Yǎ*
and *Sòng*,
their hearts were filled with utmost virtue,
and they happily returned.
This is why the four barbarian tribes admired righteousness and submitted internally,
not because they needed multiple interpreters and Dí and Dī emissaries to come and see fierce beasts and bears.
Rhinoceroses, elephants, *sì*, and tigers
are plentiful in the southern barbarian regions.
Mules, donkeys, and Bactrian camels
are commonly raised by the northern barbarians.
What China lacks,
foreign countries consider cheap.
The southern Yuè use peacocks to adorn their doorways.
Beside Mount Kūn,
they use jade to ward off crows and magpies.
Now, what the nobles despise
is abundant to the people,
which is not a way to enrich China and illuminate great virtue.
The Suí and Hé pearls
are famous treasures of the world,
but they cannot secure safety in times of peril and existence in times of ruin.
Therefore, to convey virtue and demonstrate power
depends on worthy ministers and good advisors,
not on dogs, horses, or strange creatures.
Therefore, the sagely kings regard worthiness as treasure,
not pearls and jade.
In the past, Yàn Zǐ cultivated relationships at the tables and stands
and deflected attacks from a thousand *lǐ* away.
Those who are incapable,
even if they fill chests with Suí
and Hé pearls,
will not benefit existence or avert ruin."
The Grandee said:
"Yàn Zǐ served as prime minister to three rulers of Qí.
Cuī and Qìng were without morals,
kidnapping their ruler
and disrupting their state.
Duke Líng's state was besieged;
Duke Zhuāng was murdered;
and during the time of Duke Jǐng,
the people of Jìn came to attack,
seizing Chuídū,
capturing Línzī,
diminishing border towns,
burning city walls,
destroying palaces,
and taking all the treasures.
What attacks could he have deflected?
From this perspective,
the worthy and good are saying that
worthy men are treasures,
but gain and loss have no relative importance."
The Worthy and Good said:
"When Guǎn Zhòng left Lǔ and entered Qí,
Qí became hegemon and Lǔ was diminished.
It was not because he carried his people and returned to Qí.
Wǔ Zǐxū, carrying his bow, sought an audience with Hé Lǘ
and broke into the capital of Chǔ.
It was not because he carried his soldiers and went to Wú.
Therefore, the state where worthy men are located is important,
and the state they leave is weakened.
Chǔ had Zǐyù
and Déchén,
so Duke Wén gave them the best seat.
Yú had Gōng Zhīqí,
so Duke Xiàn of Jìn could not sleep.
Where worthy ministers are located,
those who dispel obstructions and open blocked pathways are far away.
Therefore, the *Chūnqiū* says:
'If mountains have tigers and leopards,
people will not gather mallows and beans.
If a state has worthy men,
its borders will not be harmed.'"
7.2 Chapter Thirty-Eight: Preparing for the Hú
The Grandee said:
"A vulgar saying says,
'Worthy men tolerate no insult.'
Speaking in worldly terms,
if a village has a troublemaker,
people still avoid him.
Now, the enlightened Son of Heaven is above,
but the Xióngnú openly act as bandits,
invading and disturbing the borders.
This is to trample upon benevolence and righteousness and gather coarse greens.
In the past, the Dí people invaded King Tài,
and the people of Kuāng feared Kǒngzǐ.
Therefore, the unbenevolent are
the bane of benevolence.
Therefore, the government sharpens its weapons to punish injustice
and sets up mechanisms to prepare for the unbenevolent."
The Worthy and Good said:
"The Xióngnú live in the midst of the desert,
in lands that do not produce food.
Heaven despises and abandons them.
They have no altars or ancestral halls,
no distinction between men and women.
They take the open fields as villages,
and the felt tent as homes.
They wear leather and furs,
eat meat and drink blood.
They gather at markets and roam,
herdsmen reside,
like the deer and elk of China.
Benevolent officials
seek righteousness from them,
demand rites from them,
causing China's weapons to not rest to this day.
Setting up defenses for thousands of *lǐ*,
this is what the *Tù Jū* poem satirizes.
Therefore, petty men are not the confidants and protectors of dukes and marquises."
The Grandee said:
"The Son of Heaven
is the parent of the world.
The multitudes of the four directions
righteously wish to be his subjects.
Yet, he still builds city walls,
sets up gates and bridges,
trains warriors,
and prepares defenses in the palace,
so as to avert calamities and prepare for the myriad regions.
Now, the Xióngnú have not yet submitted.
Even if there is no trouble,
how can we want to abandon our preparations?"
The Worthy and Good said:
"The reason why the King of Wú was captured by Yuè
was because he favored Yuè, which was near, and slighted those who were far away.
The reason why the Qín dynasty perished
was because it prepared against the Hú
and Yuè externally, but internally lost its governance.
To use the army externally
while governance decays internally,
preparations become a source of trouble
and increase the ruler's worries.
Therefore, if the ruler of men obtains the Way,
then those far and near will all follow and return to him;
King Wén was such a ruler.
If he does not obtain the Way,
then even his subjects will become enemies;
the King of Qín was such a ruler.
When civil virtue declines, martial prowess prevails.
When virtue flourishes, preparations are few."
An official said:
"In the past,
the four barbarians were all strong,
and together they were a scourge;
Cháoxiǎn crossed the border,
seizing Yān's eastern lands;
Dōngyuè crossed the East Sea,
plundering south of the Zhèjiāng River;
Nányuè invaded internally,
causing trouble for the officials;
the Dí, Bó,
Rǎn, Máng,
Xūitáng,
and the Kūnmíng tribes
disturbed Lǒngxī,
Bā, and Shǔ.
Now the three borders have been pacified,
only the northern border remains unsettled.
If we launch a single campaign, the Xiōngnú will be terrified,
and both the interior and exterior will be relieved of their defenses,
so why do you say it is unwise?"
The Worthy and Good said:
"In ancient times,
the virtuous established benevolence and cultivated righteousness,
to pacify their people,
so those nearby learned goodness,
and those far away submitted to it.
Therefore, when Kǒngzǐ served in Lǔ,
after serving for three months, he brought peace with Qí,
and after serving for three months, he brought peace with Zhèng,
striving to use virtue to pacify those nearby and soothe those far away.
At that time,
Lǔ had no difficulties with enemy states,
nor troubles with neighboring territories.
Powerful ministers changed their disloyal ways and became loyal and obedient,
so Jì Huán demolished the walls of his capital.
Great states feared righteousness and made peace,
and the people of Qí returned the fields of Yún,
Huān, and Gūiyīn.
Therefore, governing with virtue
is not only about averting harm and warding off attacks,
but also about obtaining what you desire without seeking it.
Now the reason why the people are restless
and the interior and exterior are not at peace
is the fault of the Xiōngnú.
They have no homes to defend within,
nor fields to accumulate outside,
following the good grass and sweet water for grazing,
the Xiōngnú do not change their ways,
and China is constantly disturbed.
They gather like wind and disperse like clouds,
if you approach them, they vanish,
if you strike them, they scatter,
so it is not something that can be accomplished in one generation."
The official said:
"In ancient times,
enlightened kings attacked the tyrannical and protected the weak,
stabilized the collapsing and supported the endangered.
Protecting the weak and supporting the endangered
pleases the rulers of small states;
attacking the tyrannical and stabilizing the collapsing
causes the innocent to submit.
If we do not launch campaigns,
then violence will not cease;
if we are not prepared,
then we are abandoning the common people to the enemy.
The *Chūnqiū* criticized the descendants of the feudal lords,
and condemned those who did not complete their guard duty.
Military service and guarding the borders
have existed since ancient times,
not only today."
The Worthy and Good said:
"The territory of the Xiōngnú is vast,
and their horses are swift and agile,
so they are easily roused to action.
If there is profit, they are like tigers dragging,
if there is sickness, they are like birds with broken wings,
avoiding the sharp points and taking advantage of fatigue;
sending out a small force is not enough to change the situation,
sending out a large force is more than the people can bear.
If the labor is burdensome, then strength is exhausted,
if spending is high, then wealth is depleted.
If these two do not cease,
then the people will harbor resentment.
This is why the Qín lost the hearts of the people
and their state.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven's domain was a thousand *lǐ*,
with corvée labor required within five hundred *lǐ*,
voices of encouragement could be heard,
and illnesses were cared for.
There were no expeditions that exceeded the time limit,
nor labor that exceeded the season.
Internally, they were attuned to the hearts of the people,
and affairs were suited to their strength.
Therefore, those who traveled were encouraged to work hard,
and those who stayed were content with their jobs.
Now the soldiers from Shāndōng with their horses and armor guarding the border counties
are extremely far away,
their bodies are in Hú and Yuè,
but their hearts are with their elderly mothers.
Elderly mothers weep,
wives grieve with resentment,
imagining their hunger and thirst,
thinking of their cold and suffering.
The *Shī* says:
'When I left,
the willows were gently swaying.
Now I return,
the rain and snow are falling heavily.
The road is slow and long,
I am both thirsty and hungry.
My heart is sorrowful,
but no one grieves for me.'
Therefore, the sages pitied their situation,
and were concerned about their long absence from their parents and wives,
exposed to the open fields,
living in cold and hardship,
so in the spring they sent messengers to reward them,
and promoted those who had been dismissed from their posts,
to show compassion for the distant people and comfort the elderly mothers.
The virtue and kindness were very great,
but the officials did not properly carry out their duties and follow the orders to care for them,
or even insulted the soldiers,
bartering with them,
forcing them to work together,
treating them unjustly.
Therefore, the soldiers lost their positions,
and the elderly mothers and wives felt resentment.
Bójī of Sòng grieved and worried, and the state of Sòng burned,
a concubine of Lǔ was dissatisfied, and the Lǔ palace suffered disaster.
Now those in the world who are dissatisfied
are not only the women of the western palace,
but also the elderly mothers of Sòng.
The *Chūnqiū* recorded the mobilization of troops,
emphasizing the importance of the people.
The people of Sòng surrounded Chánggé,
criticizing the long service.
The virtuous must be mindful of this."
The official remained silent and did not reply.
7.3 "Performing Duties, Chapter Thirty-Nine"
The Prime Minister said:
"The Way of the former kings
has been lost for a long time and is difficult to restore,
the words of the Worthy and Good
are profound and difficult to implement.
To praise the high conduct of the supreme sages,
and speak of the beautiful words of utmost virtue,
is not something that can be achieved in the present age.
I wish to hear about the urgent tasks of today,
that can be implemented in government;
so that the people are all sufficient in clothing and food,
without the worry of poverty;
the wind and rain are timely,
the five grains are ripe,
and locusts do not arise;
the world is peaceful and happy,
and bandits do not rise up;
those who have fled return,
each returning to their fields and homes;
the officials are all honest and upright,
respectfully performing their duties,
and all people attain their proper place."
The Worthies said:
"Mèngzǐ said:
'The Way of Yáo and
Shùn
is not far from people;
it is simply that people do not think about it.'
The *Shī* says:
'I sought her and could not get her,
And waking and sleeping I was thinking about her.'
If one seeks as in the *Guān Jū*,
and loves virtue as in the *Hé Guǎng*,
what failure to achieve could there be?
Therefore, the high mountain is looked up to,
and the great road is followed.
Though one cannot reach it,
one is not far from the Way.'
Yán Yuān said:
'What kind of man was Shùn?
What kind of man was I?'
If one thinks of the worthy and admires the capable,
and follows goodness without ceasing,
then the customs of Chéng and
Kāng can be attained,
and the Way of Táng and
Yú can be reached.
The dukes and ministers do not think about it;
how far away is the Way of the former kings?
Qí Huán Gōng used the feudal lords to think about kingly government,
and worried about the Zhōu House,
rectified the difficulties of the various Xià states,
pacified the rebellions of the Ǐ and
Dí peoples,
preserved the dying and restored the extinct,
and his trustworthiness and righteousness were greatly practiced,
becoming evident throughout the world.
At the assembly of Shàolíng,
he was given the position of leader.
The *Zhuàn* says:
'It is through accumulation.'
Thus, soil accumulates to form hills and mounds,
water accumulates to form rivers and seas,
and good deeds accumulate to form the gentleman.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'In the *Hé Guǎng*,
I know the utmost of virtue.'
And if you wish to attain it,
each should return to its root,
and return to the past."
"In ancient times,
military service did not exceed the season;
spring service meant returning in the autumn,
and autumn service meant returning in the spring;
the cold and heat had not yet changed,
and clothes had not yet been changed,
and one was already back.
Husbands and wives did not miss the season,
and people were as peaceful and harmonious as if they were together.
Lawsuits were settled fairly,
and punishments were appropriate,
then the yin and yang were harmonized,
and wind and rain were timely.
The ruler did not harass and disturb,
and the people did not toil and labor,
each cultivating his own occupation,
and dwelling peacefully in his own nature,
then locusts would not be born,
and floods and droughts would not arise.
Taxes and levies were reduced, and farmers did not miss the season,
then the people were sufficient,
and refugees returned to their fields and villages.
The ruler was pure and tranquil and had no desires,
then the people were honest and not greedy.
But now, service and labor extend to the farthest places,
to the coldest and most bitter lands,
to dangerous and difficult places,
crossing the territories of the Hú and
Yuè peoples.
If one goes this year, he returns next year;
parents crane their necks and look west,
and men and women are lonely and think of each other.
Though one's body is in Dōngchǔ,
his mind is in Xīhé.
Therefore, when one person goes, the village hates it,
and when one person dies, ten thousand people grieve.
The *Shī* says:
'The king's business is never done,
So that we cannot plant our millet and rice.
What shall our parents rely on?'
'We think of those officers,
And the tears fall down like rain.
Do we not think of returning home?
We are afraid of these nets of crime.'
If officials do not uphold the law to care for the people,
but turn their backs on the public and take on private matters,
each using his power to satisfy his desires,
and the people are worried and resentful,
and the ruler does not sympathize and govern,
then evil policies are carried out and perverse influences arise;
when perverse influences arise,
then insects and locusts are born, and floods and droughts arise.
If this is the case,
even if one prays and sacrifices and offers supplications,
and uses all the spirits at all times,
how can he harmonize the yin and yang and stop bandits and thieves?"
7.4 《Néng Yán Dì Sìshí》
The Grandee said:
"A blind man can speak of white and black,
but has no eyes to distinguish them.
A scholar can speak of order and chaos,
but has no ability to carry them out.
If one sits and talks without acting,
then a shepherd boy has the strength of Wū Huò,
and disheveled hair covers the virtues of Yáo and
Shùn.
Therefore, if one makes words close to deeds,
then why should the scholar worry about order and chaos,
and why should the blind man worry about white and black?
If words do not come out,
one is ashamed that one's actions do not reach them.
Therefore, for the lowly to speak of the lofty,
and for those who can speak but cannot act,
the gentleman is ashamed."
The Worthies said:
"Those who can speak but cannot act are
the treasures of the state.
Those who can act but cannot speak are
the instruments of the state.
Those who combine these two are
gentlemen.
Those who have neither are
shepherd boys and
disheveled heads.
His words filled the world,
and his virtue covered the four seas:
this was Zhōu Gōng.
Instead of speaking with the mouth
and acting in person,
how about silently carrying out one's actions?
Then why should the ministers have any worries or shame?
Now, if the Way is not promoted but one strives for small gains,
and admires what is not urgent in order to disrupt the will of the group,
even if the gentleman is poor,
he should not do it.
Medicated wine is
the benefit of illness,
and correct speech is
the medicine of governance.
If the dukes and ministers can truly strengthen and restrain themselves,
eat the ultimate words of literature,
remove power and cunning,
dismiss profitable officials,
and return everything to the people,
and personally follow the Way of Zhōu Gōng,
then the world will be ordered and songs of praise will arise.
How could the scholar worry about order and chaos?"
7.5 《Qǔ Xià Dì Sìshíyī》
The Grandee said:
"Unruly people
hinder public interests
and want to monopolize the mountains and marshes.
If we follow the ideas of the scholars and
worthies,
then the benefits will go to the people below,
and the county government will have nothing to do.
They criticize what the ruler does,
and ridicule what the ruler says,
only wanting to harm the ruler and benefit the people below,
diminishing the lord and pleasing the ministers.
How can the righteousness of superior and inferior,
and the etiquette of ruler and minister, be maintained?
And how can songs of praise arise?"
The Worthies and Literati said:
"In ancient times,
the ruler took with measure,
and provided for himself with moderation.
In years of plenty, there was no stealing;
in years of famine, distribution was generous.
The use of the people's labor
did not exceed three days a year;
the land tax
did not exceed one-tenth.
The ruler was sincerely loving,
and the ministers exerted their utmost.
Superiors and inferiors yielded to each other,
and the world was at peace.
'Dredge and open your private channels'
means the superior yielding to the inferior.
'Then it will extend to my private concerns'
means putting public duties first.
Mèngzǐ 孟子 said:
'There has never been a benevolent man who abandoned his relatives,
nor a righteous man who put his ruler last.'
If the ruler acts like a ruler and the ministers act like ministers,
how could there be a lack of propriety and righteousness?
But towards the end of the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
virtue and kindness were blocked, and desires multiplied.
The ruler became extravagant and sought much from above,
while the people were distressed below,
becoming negligent in their public duties.
Therefore, there was the land tax by the *mǔ*,
and the poem 'Big Rat' was written.
Wèi Línggōng 衛靈公 mobilized the people to dig ponds in the dead of winter.
Hǎi Chūn 海春 remonstrated, saying:
'It is cold,
and the people are freezing and hungry.
I hope that Your Grace will stop the labor.'
The Duke said:
'Is it cold?
Why do I not feel cold?'
Hǎi Chūn 海春 said:
'People say:
"Those who are comfortable cannot sympathize with the distressed,
and those who are full cannot understand the hungry."'
Therefore, those who have leftover meat and rice find it difficult to talk about scarcity,
and those who live in ease and pleasure find it difficult to talk about diligence and hardship.
Those who live in high halls and deep houses,
in spacious mansions and secluded rooms,
do not know the suffering of those who live in small, cramped huts,
where the roof leaks above and the ground is damp below.
Those who have hundreds of four-horse carriages hitched,
whose wealth and goods fill their homes,
who store and display new things,
do not know the urgency of those who have no assurance of food from morning till night
and who resort to borrowing.
Those who have extensive estates and beautiful gardens,
and fields of fertile land stretching in rows,
do not know the toil of those who have no inherited occupation
and who live in cramped dwellings.
Those whose horses cover the hills
and whose cattle and sheep fill the valleys
do not know the poverty of those who have no orphaned piglet or scrawny calf.
Those who lie on high pillows, talking and sleeping,
with no cries of distress,
do not know the sorrow of those who are worried about private debts and the harshness of officials.
Those who wear fine silk and leather shoes
and who eat the finest grains and fatty meats
do not know the cold of short hemp garments
and the bitterness of bran and chaff.
Those who leisurely stroll in their private chambers
and sit with folded hands, holding a table to eat,
do not know the toil of those who push plows and till the fields themselves.
Those who ride strong horses and drive good carriages,
with rows of riders in formation,
do not know the labor of those who carry burdens and walk on foot.
Those who have fancy beds and felt mats
and who are served by attendants on all sides
do not know the difficulty of those who haul carts and tow boats
and who climb high and cross swift currents.
Those who wear light, warm clothing,
cover themselves with fine furs,
live in warm rooms,
and ride in comfortable carriages
do not know the perilous cold of those who patrol the borders,
exposed to the north wind,
in the regions of Dài 代 and Xiāng 鄉.
Those whose wives and children are happily united
and whose descendants are secure
do not know the withered appearance of old mothers
and the sorrowful resentment of lonely women.
Those whose ears listen to music
and whose eyes watch performers
do not know the death of those who face flying arrows
and stand against the enemy on the battlefield.
Those who face east and lean on desks,
wielding their pens as if composing literature,
do not know the tightness of ropes
and the pain of whips and canes.
Those who sit on felt carpets
and calmly discuss the words in books as if it were easy
do not know the difficulty of those who wade through water.
In the past, when Shāng Yāng 商鞅 was in charge of Qín 秦,
he executed people as if cutting reeds and rushes
and used the army as if shooting pellets.
Those who followed the army had their bones exposed on the Great Wall,
and those who transported grain had carts stretching as far as the eye could see.
They went to their deaths
and were brought back only as corpses.
Were they not human beings too?
Therefore, the superior man is benevolent with compassion
and righteous with moderation.
He shares his likes and dislikes with the world
and does not inflict inhumanity on others.
Gōng Liú 公劉 loved goods,
so those who stayed at home had savings,
and those who traveled had bags.
Tài Wáng 大王 loved beauty,
so there were no resentful women within
and no unmarried men without.
Wén Wáng 文王 established laws,
so there were no unjust imprisonments in the country.
Wǔ Wáng 武王 led his army,
so the soldiers gladly died for him,
and the people gladly served him.
If it were like this,
then why would the people suffer and complain,
or seek and criticize?"
The dukes and ministers looked sorrowful,
silent as if no one were there.
Thereupon, the debate was dismissed and the arguments ceased.
The memorial stated:
"The Worthies and Literati do not understand the affairs of the government
and presumptuously consider salt and iron to be inconvenient.
It is requested that the state monopoly on liquor in the commanderies and kingdoms
and the iron officials within the passes be temporarily abolished."
The memorial was approved.
7.6 *Jí Zhī Dì Sìshíèr* 擊之第四十二
After the Worthies and Literati were appointed,
they were all granted the rank of grand master,
and they resigned from the positions of chancellor
and imperial historian.
The grand master said:
"In the previous discussion of public affairs,
the Worthies and Literati cited ancient times,
which deviated somewhat from the needs of the present.
Those who argue do not necessarily have to contradict each other;
the goal is to achieve what is feasible.
In the past,
when the government had not yet dealt with the affairs of the Hú 胡 and Yuè 越,
the border cities were attacked on all sides,
and the northern border suffered especially.
The late emperor ended the troubles on three fronts,
pacified and won over the neighboring countries,
and used them as a protective barrier,
exhausting the commanderies and kingdoms
to attack the Xiongnu.
The Xiongnu's territory is like an animal pen,
isolated and weak, with no allies.
This is a time of distress and ruin for them.
If we do not pursue them from afar
and allow them to catch their breath again,
to rest and train their soldiers and horses,
and to deceive the Western Regions,
the Western Regions, being close to the Hú 胡 bandits
and disheartened within,
will surely become a source of trouble.
Therefore, the sovereign desires to sweep them away,
even at the cost of depleting the granaries.
To chase after birds all day
and then release them when tired is not a good plan.
Shùn 舜 continued the legacy,
and Yǔ 禹 completed the task.
How about attacking them now in a military campaign?"
The Literary Man said:
"In the past,
when the county officials reduced the light taxes,
public expenses were ample,
and the people were rich and well-supplied.
Later,
guarding against the Hú (胡) and
Yuè (越), and communicating with the four barbarian tribes,
expenses became insufficient.
Therefore, they promoted profit-making,
assessed taxes on carriages and boats,
using the proceeds to aid the border,
redeem crimes, and collect wealth through cáo mǐn (告緡),
causing the people to suffer.
Soldiers died in military campaigns,
middle-ranking officers were exhausted by transporting supplies,
and this was followed by kě zhé (科適),
and the officials' levies reached their limit.
To labor and then rest,
to reach the extreme and then return to the origin,
this is the ancient way,
even if Shùn (舜) and
Yǔ (禹) were to rise,
they could not change it."
The Grandee said:
"In the past, Xià Hòu (夏后) controlled the disasters of the flood,
the people worked diligently,
exhausted by baskets and shovels,
but later,
they all enjoyed the benefits of their labor.
During the time of the late emperor,
the commanderies and kingdoms were somewhat burdened by military affairs,
but the labor of the three borders was also reduced.
The saying goes:
'Those who do not seize the opportunity when they see it will lose their accomplishments.'
One day of failing to resist the enemy
will bring trouble for generations.
Rest and labor are used to supply needs,
taking advantage of weaknesses and seizing the opportune time.
The way of emperors and kings
is what sages and worthies cannot lose sight of.
When achievements have a beginning,
to dislike labor and not finish them
is like a farmer growing tired of rest and stopping in difficulty.
Those who stop working achieve nothing,
those who are lazy in farming gain nothing."
The Literary Man said:
"A country that is broad in land but does not secure it is in danger,
soldiers who are strong but bully the enemy will perish.
When tigers and rhinoceroses fight each other,
ants and mole crickets can achieve their ambitions.
When two enemies resist each other,
a common man can take advantage of the gap.
Therefore, the sage kings see the harm in advantages
and preserve the near while seeing the far.
Those who plan for the county officials now
should stop the fighting and let the soldiers rest,
use generous gifts to establish peaceful relations,
and cultivate moral virtue.
If they do not care about the people's urgent needs,
do not consider their difficulties,
exhaust what they rely on in useless lands,
losing ten to gain one,
this is not what the Literary Man knows."
8.1 《Jié Hé Dì Sìshísān》 (結和第四十三)
The Grandee said:
"Since the rise of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
in cultivating good relations and establishing peaceful alliances,
the gifts sent to the Chányú (單于) have been very generous;
however, they have not changed their behavior because of the heavy gifts and bribes,
and their violent harm has increased even more.
The late emperor saw that they could be subdued by force
but not won over by virtue,
so he expanded the generals and leaders,
recruited brave fighters,
to punish their crimes;
their achievements were brilliant,
known throughout the country,
and stored in the historical archives.
How can you call it
'losing ten to gain one'?
Those who steal peace are in later danger,
those who worry about the near are concerned about the immediate,
the virtuous separate themselves from the common,
the wise act according to circumstances,
what the gentleman worries about,
the common people doubt.
Therefore, the people can be shown the completed result,
but cannot be involved in planning the beginning.
This is what the officials alone see,
and what the Literary Man does not see."
The Literary Man said:
"In the past,
the Xióngnú (匈奴) established peaceful alliances,
the various barbarian tribes paid tribute,
and the ruler and his subjects trusted each other both internally and externally,
without the troubles of the Hú (胡) and
Yuè (越).
At that time,
the demands of the superiors were few and easily met,
the people were peaceful and happy without incident,
tilling the fields and eating,
growing hemp and wearing clothes,
each family had several years' worth of savings,
the county officials had surplus goods and wealth,
and the elders in the villages
all benefited from their benevolence.
Since then,
they have retreated from civil affairs and appointed military men,
tormenting the teachers and exhausting the masses,
to conquer useless lands,
establishing commanderies among the sand and stones,
the people cannot defend themselves,
so they are sent to garrison and defend the cities,
pulling carts and providing for them.
I foolishly see its ruin,
and do not see its success."
The Grandee said:
"The Xióngnú (匈奴) used empty reputations to trade with the Hàn (漢),
but did not follow through in reality;
they were repeatedly deceived by the Mán (蠻) and
Mò (貊) tribes,
but they did not feel the pain,
why is that?
Emperor Gāo (高) held his sword and pacified the nine provinces;
now, with the nine provinces, he cannot control the Xióngnú (匈奴).
Even ordinary people in the villages
still have those who scatter and flee,
how much more so the master of ten thousand miles and the small country of the Xióngnú (匈奴)?
With the strength of the empire, what can't be crushed?
With the soldiers and people of the empire, who can't be subdued?
Now we have the name of an emperor,
but his power is not trusted beyond the Great Wall,
instead we give bribes and they still sit arrogantly,
this is what the Five Emperors could not bear,
and what the Three Kings would be completely enraged by."
The Literary Man said:
"Tāng (湯) served the Xià (夏) and finally subdued it,
King Zhōu (周) served the Yīn (殷) and finally destroyed it.
Therefore, those who use the great to control the small become kings,
those who use the strong to bully the weak perish.
The sage does not exhaust his people to annex a country,
the good driver does not exhaust his horses to cover a road.
Therefore, the driving of Zàofù (造父) did not lose harmony,
the governance of the sage did not betray virtue.
The Qín (秦) dynasty used sharp bits to control the world,
held a repaired whip to lash the eight extremes,
the chariot horses were exhausted,
and the whip was applied even more,
therefore there was the change of breaking the bit and dropping the whip.
It was not that the soldiers and people were not numerous,
or that the labor was not diligent,
but that they all betrayed internally and rebelled externally and were of no use.
This is why Emperor Gāo (高) held his sword and took the world.
When two rulers are on good terms,
internal and external communications are open,
the world is peaceful,
and there are no worries for generations,
what would the soldiers and people be concerned about?
Why would the Three Kings be angry?"
The Grand Secretary said:
"When Bó Yì 伯翳 was first enfeoffed in Qín 秦,
his land was seventy *lǐ* 里.
Mù Gōng 穆公 initiated hegemony,
and Xiào Gōng 孝公 expanded the enterprise.
From low to high,
from small to large.
Thus, the ancestors laid the foundation,
and the descendants accomplished it.
Xuānyuán 軒轅 fought at Zhuōlù 涿鹿,
killed the two Hào 皞,
and Chīyóu 蚩尤 to become emperor;
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武 attacked Xià 夏
and Shāng 商, executing Jié 桀
and Zhòu 紂 to become kings.
The Yellow Emperor succeeded through battle,
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武 achieved filial piety through conquest.
Therefore, the labor of hands and feet
is for the nourishment of the belly and intestines.
The tasks of the present age
are for the benefit of future generations.
Now that the four barbarians are invading internally,
if we do not resist,
ten thousand generations will surely suffer this long-term trouble.
The late emperor raised righteous armies to punish the violent and strong,
destroyed Cháoxiǎn 朝鮮 in the east,
pacified Rǎn 冉 and Máng 駹 in the west,
captured the Bǎiyuè 百越 in the south,
defeated the powerful Hú 胡 in the north,
pursued the Xiōngnú 匈奴 to expand the northern provinces—
the actions of Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武
were like the armies of Chīyóu 蚩尤.
Therefore, the sage ruler expands the territory,
not for personal gain;
using armies
is not merely to vent anger,
but to rectify difficulties, avoid harm,
and plan for the long-term benefit of the common people."
The Literary Scholar said:
"Qín 秦 in the south captured the strong Yuè 越,
and in the north repelled the powerful Hú 胡,
exhausting the central states to employ the four barbarians.
The people were weary and exhausted, yet the ruler did not care,
the country collapsed internally, yet the ruler did not know.
Therefore, one man initiated rebellion, and the whole world responded;
the armies were defeated by Chén Shè 陳涉,
and the land was seized by the various lords.
What benefit did it bring to future generations?
*The Book of Odes* says:
'The wild geese cry *yōng yōng*,
the rising sun begins to dawn.'
Gaining immediate benefits,
they do not think of future troubles.
Thus, the King of Wú 吳 knew the convenience of attacking Qí 齊,
but did not know the trouble from Gàn Suì 干遂.
Qín 秦 knew the benefit of advancing and seizing,
but did not know the difficulty of Hóngmén 鴻門.
Therefore, they knew one thing but not ten.
The Zhōu 周 were careful in small matters and gained big things,
Qín 秦 desired big things and lost small ones.
The saying goes:
'If the cart in front overturns,
the cart behind takes warning.'
'The example of Yīn 殷 is not far off,
it lies in the era of the Xià 夏 rulers.'"
8.2 《Zhū Qín Dì Sìshísì 誅秦第四十四》 (Punishing Qin, Chapter 44)
The Grand Secretary said:
"Qín 秦, Chǔ 楚, Yān 燕,
and Qí 齊 were enfeoffed by Zhōu 周;
the rulers of the three Jìn 晉
and the Tián 田 family of Qí 齊
were all household ministers of the feudal lords.
Guarding their countries internally
and attacking injustice externally,
their territories expanded,
so they established the title of ten thousand chariots
and became feudal lords.
The Zhōu 周 court cultivated rites and emphasized writing,
but the country was weakened
and could not sustain itself.
In the east, it was restrained by the six states,
and in the west, it was feared by Qín 秦.
The ruler himself was exiled,
and the ancestral temples were cut off from sacrifices.
Thanks to the great favor of the late emperor,
he revived their descendants,
enfeoffing Jiā 嘉 in Yǐngchuān 潁川,
with the title of *Zhōu Zǐ Nán Jūn* 周子男君.
Qín 秦, having unified the world,
in the east cut off the Pèi 沛 River,
also destroyed Cháoxiǎn 朝鮮,
in the south seized Lùliáng 陸梁,
in the north repelled the Hú 胡 and Dí 狄,
and in the west subdued the Dī 氐 and Qiāng 羌,
establishing the title of Emperor
and holding court for the four barbarians.
Wherever boats and carriages could reach,
wherever footprints could be found,
all came to pay tribute.
It was not that they submitted to his virtue,
but that they feared his power.
If one has more power, others will pay court;
if one has less power, one will pay court to others."
The Literary Scholar said:
"Yǔ 禹 and Shùn 舜 were assistants to Yáo 堯;
Tāng 湯 and Wén 文 were ministers to Xià 夏 and Shāng 商.
The reason they were followed from the eight limits to the four seas
was not because of the land of Lùliáng 陸梁
or the might of weapons and armor.
Qín 秦, Chǔ 楚,
and the three Jìn 晉, though calling themselves rulers of ten thousand chariots,
did not focus on accumulating virtue but focused on invading each other,
provoking wars and competing for strength, and ultimately all perished together.
Although they advanced territories and expanded lands,
it was like eating *zè* 萴 to fill the stomach;
to desire their peace and survival,
how could it be possible?
Governing a country with ritual propriety and yielding is like the Jiāng 江 and Hǎi 海 Rivers;
flowing and spreading for a long time without drying up,
its foundation is good.
If one acts without a foundation,
like a fire of artemisia that flares up suddenly and has no continuation,
its destruction can be established and awaited;
this is what happened in the Warring States period.
The virtue of the Zhōu 周 declined,
and then it was listed among the feudal lords,
yet it has not been cut off to this day.
Qín 秦 exhausted its strength and annihilated its clan;
how could it obtain the allegiance of others?"
The Grand Secretary said:
"The central states and the border regions
are like the limbs and the heart of the body.
If the skin and flesh feel cold on the outside,
or the heart suffers illness inside,
the mutual labor of inside and outside
is not a bestowal for each other!
If the lips are lost, the teeth will feel cold;
if the limbs are injured, the heart will be grieved.
Therefore, without hands and feet, the limbs are crippled;
without border regions, the inner country is harmed.
In the past,
the Róng 戎 and Dí 狄 attacked Tài Wáng 太王 at Bīn 邠,
crossing Qí 岐 and Liáng 梁 and bordering Qín 秦 at the Jīng 涇 and Wèi 渭 Rivers,
reaching Lùhún 陸渾 of Jìn 晉 in the east,
invading and oppressing the central states,
and the central states suffered from it.
Now, the Xiōngnú 匈奴 gradually encroach and invade internally;
those far away do not experience their suffering,
only the border regions suffer their defeat.
*The Book of Odes* says:
'My heart is full of sorrow,
thinking of the evil done to the country.'
If we do not prepare defenses,
violent harm will not cease.
Therefore, the late emperor raised righteous armies to punish their crimes,
and then broke Qílián 祁連 and Tiānshān 天山,
dispersing their assembled parties,
and in the north, he raided as far as Lóngchéng 龍城,
greatly encircling the Xiōngnú 匈奴.
The *chányú* 單于 lost his soul,
barely escaping with his life,
pursuing the fleeing north,
beheading and capturing over ten thousand.
The people who drew bows
and the leaders in felt clothing
were all dismayed,
frustrated, and fled far away,
and then we returned with our troops.
Húnyē 渾耶 led his people to surrender,
and five dependent states were established to resist the Hú 胡,
so that within the Great Wall
and beyond the Hé 河 and Shān 山,
attacks were rare.
Then the decree was issued,
reducing the garrison and transportation,
and easing corvée labor.
Although it was initially arduous,
they ultimately obtained its blessings."
The Literary Man said:
"The Zhōu 周 dynasty accumulated virtue over generations;
everyone in the world wanted them as their ruler;
therefore, they became kings without effort.
Their benevolence spread from near to far,
and the Mán 蠻 and
Mò 貊 peoples came of their own accord.
The Qín 秦 dynasty relied on military victories to unify the world,
belittled the interior and coveted the lands of the Hú 胡 and
Yuè 越 peoples.
They sent Méng Tián 蒙恬 to attack the Hú,
taking the area south of the Yellow River and making it 'New Qín,'
while losing the original Qín.
They built the Great Wall to defend against the Hú,
but lost what they were supposed to defend.
In the past,
wars were frequent,
armies rose up repeatedly.
North of the Great Wall,
broken chariots and lost arrowheads could be seen everywhere.
When Lǐ Guǎnglì 李廣利 and others acted rashly,
calculating only what their horses could manage,
everyone was disheartened.
Even though they captured Hún Yé 渾耶,
they could not recover what they had lost.
This was hardly a sound plan for the state. "
8.3 《Chapter 45: Attacking Merit》
The Grandee said:
"Qí Huán Gōng 齊桓公 crossed Yān 燕 to attack the Shān Róng 山戎,
defeated Gūzhú 孤竹,
and devastated Lìngzhī 令支.
Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng 趙武靈王 crossed Jùzhù 句注,
passed through Dài Gǔ 代谷,
and nearly destroyed the Lín Hú 林胡 and
Lóufán 樓煩.
Yān ambushed and routed the Dōng Hú 東胡,
expanding their territory by a thousand *lǐ*,
crossing Liáodōng 遼東 to attack Cháoxiǎn 朝鮮.
Lord Méng 蒙 defeated the Xiōngnú 匈奴 for Qín,
like a hawk chasing a flock of sparrows.
The Xiōngnú were terrified
and dared not face south for more than ten years.
Later,
when Lord Méng died and the nobles rebelled against Qín,
China was thrown into turmoil,
and the Xiōngnú, in disarray,
dared to become border raiders again.
Even the small states of Yān 燕 and
Zhào 趙 were able to repel the invaders and expand their territories.
Now, with the might of the Hàn 漢 state,
and the strength of its soldiers and people,
it is not merely the forces of Qí Huán Gōng,
or the armies of Yān and Zhào.
Yet, the Xiōngnú have not been subdued for a long time
because the ministers do not work together
and there is a lack of harmony between the superiors and subordinates."
The Literary Man said:
"In ancient times, the use of armies
was not for the sake of seizing land and resources,
but to relieve the people's suffering.
The people thought of them
as one thinks of rain in a drought,
bringing baskets of food and pots of drink
to welcome the royal army.
Therefore, those who worried about the people's suffering
were united with the people in heart and mind, and the people returned to them.
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武 were such rulers.
Those who did not cherish the lives of the people,
whose strength was exhausted and were thus defeated and betrayed,
were like the king of Qín.
Mèngzǐ 孟子 said:
'If a ruler does not follow the Way,
does not adhere to benevolence and righteousness,
and engages in forceful warfare,
he will surely perish, even if he is victorious.'
This is why China was thrown into turmoil,
not because Méng Tián died and the nobles rebelled against Qín.
In the past, during the height of the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
the Yuèshāng 越裳 people came to offer tribute,
and the various Mán 蠻 brought their contributions.
Later, as the Zhōu declined,
the nobles engaged in forceful conquests,
and the Mán 蠻 and Mò 貊 scattered,
each forming their own factions,
unable to unite with each other.
This is why Yān 燕 and
Zhào 趙 were able to gain advantages.
Later,
the Xiōngnú gradually grew stronger,
nibbling away at the territories of the nobles.
Thus, they defeated and drove away the Yuèzhī 月氏.
Relying on their military might,
they relocated small states
and the people who drew bows
were united as one family,
with one mind and unified strength.
Therefore, they were difficult to control.
The previous ruler devised a strategy against the Xiōngnú for the late emperor:
'Establish military bases in the Western Regions,
seize strategic locations,
and await their changes.
With the strength of the Hàn,
attacking the masses of the Xiōngnú
would be like using a powerful crossbow to burst a boil.
The state of Yuè's 越 capture of Wú 吳,
is hardly worth mentioning!'
The emperor thought this was right.
Using your righteousness,
listening to your plans,
even if King Yuè 越 employed Zhǒng 种 and
Lí 蠡, it would not surpass this.
Promoting the Grain Collecting Commandant to the position of Imperial Counselor,
holding office for more than ten years,
I have not seen the merits of Zhǒng 种 and
Lí 蠡,
but I have seen the effects of exhaustion and decay.
The Xiōngnú have not become more submissive,
but the common people are exhausted.
This is because your strategy cannot weaken the Xiōngnú,
but instead weakens China.
Is this how someone skilled in planning should act?"
8.4 《Chapter 46: The Western Regions》
The Grandee said:
"In the past,
the Xiōngnú occupied the strategic passes of the Yellow River and mountains,
monopolized the benefits of farming and grazing,
their people were wealthy, and their army was strong.
When they raided,
the area within Jùzhù 句注 was alarmed,
and the area south of Shàngjùn 上郡 was in a state of complete defense.
During the time of Emperor Wén 文帝,
the barbarians entered Xiāo Pass 蕭關,
and beacon fires reached Gānquán 甘泉,
the ministers were afraid and did not know what to do,
so they requested to station troops in the capital to prepare for the Hú.
The Hú allied with Dàyuān 大宛,
Kāngjū 康居, and others in the west,
and communicated with the various Qiāng 羗 in the south.
The late emperor yielded and took away the broad and abundant land,
establishing the area west of Zhāngyè 張掖,
isolating the Qiāng 羗 and
Hú, and dividing their support.
Therefore, the countries of the Western Regions
all resisted the Xiōngnú from within,
severing their right arm,
causing them to drag their swords and flee.
Therefore, we recruited people to farm and raise livestock to expand our resources.
South of the Great Wall,
in the counties along the border,
horses and cattle roamed freely,
and accumulations were spread across the fields.
I have not seen the mistakes of this plan.
For a weak Yuè 越 state to achieve its aims against the strong Wú 吳,
it was not equal in terms of talent, land, and number of people.
If the ruler thinks and the ministers plan,
success will surely come."
The Literati said:
"Wú and
Yuè are pressed by the Jiāng and
Hǎi rivers, and the three rivers cycle around them,
situated among the five lakes.
Their lands are close,
their borders adjoining,
so it is easy for them to seize each other.
Before the sound of drums and gongs is heard,
before banners and flags are unfurled,
before battle formations are established,
the armies are already engaged.
The army has no expenses for baggage trains,
the soldiers have no hardship of lacking supplies,
this is what is meant by 'eating from the kitchen and fighting at the city gates.'
Now, the Xiōngnú graze on boundless marshes,
stretching east, west, north, and south,
with no end in sight.
Even with light carriages and swift horses,
they cannot be reached,
much less pursued by troops burdened with heavy armor and supplies.
It is impossible to reach them.
Vaguely, it is like traveling in the deep marshes, not knowing where to stop,
clearly, it is like fishing in the rivers and seas without a net.
Even if they are reached,
the armies will be exhausted,
merely leaving them bait.
Therefore, the wise kings knew there was no profit in it,
thinking that campaigns should not be launched frequently,
and power should not be exerted for long.
Therefore, they summoned the gōngqīng, dàfū,
xiánliáng,
and wénxué,
in order to restore the path of correcting wrongs and promoting the insignificant.
The gōngqīng should consider the needs of the people and
the harm caused by the Xiōngnú,
follow the heart of the sage ruler,
and establish lasting peace.
Now you focus on trivial matters,
reject fundamental proposals,
and do not follow the emperor's will,
which is not fulfilling your loyalty."
The Grandee said:
"Initially,
Èr Shī failed to conquer Yuān and returned.
Those who advised wanted the ruler not to give in to anger,
otherwise the Western Regions would all collapse and attach themselves to the Hú,
and the Hú would gain strength by acquiring more states.
The late emperor made extraordinary decisions,
exercised military might,
and launched a surprise attack on Yuān,
and Yuān surrendered its entire country,
offering its weapons,
and presenting its precious horses.
The tribes of Wūsūn were terrified
and asked to become vassals.
The Xiōngnú lost their courage,
fleeing in all directions.
Although they were not completely subdued,
they were driven to remote, cold, barren lands.
The strong died in Qílián and
Tiānshān,
and their offspring have not recovered.
Therefore, the ministers advised that the Xiōngnú were weakened by the Hàn army,
with broken wings and injured flanks,
and could be completely defeated by attacking them.
Then the late emperor abandoned his ministers,
and therefore the Xiōngnú were not reformed.
It is like building a mountain,
stopping before completing a single basket of earth,
judging that the work has no chance of being completed,
which is abandoning them to the Hú and strengthening the enemy.
Stopping halfway and abandoning success,
planning for the ruler in this way,
cannot be called fulfilling your loyalty."
The Literati said:
"The officials speak of foreign affairs,
and those who advise seek temporary advantages,
without considering the consequences.
Zhāng Qiān spoke of the heavenly horses of Dàyuān that sweat blood,
and the true jade and giant birds of Ānxī.
When the government heard of it, they were as delighted as if they had tasted something sweet.
Then they launched a large-scale campaign to attack Yuān,
which took several years to conquer.
To attack a country ten thousand *lǐ* away,
where more than half of the army's supplies are lost without even fighting,
even if Yuān is defeated and precious horses are obtained,
is not a good plan.
At that time,
the generals and soldiers were turning red in the face while dealing with the four barbarian tribes,
armies stretched as far as the eye could see,
and commanderies and kingdoms were mobilized together,
the common people were in hardship,
deception and treachery arose,
and bandits rose up everywhere,
which the garrison commanders could not suppress,
and the cities could not stop.
Then they sent a senior official wearing embroidered robes to investigate and strike down.
At that time,
the common people,
none could be sure of their lives,
and therefore the heroes of Shāndōng
harbored discontent.
Relying on the late emperor's divine spirit, it was magnificent.
The blame all lies in wanting to completely defeat the Xiōngnú and neglecting the consequences.
Planning for the ruler in this way,
can it be called loyalty?"
8. 5 "Worldly Affairs, Chapter Forty-Seven"
The Grandee said:
"You scholars speak recklessly!
The advisors' suggestions should be carefully followed,
and not simply guarding the ancient words of Chuí Chē,
which are foolish and cannot be followed.
The Hàn's existence with the Xiōngnú
is like a tree with termites,
or a person with a disease,
which will only deepen if not treated.
Therefore, the strategists believe in attacking and seizing to exhaust them.
The scholars speak of embracing them with virtue,
but these are just words and cannot be put into practice.
The scholars above cannot imitate the three kings,
and below cannot imitate the nearing Qín,
but allow the officials to implement and carry out what is appropriate for the present time,
to secure the multitude of commoners and pacify the borders?"
The Literati said:
"In the past, Qí Huán Gōng internally attached the people,
and externally appeased the dukes,
preserved the perishing and connected the severed,
and the world followed like the wind.
Later,
his virtue declined and his actions weakened,
at the Kuíqiū assembly,
he asserted himself and boasted,
and nine states rebelled.
The *Chūnqiū* criticized him for not valuing virtue and valuing strength.
Therefore, relying on virtue,
the strong Chǔ confessed submission,
and distant countries arrived without being summoned;
relying on strength,
those nearby do not become close,
and small countries do not attach themselves.
This is the result.
Truly, if you look at how the three kings prospered above,
and discuss how Qín perished below,
and in the middle relate how Qí Huán Gōng rose,
abandoning military force and practicing civil administration,
abolishing strength and valuing virtue,
closing the passes and bridges,
and removing the barriers,
and guiding them with benevolence and righteousness,
then there would be no worries about the barbarians on the northern borders,
and no wars in the central states."
The Grandee said:
"If matters are not discussed beforehand,
they cannot be handled in emergencies.
If there is no internal preparation,
enemies cannot be defended against.
The *Shī* says:
'Instruct your people,
be careful of your boundaries,
and use them to guard against the unexpected.'
Therefore, where there are civil affairs,
there must be military preparations.
In the past, Sòng Xiāng Gōng trusted Chǔ without preparing,
and suffered great humiliation,
being imprisoned and the state nearly destroyed.
Therefore, even with sincere trust,
if one does not know how to adapt to changes,
it is the path to danger and destruction.
The *Chūnqiū* does not approve of the 夷 and
狄 controlling the central states,
because they are untrustworthy.
The Xiōngnú are greedy and wolfish,
acting according to the times,
and striking when there is an opportunity,
swooping down like a whirlwind or lightning.
To try to trust the deceit of the unrighteous with a sincere heart
and treasures of gold and silk,
is like befriending Zhí and
Qiáo and supporting a fierce tiger."
The Literary Scholar said:
"The *Chūnqiū*
states, 'A true king has no enemy.'
This means his benevolence is profound,
his virtue is beautiful,
and the world submits to him,
with no one daring to contend with him.
His virtuous conduct extends beyond the borders,
to where ships and carts reach,
and where footprints tread,
all are showered with his grace.
Even distant foreign lands like the Mán and Mò
require multiple interpreters to arrive.
At such a time,
the world is harmonious and unified,
ruler and subjects are of one mind,
there is mutual trust within and without,
and harmony prevails above and below.
Weapons are readied but not tested,
shields and spears are locked away and not used.
Lǎozi said:
'The rhinoceros has no need for its horns,
and stinging insects have no need to release their poison.'
Therefore, if the ruler is benevolent, all are benevolent;
if the ruler is righteous, all are righteous.
How could the world embrace the likes of Zhí
and Qiāo? "
The Grandee said:
"Revealing one's innermost thoughts,
showing one's true feelings and sincerity,
with genuine trust felt inwardly,
and righteousness displayed outwardly.
When Sòng’s Huá Yuán
and Chǔ’s Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn met,
their inner beliefs aligned like matching tallies,
and they trusted each other sincerely.
Now, the Xiongnu harbor untrusting hearts
and conceal treacherous schemes.
They see profit before them
and seize opportunities as they arise,
secretly advancing near market areas
to attack the unprepared.
This is like leaving valuable treasures on the road without anyone guarding them.
To expect them not to be lost,
how is that possible?"
The Literary Scholar said:
"If sincerity and trustworthiness are evident throughout the world,
and pure virtue flows to the four corners of the sea,
then those nearby will sing and rejoice,
and those far away will bring tribute and come to court.
Therefore, one rectifies those nearby not with force,
and attracts those far away not with arms,
but by cultivating virtue and righteousness and employing the wise and capable.
Thus, when it comes to service, the people
decline ease and embrace labor;
and when it comes to wealth,
they decline abundance and embrace scarcity.
Superiors and inferiors yield to each other,
and people yield to each other on the roads.
At such a time,
valuables are disdained while virtue is esteemed,
righteousness is valued while profit is slighted,
and rewards are not stolen.
What need is there for guarding treasures!"
8.6 *Hé Qīn Dì Sìshíbā* (Harmonious Relations, Chapter 48)
The Grandee said:
"In the past, Xú Yǎn Wáng practiced righteousness and was destroyed,
and Lǔ Āi Gōng favored Confucianism and was weakened.
They knew culture but not martial affairs,
they knew one but not two.
Therefore, a gentleman earnestly practices benevolence,
but he must also build walls to defend himself
and set up defenses to prepare himself,
guarding against the harm that unrighteous people might inflict.
Thus, in ancient times,
hunts and military exercises were held to review military strength,
fearing that the people would become too complacent and forget the dangers.
Therefore, weapons and armor
are the tools of the state,
and city walls and fortifications
are the state's defenses;
to want to abandon them
is to remove the outer garments and expose the inner body,
revealing one's heart to the Xiongnu.
If the Xiongnu lightly advance and secretly attack,
taking advantage of our emptiness and weakness,
it would be like facing arrows and stones without armor,
and disaster would surely follow.
This is what the border regions fear
and what the officials worry about."
The Literary Scholar said:
"In the past,
trade routes were opened,
and goods were exchanged.
From the *chányú* downwards,
all were close to the Hàn and attached themselves,
coming and going below the Great Wall.
Later,
Wáng Huī mistakenly plotted the Màiyì campaign,
and the Xiongnu severed the harmonious relations,
attacking the key passes,
disasters arose and were not resolved,
wars continued without end,
and the border people did not remove their armor or loosen their crossbows.
For decades,
they plowed and cultivated in armor,
hoeing and weeding while keeping watch,
with signal fires lit and beacons raised.
Strong men armed with bows and arrows went out to fight,
while the old and weak fled into the fortresses.
Speaking of it is enough to bring tears and chills to the heart,
and the benevolent cannot bear it.
The *Shī* says:
'They give me a peach,
and I return a plum.'
I have never heard of good intentions being met with evil returns.
Therefore, if a gentleman is respectful and makes no mistakes,
and treats others with courtesy and propriety,
then within the four seas,
all will be brothers.
If one examines oneself and finds no fault,
what is there to worry about or fear!"
The Grandee said:
"Since the Spring and Autumn period, the lords of the various Xia states
have gathered and allied themselves,
but after a few meetings,
they grew estranged and suspicious of each other,
and wars did not cease.
The six states formed alliances,
with officials meeting frequently,
but they never had firm agreements.
How much more so with the states of beasts!
The *Chūnqiū* preserved the ruler in Chǔ,
and the Guìyóu gathering recorded the duke,
deceiving the Ì and Dí.
The Xiongnu have frequently sought harmonious relations,
but they always break their agreements first,
driven by greed and theft,
a state with long-standing treacherous schemes.
They are fickle and untrustworthy,
breaking every agreement,
like Zhū and Xiàng,
who cannot be changed,
and Shāng Jūn, who cannot be transformed.
To trust their military preparations
and treat them with kindness and virtue
is indeed difficult."
The Literary Scholar said:
"A true king stands in the center and listens to the world,
his virtue extending beyond the borders.
Distant lands and different customs
come to his court.
The phoenixes are in the courtyard,
and the qílín are in the suburban swamps.
All living beings and creatures
are showered with his grace.
It is not by personally traveling and managing everything with benevolence,
