but by extending his benevolent grace and embracing them.
That is sincerity.
Fàn Lǐ came from Yuè,
and Yóu Yú grew up among the Hú,
yet both became worthy advisors to hegemons and kings.
Therefore, there may be teachings that are not followed,
but there are no people in the world who cannot be transformed.
The *Shī* says:
'Draw from those puddles,
pour from them into these.'
Thus, when Gōng Liú lived among the Róng and Dí,
the Róng and Dí were transformed.
When Dà Wáng left Bīn,
the people of Bīn followed him.
The Duke of Zhōu cultivated virtue,
and the Yuèshāng clan came to court.
Their embracing goodness was like an echo.
Governing should focus on being kind and close to the people.
Why worry that they will not change?"
9.1 *Yáo Yì Dì Sìshíjiǔ* (Corvée Labor, Chapter 49)
The Grandee said:
"A butcher understands the principles of dissection and can separate [meat] with his hands.
But when it comes to extracting marrow and chiseling bones,
one cannot do it without metal axes.
A sagacious ruler transforms [people] by following their nature;
if there are those who do not comply,
he will raise troops and punish them.
Therefore, Tāng 湯 punished Gé Bó 葛伯,
and King Wén 文王 punished the Qúan Yí 犬夷.
Later, when the Róng 戎 and
Dí 狄 disturbed the Xià 夏 [territories],
Zhōngguó 中國 was not at peace.
King Xuān of Zhōu 周宣王 and
Zhòng Shānfǔ 仲山甫 planned to curb the invading cruelty.
The *Shī* says:
'We strike at the Xiǎn Yǔn 獫狁,
as far as Tàiyuán 太原.'
'The chariots come forth in force,
to build our city in the northern region.'
Since ancient times, enlightened kings have had to conduct punitive expeditions to subdue the unjust
and build ramparts to defend against the violent."
The Literary Man said:
"Shùn 舜 held his shield and axe, and the Miáo 苗 people submitted;
King Wén 文王 cultivated virtue and won over the four barbarians.
The *Shī* says:
'The Pì Yōng 辟雍 of Hào Jīng 鎬京,
from west, from east,
from south, from north,
there is no one who does not think of submitting.'
Under the vast sky,
among all those with human faces,
there is none who does not crane their necks and return to righteousness.
Therefore, drawing a line on the ground as a border,
no one dares to cross it.
The Master said:
'One can brave a gleaming blade,
but one cannot enter the [doctrine of] the Mean.'
This speaks of ultimate virtue.
Thus, those skilled in attack do not need strong armor to conquer,
and those skilled in defense do not need Qú Liáng's 渠梁 fortifications to be secure.
When King Wǔ 武王 attacked the Yīn 殷,
he held the yellow battle-axe
and swore an oath in the fields of Mù 牧,
and all the warriors of the land wished to be employed by him.
Then he sheathed his weapons,
grasped his tablet and held court,
and all the people of the land wished to be his subjects.
He took it by righteousness
and guarded it with virtue.
The Qín 秦 took it by force
and guarded it by law.
Failing to grasp the fundamentals,
they perished.
Civil administration can be employed for a long time,
but military force is difficult to maintain for long."
The Grandee said:
"The *Shī* says:
'The Xiǎn Yǔn 獫狁 are fiercely blazing,
so we are on guard.'
'The warriors are bold and strong,
managing all the four quarters.'
Therefore, defense and punitive expeditions
have a long history.
The *Chūnqiū* prevented the arrival of the great Róng 戎 by preparing for it in advance.
Thus, if the limbs are strong, the body is firm;
if the blossoms and leaves are lush, the roots are strong.
Therefore, fortifying the borders is the way to secure Zhōngguó 中國,
and deploying troops and transporting grain is the way to assess labor and leisure.
When the ruler worries, the ministers labor;
when the sovereign is in danger, the subjects die.
The late emperor worried that the common people were not well-provided for,
so he released restricted funds,
unharnessed the imperial carriage's outrider horses,
reduced musical performances, and decreased meals
to relieve the poor and prepare for border expenses.
To see the principle of obstructing success,
rather than the righteousness of rewarding [such actions],
is unheard of."
The Literary Man said:
"The ways of Zhōu 周 declined,
the traces of the [true] king faded,
the feudal lords contended for power,
and the great oppressed the small.
Therefore, strong states made it their business to invade,
and weak states prepared their defenses.
Armored soldiers toiled in battle formations,
serving with weapons and armor,
therefore, the ruler was burdened, and the people suffered.
Now, Zhōngguó 中國 is unified,
but the region within is not at peace;
corvée labor is distant, and both the outside and inside are troubled.
In ancient times,
there were no levies that lasted over a year,
nor corvée labor that exceeded its time.
Now, the near ones are several thousand *lǐ* 里 away,
the far ones are over ten thousand *lǐ* 里,
lasting two terms.
When the eldest son does not return,
the parents worry,
the wives and children sigh,
and the resentment and bitterness ferment in their hearts,
and the longing and yearning cause pain in their bones.
This is why the *Dì Dù* 杕杜 and
*Cài Wēi* 采薇 were composed."
9.2 *Dangerous Defenses*, Section 50
The Grandee said:
"The reason why tigers and rhinoceroses can capture bears and brown bears
and subdue the beasts
is that their claws and teeth are sharp and their grasp is strong.
The reason why Qín 秦 surpassed the feudal lords,
swallowed the world,
and annexed enemy states
is that its passes were secure and its power was overwhelming.
Thus, the tortoise has a shell,
so foxes and badgers cannot seize it;
the viper has a sting,
so people fear it and do not take it lightly.
Therefore, having defenses allows one to control others,
while lacking defenses allows one to be controlled by others.
Thus, Zhòng Shānfǔ 仲山甫 filled the gaps in the royal duties,
and Méng Gōng 蒙公 built the firmness of the Great Wall.
This is how they prepared for bandit troubles
and parried attacks from ten thousand *lǐ* 里 away.
Now, not securing the outside
while wanting to secure the inside
is like a family not strengthening its walls,
with dogs barking and startling them at night
and blindly acting in the dark."
The Literary Man said:
"Qín 秦 had the Háo 殽 and
Hán 函 on its left, the Lǒng 隴 and Dǐ 阺 on its right,
the Shǔ 蜀 and
Hàn 漢 in front, and mountains and
rivers behind, using these four strongholds for defense,
a golden city stretching for a thousand *lǐ* 里,
with capable generals and brave soldiers,
setting up sharp weapons and guarding the mountain passes.
Mòzǐ 墨子 defended against cloud ladder siege engines.
They believed that even if Tāng 湯 and
Wǔ 武 were to be reborn
or Chī Yóu 蚩尤 were to rise again,
they would not lightly attack.
Yet, the garrison soldier Chén Shèng 陳勝, without the position of a general or commander
or the multitude of an army,
with empty fists, broke a million soldiers,
without the difficulty of walls and fences.
Therefore, security lies in virtue, not in defenses.
If one truly uses benevolence and righteousness as barriers,
morality and virtue as ramparts,
worthy men as soldiers,
and sages as guards,
then no one can enter.
In this case, Zhōngguó 中國 would have no alarms of barking dogs,
and the borders would have no worries of deer startled and wolves looking back.
What need would there be for blind action?"
The Grandee said:
"In ancient times,
to govern a state, one must investigate the land,
mountain ranges, obstacles, and dangers,
the timing of the heavens, and the advantages of the earth,
and then one could become a king or hegemon.
Therefore, one regulated the land and built city walls,
repaired ditches and ramparts,
to defend against bandits and secure the state.
The *Chūnqiū* says:
'In winter, dredge the Zhū 洙.'
This is to improve the advantages of the land.
If the three armies conform to the timing of the heavens,
using the substantial to strike the empty,
they are then trapped by obstacles and dangers
and opposed by golden cities.
This is like when Lord Zhuāng of Chǔ 楚莊 besieged Sòng 宋,
and the Qín 秦 army was defeated at the Xiáo Qīn Yín 崤嶔崟 mountain range.
This is what I mean.
Therefore, it is said:
'The timing of the heavens and the advantages of the earth.'
The Qiāng 羗 and Hú 胡 are inherently
close to the border.
If we do not take them now,
they will surely become a long-term problem for the four borders.
This is why Jì Sūn 季孫 worried about Zhuān Yú 顓臾,
and there was the change brought about by Gōu Jiàn 勾踐,
which became a regret for the powerful Wú 吳 state."
The Literary Man said:
"Advantageous terrain is not as good as popular support;
military force is not as good as civil virtue.
The Zhōu 周 dynasty's ability to reach far
was not due to advantageous terrain,
but due to popular support.
What cannot be taken away in a hundred generations
is not due to defensible passes,
but due to virtue.
Wú 吳 had the difficulties of the Three Rivers (Sān Jiāng)
and Five Lakes (Wǔ Hú),
yet it was annexed by Yuè 越.
Chǔ 楚 had the strength of the Rǔ Yuān 汝淵
and Liǎng Táng 兩堂,
yet it was destroyed by Qín 秦.
Qín 秦 had the Lǒng Dǐ 隴阺
and Xiáo Sāi 崤塞,
yet it was destroyed by the feudal lords.
Jìn 晉 had the Yellow River (Hé 河), Huá 華, and Nine Rivers (Jiǔ Hé),
yet it was seized by the Six Ministers (Liù Qīng).
Qí 齊 had Mount Tài (Tài Shān)
and the vast sea,
yet it was threatened by Tián Cháng 田常.
Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂 possessed the empire,
controlling Hào 滈
and Bó 亳. The King of Qín 秦 was trapped by Chén Shè 陳涉 with all the land within the six directions.
It was not that the advantage of terrain was not strong,
but that there was no art to defend it.
Neglecting what is near and worrying about what is far away
is like Wú 吳 not settling its own country internally,
but westward cutting off the Huái River (Huái Shuǐ) to contend for supremacy with Qí 齊 and Jìn 晉;
Yuè 越 took advantage of their exhaustion and
attacked their weak points.
If the King of Wú 吳 had used Shēn Xū 申胥,
cultivated virtue,
and not relied extremely on his multitude,
then Gōu Jiàn 勾踐 would not have avoided becoming a border servant on the seacoast,
what schemes would he have dared to contemplate?"
The Grandee said:
"Chǔ 楚, from Mount Wū (Wū Shān), built Fāng Chéng 方城,
attaching Wū 巫
and Qián Zhōng 黔中,
setting up Hán Passes (Hàn Guān) to resist Qín 秦.
Qín 秦 surrounded Shāng 商
, Luò 洛, Xiáo 崤,
and Hán 函, to defend against the feudal lords.
Hán 韓 blocked Yíyáng 宜陽
and Yī Quē 伊闕,
controlled Chéng Gāo 成皋
and Tài Háng 太行,
to secure Zhōu 周 and Zhèng 鄭.
Wèi 魏 built cities along the Luò River (Luò Hé),
blocking mountains and using the river as a belt,
to protect the state of Jìn 晉.
Zhào 趙 connected Fēi Hú 飛狐,
Jù Zhù 句注,
and Mèng Mén 孟門,
to preserve Xíng 邢 and Dài 代.
Yān 燕 fortified Jié Shí 碣石,
cut off Xié Gǔ 邪谷,
and surrounded Yuán Liáo 援遼.
Qí 齊 pacified Ā 阿
and Zhēn 甄, closed Guān Róng 關榮
and Lì 歷, relied on Mount Tài (Tài Shān),
and faced the sea and the Yellow River (Hé 河).
Passes and bridges
are the fortifications of a state,
and mountains and rivers
are the treasures of the nation.
When the people of Xú 徐 destroyed Shū 舒,
the *Chūn Qiū* 春秋
called it 'taking',
disliking their lack of preparedness,
and the ease of obtaining the object.
Therefore, being concerned about invading armies is
like benevolence being wounded by punishment.
A gentleman governing a state
must have impregnable defenses.
The *Yì* 易 says:
'Double gates and striking the clapper
to await violent guests.'
It speaks of the constant cultivation of preparedness."
The Literary Man said:
"Obstructing with defenses is not as good as obstructing with righteousness.
In the past, Tāng 湯, with seventy *lǐ* 里,
governed the empire,
while Shū 舒, with a hundred *lǐ* 里,
was destroyed by an enemy state.
This is why they were seen as bad.
If passes and bridges were reliable enough to depend on,
the Six States (Liù Guó) would not have been annexed by Qín 秦;
if the Yellow River (Hé Hé) and mountains were sufficient to protect,
Qín 秦 would not have been destroyed by Chǔ 楚 and Hàn 漢.
From this perspective,
fortifications are not enough to make one strong,
and high walls are not enough to make one secure.
Doing good leads to prosperity,
doing evil leads to ruin.
The true king widely loves and bestows favor far and wide;
internal and external are of one mind;
all within the four seas come to offer sacrifices according to their duties;
why strike the clapper and wait?
The *Zhuàn* 傳 says:
'The feudal lords having passes and bridges,
and the common people having rank and emolument,
is not a flourishing of peace,
but originated from the Warring States period.' "
9.3 Discourse on Courage, Fifty-First
The Grandee said:
" Jīng Kē's 荊軻 plan, cherished for several years, did not succeed
because a short eighteen-inch dagger is not enough to rely on.
The King of Qín 秦, fearing the unexpected,
and Liè Duàn 列斷 and Bēn Yù 賁育, who could tear apart
wore armor of seven *chǐ* 尺.
If Zhuān Zhū 專諸 had empty hands,
he could not have avoided being captured;
if Yào Lí 要離 had no water,
he could not have accomplished his task.
The world speaks of the strong Chǔ 楚 and the mighty Zhèng 鄭,
having rhinoceros and armored
and the Tangxi 棠谿 [swords].
Relying internally on Jin Cheng (Jīn Chéng) 金城,
and externally employing sharp weapons,
they were able to exert their authority over all the Xia 夏,
and strongly subdue enemy states.
Therefore, when Mèng Bēn 孟賁 flexes his arms,
the crowd looks down on him;
but a coward with preparations
has his courage doubled.
How much more so with the soldiers of Wú 吳
and Chǔ 楚,
brandishing sharp swords,
and triggering strong crossbows,
to compete with the northern barbarians (Hé Lǔ) 貉虜 in the Central Plains (Zhōng Yuán)?
One man being equal to a hundred
is not worth mentioning!
If this were the case,
then the Huns (Hú) 胡, without defending the Gu Xi 谷谿,
without engaging in battle,
and lacking the strength to support the Hàn 漢,
would inevitably surrender.
This is like Shāng Jūn's 商君 fleeing to Wèi 魏,
and Sūn Bìn's 孫臏 defeating Liáng 梁."
The Literary Man said:
"The Táng Xī 棠谿 [swords] of Chǔ 楚
and Zhèng 鄭
, and the Mò Yáng 墨陽 [swords],
are not without their sharpness;
rhinoceros hide and armored armor
are not without their strength;
yet the reason they could not survive
is that sharpness is not enough to rely on.
Qín 秦 annexed the armies of the Six States (Liù Guó),
and, relying on Xiáo 崤
and Hán 函, ruled within the universe.
The strength of metal and stone
and the sharpness of Mò Yé (Mò Yé) 莫耶 [swords] were theirs.
Yet Chén Shèng 陳勝, without the resources of soldiers and people,
and the use of armor and weapons,
used hoes and thorny branches
to break through fortifications.
The Wǔ Zhāo 武昭 [bows] did not strike,
and the Wū Hào 烏號 [arrows] were not fired.
The so-called Jīn Chéng 金城
does not refer to building earthworks high,
and digging deep moats.
The so-called sharp weapons
do not refer to the swords of Wú 吳
and Yuè 越
or the swords of Gān Jiàng 干將.
It means taking morality as the city walls,
and benevolence and righteousness as the outer walls.
No one dares to attack it,
no one dares to enter it.
This is [what characterized] King Wén (Wén Wáng) 文王.
Taking morality as armor,
and benevolence and righteousness as swords,
no one dares to resist it,
no one dares to oppose it.
This is [what characterized] Tāng 湯 and King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) 武王.
Now, not building an impregnable city
and irresistible weapons,
but wanting to rely on the efforts of a single man
and wielding a three-foot blade,
is too trivial!"
The Grandee said:
"[Jīng Kē] carried a dagger and entered the unfathomable and powerful [Qín];
the King of [Qín] panicked, lost his composure, and abandoned his defenses;
the guards were all frightened.
[Zhuān Zhū] wielded a sword to assassinate the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
assassinating King [Wú];
his corpse stood upright,
with his tall hat visible for a thousand *lǐ*.
[Niè Zhèng], from [Wèi],
assassinated his lord in the [Hán] court;
after achieving his goal, he got what he wanted,
retreated, and committed suicide in the court,
exposing his corpse in the market.
Now, if we could truly obtain a brave warrior,
relying on the power of the strong [Hàn],
attacking the [Xiōngnú], who are devoid of righteousness,
controlling their life and death,
and holding them accountable for their transgressions,
like [Cáo Guì] threatening [Qí Huán Gōng],
fulfilling our demands.
Pushing the attack, blunting their sharp edges,
throwing the [Xiōngnú] into chaos,
causing superiors and inferiors to flee from each other,
and then following them closely with light cavalry.
The [Xiōngnú] will surely cross their arms and dare not resist."
The Literary Man said:
"[Tāng] obtained [Yī Yǐn],
and with a small [Bó], he subjugated all within the seas;
King [Wén] obtained [Tài Gōng],
expanding [Fēng] and
[Hào] to encompass the world;
Duke [Huán] of [Qí] obtained [Guǎn Zhòng] and became hegemon over the feudal lords;
Duke [Mù] of [Qín] obtained [Yóu Yú],
and the eight western [Róng] states submitted.
I have heard of attracting the [Mán] and
[Mò] peoples with virtuous sages,
but I have never heard of coercing and killing their rulers to pacify those far away.
The *Shī* says:
'Cherish this central kingdom,
so as to pacify the four quarters.'
Therefore,
'From those [Dǐ] and
[Qiāng], none dare not come to submit.'
It is not because they fear our might,
but because they fear our virtue.
Therefore, the submission of the unrighteous to the righteous
is faster than a fine horse and good bow;
the summoning of the distant by virtue
is faster than fast messengers and relay stations."
9.4 On Meritorious Service, Chapter 52
The Grandee said:
"The [Xiōngnú] have no walls to defend,
no moats to hold,
no long spears and strong crossbows to use,
no accumulated granaries and storehouses,
superiors have no righteous laws,
inferiors have no literate principles,
rulers and ministers are disrespectful and easygoing,
superiors and inferiors have no propriety,
weaving willow branches for houses,
using felt as coverings.
Their bows are plain, their arrows are bone-tipped,
and their horses do not eat grain.
Internally, their defenses are not worth fearing;
externally, their etiquette is not worth mentioning.
The Central Kingdom is the heart of the world,
the gathering place of virtuous scholars,
the assembly of propriety and righteousness,
and the place where wealth is cultivated.
To overcome foolishness with wisdom,
to attack unrighteousness with righteousness,
is like shaking fallen leaves with autumn frost.
The *Chūnqiū* says:
'Duke [Huán] dealt with the [Róng] and
[Dí], driving them away.'
How much more so with the strength of the world?"
The Literary Man said:
"The [Xiōngnú] vehicles have no silver, yellow, silk, or lacquer decorations;
they are simply made for durability;
their silk has no woven patterns or elaborate skirt and collar designs;
they are simply made for completeness.
The men have no carved or ingenious crafts,
or palace or city wall construction;
the women have no embroidered or extravagant tributes,
or delicate silk gauze creations.
They simplify their affairs and focus on utility,
making them easy to produce and difficult to damage.
Although they have no long spears and strong crossbows,
they have war horses and good bows;
every household has them prepared,
and everyone has their uses.
In case of emergency,
they simply draw their bows and mount their horses.
Provisions are not obvious,
but they can provide food for dozens of days.
They use mountains and valleys as city walls,
and use water and grass as granaries.
Their laws are simple and easy to understand,
their demands are few and easy to supply.
Therefore, their punishments are lenient and rarely needed,
and their commands are obeyed with a gesture.
They may be lax in etiquette, but they are steadfast in trust;
they may be lacking in writing, but they are quick in action.
Therefore, although they have no books on propriety and righteousness,
they carve bones and inscribe wood;
the officials have ways to remember,
and superiors and inferiors have ways to command and serve each other.
The officials who plan for the county government
all say it is easy,
but in reality it is difficult;
this is why [Qín] wanted to drive them away but instead suffered its own demise.
Therefore, weapons are instruments of ill omen
and should not be used lightly.
Turning strength into weakness and
turning survival into ruin can happen
in a single morning."
The Grandee said:
"[Lǔ Lián] said:
'The [Qín] court used its scholars like tools and
enslaved its people.'
Therefore, its policies were harsh and short-lived.
[Gāo Huángdì] received the mandate to pacify the violence and chaos,
and his achievements and virtue were lofty and grand,
as great as Heaven itself.
Then [Wén] and
[Jǐng] continued his legacy and embellished it.
As for the late emperor, he attacked the unrighteous and
expelled the unworthy,
to reveal the path of benevolence and sagacity,
the pure foundation of perfect virtue.
This is the accumulation of many years of benevolence and righteousness by the sage kings.
Now, the Literary Man cites the governance of a lost and failed state
and compares it to the present,
saying that the [Xiōngnú] are difficult to deal with,
which is quite appropriate!"
The Literary Man said:
"During the time of [Yú Shì],
the [Sān Miáo] did not submit,
and [Yǔ] wanted to attack them.
[Shùn] said:
'It is because my virtue has not yet been understood.'
He retreated and cultivated his government,
and the [Sān Miáo] submitted.
For lands that cannot be pastured
and peoples that cannot be governed,
the sage kings do not use weapons
or engage in forceful measures,
considering it unworthy to trouble the common people and burden the Central Kingdom.
Now, the enlightened king cultivates the legacy of the sages,
propagates virtue and transformation,
yet the court has schemes to use coercion
and values meritorious service;
I truly find this strange.
When ministers rely on the power of the realm,
exploit the resources of the state,
enjoy the benefits for themselves, and disregard their ruler,
this is how [Wèi Tuó] and
[Zhāng Hán] became kings,
and [Qín] lost its government.
[Sūnzi] said:
'Now, affairs of state
change a hundred times a day,
yet if it does not perish,
it can be reformed.
But once the troops are sent out into the plains and open pastures,
and the drums sound and arrows fly,
even if you have the wisdom of [Yáo] and
[Shùn],
it cannot be changed.'
If you fight and win,
retreat and cultivate propriety and righteousness,
following the example of the three dynasties,
benevolence and righteousness will be attached to you.
To win battles and not rest,
resulting in personal death and national destruction,
King [Wú] is an example."
The Grand Master said:
"He who shouts with the wind easily projects his voice;
he who acts according to the times easily exerts his strength.
Wén (文) and Wǔ (武) retained surplus strength
and did not plan for their descendants,
therefore their virtue declined in three generations.
Zhāo Wáng (昭王) campaigned south
and died without returning.
Fán Bó (凡伯) was imprisoned
and prevented from communicating.
Jìn (晉) took Jiāo (郊) and
Pèi (沛), and the royal army was defeated at Máoróng (茅戎).
Now, the southwestern barbarian tribes
are descendants of Chǔ Zhuāng (楚莊);
the king of Cháoxiǎn (朝鮮)
is a refugee from Yān (燕).
Nányuè Wèi Tuó (南越尉佗) rose up in the Central Kingdom
and established himself as king.
Their virtue is extremely thin,
yet they all reject the greatness of the empire,
each considering himself the master of a single province,
stubborn and arrogant,
calling themselves 'old men.'
The late emperor planned for ten thousand generations,
fearing the troubles of Jìzhōu (冀州)
and the calamities of Nán Jīng (南荊).
Therefore, he sent the Left General with ships to pacify them.
Without the bloodshed of a single blade,
they all became officials of the central government.
During the time of the Seven Kingdoms,
each possessed ten thousand chariots,
faced south and called themselves kings,
raised battle-axes and threatened the enemy states for generations,
but in the end, they could not avoid bowing their heads and being captured by Qín (秦).
Now, the Xiongnu (匈奴) do not consider themselves vassals and subjects of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
nor do they possess the resources of the Six Kingdoms
or the plans of wise men.
From this perspective, the difficulty or ease
can be clearly seen."
The Literary Man said:
"Qín (秦) destroyed the Six Kingdoms,
captured the seven kings,
and clearly had strength to spare.
They thought that Chīyóu (蚩尤) could not harm them,
nor could the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì 黃帝) reprimand them.
But by the time of the Second Emperor, he was assassinated at Wàngyí (望夷),
and Ziyīng (子嬰) surrendered to Chǔ (楚) with a rope around his neck.
They did not even achieve the bowing of the heads of the seven kings.
Had the Six Kingdoms existed in parallel,
Qín (秦) would still have been in the Warring States period,
and certainly would not have perished.
How can this be demonstrated?
From Xiào Gōng (孝公) to Shǐ Huáng (始皇),
generation after generation, they were the heroes among the feudal lords,
for over a hundred years.
But after unifying the empire,
it perished in fourteen years.
Why?
Because there was no external worry of enemy states,
and internally they indulged themselves.
Except for sages,
there has never been anyone who achieved their ambitions without becoming arrogant and dissolute."
9.5 On Zōu (鄒), Chapter 53
The Grand Master said:
"Zōu Zǐ (鄒子) criticized the scholars and Mohists of later generations
for not understanding the vastness of Heaven and Earth,
the clarity and expansiveness of the Way.
They wanted to explain nine turns with one note,
and know all directions by guarding one corner,
just as they want to know the height and depth without a level,
and know the square and round without a compass and square.
Therefore, he deduced the cycle of beginning and end of great sages
to enlighten kings and dukes.
First, he listed the famous mountains and valleys of the Central Kingdom,
extending to overseas.
What is called the Central Kingdom
is one eighty-first of the world,
named the Red County Divine Continent (Chìxiàn Shénzhōu 赤縣神州),
and divided into nine provinces.
Continuous mountains and lands are not connected,
so it forms one province,
with a large ocean encircling its exterior.
This is what is called the Eight Extremes,
where the boundaries of Heaven and Earth meet.
The *Yǔ Gòng* (禹貢) also recorded the height and depth, plains and marshes of mountains and rivers,
but did not understand the distance of the Great Way.
Therefore, Qín (秦) wanted to reach the nine provinces and the surrounding ocean,
to govern the barbarians and receive homage from all nations.
The scholars guarded the concerns of their fields
and the solidity of their neighborhoods,
not understanding the meaning of the world."
The Literary Man said:
"Yáo (堯) employed Yǔ (禹) as Minister of Works
to regulate the water and land,
cutting down trees along the mountains,
determining heights and depths, and ordering the nine provinces.
Zōu Yǎn (鄒衍) was not a sage;
he created strange errors
to confuse the rulers of the Six Kingdoms
in order to have his theories accepted.
This is what the *Spring and Autumn Annals* calls
'a commoner confusing the feudal lords.'
Confucius (Kǒngzǐ 孔子) said:
'If you cannot serve men,
how can you serve spirits?'
If you do not understand what is near,
how can you know the surrounding oceans?
Therefore, what is of no use,
the gentleman does not do;
what is of no benefit to governance,
the gentleman does not follow.
The Three Kings believed in the classics and the Way,
and their virtue shone over the four seas;
the Warring States believed in flowery words,
and their destruction was like a collapsing mountain.
In the past, Emperor Shǐ (始) of Qín (秦) had already swallowed the empire
and wanted to annex all nations,
but lost his thirty-six commanderies;
he wanted to reach the surrounding oceans,
but lost his prefectures and counties.
To understand the greater meaning like this,
is not as good as sticking to a small plan."
9.6 On Zī (菑), Chapter 54
The Grand Master said:
"Witches and ritualists cannot be worshipped alongside [proper deities],
and scholars cannot be argued with at length.
They believe in the past and doubt the present,
affirming themselves and denying others.
For one who speaks of antiquity, examine it in the present;
for one who speaks of the distant, compare it to the near.
The sun and moon are in the sky,
their evidence is in man.
Calamities and anomalies,
periods of early death,
the transformations of Yin and Yang,
the order of the four seasons,
water, fire, metal, wood,
omens of good and bad fortune,
the intelligence of ghosts and spirits,
the blessings of sacrifices,
the movements of the sun and moon,
the records of the stars,
the reasons for indirect speech—
what is their origin?
If you don't know, be silent;
do not recklessly disturb the ears."
The Literary Man said:
“At the beginning, Xiāng Dū’s chancellor, Dǒng Shēng, promoted the doctrine of *yīn* and *yáng*,
that the four seasons follow each other,
the father gives birth to it,
the son nourishes it,
the mother completes it,
and the son stores it away.
Therefore, spring brings forth life,
representing benevolence; summer causes growth,
representing virtue; autumn brings about completion,
representing righteousness; winter stores away,
representing propriety. This is the order of the four seasons,
which the sages take as their model.
Punishment cannot be relied upon to bring about transformation,
therefore, widespread moral education is essential.
When speaking of the distant, one must examine the near,
therefore, one must act with inner consideration.
Thus, punishments are applied as if they were applied to oneself,
and diligent labor is done as if it were done on one's own body.
How could one bear to kill one's innocent children
to pursue useless endeavors,
exhaust what one relies on,
and reach the Yíng Hǎi?
Indeed, the people of Yuè admire shellfish and simplify the grand offerings of oxen,
and the vulgar enjoy *zazhe* music and find *sháohù* music strange.
Therefore, those who do not know flavors
consider fragrance to be stench;
those who do not know the Way
consider beautiful words to be disturbing to the ears.
People do not have predetermined lifespans;
each determines their fate based on their likes and dislikes.
Yì and Ào did not die natural deaths despite their skill and strength,
and Zhì Bó ruined himself through greed and ruthlessness.
The evidence of heavenly calamities
and the response of auspicious omens
are like expecting repayment for giving,
each comes according to its kind.
Therefore, those who are fond of doing good
are aided by heaven with blessings,
which are symbolic omens.
The *Yì* says:
'Heaven aids them,
good fortune will bring success in everything.'
Those who are fond of doing evil
are repaid by heaven with misfortune,
which are demonic calamities.
The *Chūnqiū* says:
'In response to this, there will be heavenly calamities.'
Zhōu Wén and
Wǔ respected the virtuous and accepted admonishments,
reverently guarded against danger,
possessed pure virtue and received supreme blessings,
and the deities assisted them.
The *Shī* says:
'Sending down abundant blessings,
sending down great blessings.'
The sun is *yáng*,
and the way of *yáng* is clear;
the moon is *yīn*,
and the way of *yīn* is obscure;
these exemplify the righteousness of the sovereign being superior and the minister being inferior.
Therefore, when the sunlight is strong above,
the kinds of *yīn* disappear below;
when the moon is full in the sky,
shellfish are abundant in the depths.
Therefore, if ministers are not subservient,
then the *yīn* and *yáng* will be out of harmony,
and the sun and moon will undergo changes;
if government policies are not fair,
then floods and droughts will be untimely,
and locusts will be born.
These are the responses of disasters and abnormalities.
The four seasons follow their order,
and people take their work from them;
stars are arrayed in the sky,
and people model their actions on them.
The constant stars are like dukes and ministers,
and the numerous stars are like the myriad people.
If the arrayed stars are correct, then the numerous stars are orderly;
if the constant stars are in chaos, then the numerous stars will fall.”
The Grandee said:
“The Literary Man speaks of the kinds of hardness and softness,
and the five phases give rise to each other in turn.
The *Yì* illuminates *yīn* and *yáng*,
and the *Shū* excels in the five elements.
Spring generates and summer grows,
therefore fire is generated from *yín* wood,
which is a *yáng* category;
autumn generates and winter dies,
therefore water is generated from *shēn* metal,
which is a *yīn* thing.
The four seasons and five elements
alternately decline and rise,
*yīn* and *yáng* are different categories,
and water and fire cannot be contained in the same vessel.
Metal is completed by earth
and dies by fire;
metal is generated from *sì*,
what reasoning or words can explain this?”
The Literary Man said:
“Weapons
are instruments of ill omen.
Strong armor and sharp weapons
are a disaster for the world.
Using the mother to control the son
allows for long duration.
The sages imitate this,
suppressing rather than flaunting them.
The *Shī* says:
'We store away shields and spears,
we sheath bows and arrows,
we seek excellent virtue,
extensively throughout this Xia.'
The declining age is not so.
Going against the way of heaven to satisfy violent hearts,
corpses pile up and blood flows,
to contend for land.
Treating their people like prisoners,
destroying people's sacrifices,
killing people's children,
as if eradicating grass and trees,
and those punished are crowded on the roads.
Applying what they hate to others.
Therefore, the state is destroyed,
and they themselves suffer misfortune,
as was the case with the Qín king.”
The Grandee said:
“Metal is generated from *sì*,
and punishments are slightly increased,
therefore shepherd's purse and barley die in summer.
The *Yì* says:
'When you step on frost,
solid ice will come.'
Autumn begins to bring frost,
and plants wither and fall;
combine winter with carrying out executions,
and all things will be stored away completely.
Spring and summer generate and grow,
and it is beneficial to practice benevolence.
Autumn and winter kill and store away,
and it is beneficial to implement punishments.
Therefore, if one plants out of season,
it will not grow even if it sprouts.
Practicing virtue in autumn and winter
is called going against the way of heaven.
The *Yuèlìng* states:
'Cool winds arrive,
a killing atmosphere moves,
crickets chirp,
and clothes of fur are made.
The Son of Heaven carries out minor punishments,
beginning with offering prey to the tiger,
in order to comply with the heavenly order.'
The Literary Man harmonizes with the four seasons,
unites *yīn* and *yáng*,
values virtue and eliminates punishments.
If it were like this,
then hawks and falcons would not be fierce,
wild beasts would not seize,
there would be no autumn hunts,
and no winter field hunts.”
The Literary Man said:
“The way of heaven favors life and dislikes killing,
favors rewarding and dislikes punishing.
Therefore, it causes *yáng* to reside in fullness and proclaim virtue and bestow blessings,
and *yīn* to be hidden in emptiness and to act as the assistant and helper of *yáng*.
*Yáng* is firm, and *yīn* is gentle;
the last season cannot surpass the first.
This is because heaven despises winter and values spring,
extending *yáng* and suppressing *yīn*.
Therefore, the king faces south to listen to the world,
turning his back on *yīn* and facing *yáng*,
prioritizing virtue and relegating punishment.
If frost and snow arrive late,
the five grains can still mature.
If hail and fog fall in summer,
all things will be harmed.
From this, one can see that
using strict punishments to govern the state
is like relying on autumn and winter to make grains mature.
Therefore, laws and ordinances
are the tools for governing evil,
and not the wind of supreme governance.
Therefore, in ancient times,
enlightened kings enriched their moral education
and relaxed their punishments.
Nets leaked fish large enough to swallow boats,
and punishments were applied outside the strict boundaries of the plumb line and ink marker,
and when it reached its end,
the people did not violate the prohibitions.”
10.1 *Xíng Dé* (Punishments and Virtue) 55
The Grandee said:
"Regulations are for teaching the people,
and laws are for restraining the wicked.
When regulations are strict, the people are cautious;
when laws are established, wickedness is forbidden.
If the net is sparse, beasts escape;
if the law is lax, crimes are overlooked.
If crimes are overlooked, the people become unrestrained and lightly break the prohibitions.
Therefore, if prohibitions are not enforced,
even the timid will seek luck;
but if punishments are certain,
even Zhí (蹠) and Qiāo (蹻) will not offend.
Therefore, the ancients created the five punishments
that cut the skin, yet the people did not overstep the bounds."
The Literatus said:
"If the road is too winding,
people do not know which way to go;
if the laws are too numerous,
the people do not know how to avoid them.
Therefore, the way a king establishes laws
should be as clear as the sun and moon,
so the people are not confused;
as broad as the great road,
so the people are not deluded.
Even in the hidden and distant regions,
even the wise can discern them,
and even young women and children
all know how to avoid them.
Thus, the laws are not violated,
and prisons are not needed.
In the past, the laws of the Qín (秦) dynasty were as numerous as autumn tea
and as tightly knit as congealed fat.
Yet superiors and inferiors evaded each other,
and deceitful practices arose.
When officials tried to govern,
it was like trying to put out a fire with rotten wood:
they could not stop it.
It was not that the net was sparse and crimes leaked through,
but that ritual propriety and righteousness were abandoned and reliance was placed on punishments.
Today, there are more than a hundred chapters of statutes and ordinances,
the writing is verbose,
and the names of crimes are severe.
When the commanderies and states use them,
they are sometimes puzzled to a greater or lesser degree.
Even officials who are learned and familiar with them
do not know how to act,
let alone the ignorant people!
Statutes and ordinances collect dust in the storerooms,
and officials cannot even read them all,
let alone the ignorant people!
This is why judgments increase in number
and the people violate prohibitions more and more.
'It is appropriate to imprison, it is appropriate to jail,
clutching millet, they go out to divine;
from where can they get grain?'
This is a criticism of the proliferation of penal laws.
There are a great many categories of mourning garments for relatives;
from above to below, those who kill are killed,
but the mourning grades do not exceed five.
There are three thousand types of the five punishments,
from above to below, attaching to each,
but the number of crimes does not exceed five.
Therefore, the way to govern the people
is to focus on enriching their education."
The Grandee said:
"The Literatus says that the way a king establishes laws
should be as broad as the great road.
Now, the imperial highways are not small,
but the people openly violate them
because the penalties are too light.
From a height of a thousand *rèn* (仞),
people do not lightly jump;
from a weight of a thousand *jūn* (鈞),
people do not lightly lift.
Shāng Jūn (商君) punished someone for scattering ashes on the road,
and the people of Qín (秦) were well-governed.
Therefore, those who steal horses are put to death,
and those who steal cattle are punished severely,
in order to emphasize the fundamental and cut off the means of minor offenses.
Military weapons are named food,
in order to assist the frontier and emphasize military preparedness.
Wounding and killing receive the same punishment
in order to weigh down their minds and examine their intent.
It is like the *Lǔ* (魯) state using the *Chǔ* (楚) army to attack *Qí* (齊),
which the *Chūnqiū* (春秋) chronicles condemned.
Therefore, making the light into the heavy
and the shallow into the deep
has a cause and effect.
The subtle aspects of the law
are certainly not known by the masses."
The Literatus said:
"The *Shī* (詩) says:
'The Zhōu (周) road is like a whetstone,
as straight as an arrow.'
This speaks of its ease.
'The gentleman walks on it,
the common man sees it.'
This speaks of its clarity.
Therefore, when virtue is clear, it is easy to follow,
and when laws are concise, they are easy to implement.
Now, the imperial highways wind through hills and valleys,
snaking around the world,
making them a trap for the people for ten thousand *lǐ*.
If you spread nets and hang their grain,
set up pitfalls and block their paths,
and adorn them with arrows and spears on top,
how can they avoid them?
If you gather what they desire,
open up what benefits them,
and decline benevolence and righteousness,
how can they not cross the line?
Therefore, in the end,
they go so far as to attack cities and enter towns,
damage the gold in the treasuries,
and steal the ritual vessels of the ancestral temples.
How can this be merely the height of a thousand *rèn* (仞)
or the weight of a thousand *jūn* (鈞)!
Guǎnzi (管子) said:
'If the four cardinal principles are not upheld,
even Gāoyáo (皋陶) cannot be an officer.'
Therefore, when moral education is abandoned, fraud and deceit prevail,
and when ritual propriety and righteousness are destroyed, wickedness arises.
This means there is no benevolence or righteousness.
Benevolence
is the effect of love,
and righteousness
is the appropriateness of things.
Therefore, the gentleman loves benevolence and extends it to things,
governing the near and extending it to the far.
The *Zhuàn* (傳) says:
'Of all living things,
none is more precious than man;
and of what a ruler values,
nothing is more important than man.'
Therefore, Heaven produces all things to serve man,
and the ruler loves man to accord with Heaven.
I have heard of using the six domestic animals and birds to nourish man,
but I have never heard of using what nourishes man to harm him.
When the stables of Lǔ (魯) burned down,
Confucius dismissed the court
and asked about the people but not the horses,
valuing people over animals.
Now, those who steal horses are put to death,
and those who steal cattle are punished severely.
If someone rides a horse-drawn carriage in the middle of the imperial highway,
the officials raise a fuss and do not stop,
considering it the same as stealing a horse,
and the punishment is also death.
Now, if someone injures another and flees with his sword,
can he also be considered to have stolen weapons from the armory and be killed for it?
If a ruler establishes laws and the people violate them,
can it also be considered rebellion and lightly break the ruler's promise?
If it is serious, it can result in death,
and if it is light, it can be avoided;
this is not the intention of forbidding transgressions through law.
Law
is established based on human nature,
not to set up crimes to entrap people.
Therefore, in the *Chūnqiū* (春秋)'s adjudication of cases,
they judged the crime based on the intention.
Those whose intentions were good but violated the law were acquitted,
and those whose intentions were evil but conformed to the law were punished.
Now, if someone injures another without causing any harm,
his intention is not very evil, but he conforms to the law,
is he to be considered a thief and injurer?
Or is it the fault of the enforcer of the law?
Why is there no satisfaction in people's hearts!
In ancient times,
those who wounded others and caused a wound were punished,
those who stole and had stolen goods were fined,
and those who killed were put to death.
Now, taking someone's weapon to injure him,
the crime is the same as killing someone;
is this not missing the ultimate intention?"
The Grandee bowed his head and did not respond.
The Yùshǐ said:
"Those who enforce the law are the reins and bit of the state,
and punishments are the rudder and oars of the state.
Therefore, if the reins and bit are not well-maintained,
even Wáng Liáng cannot go far;
if the rudder and oars are not set,
even skilled craftsmen cannot cross the water.
Hán Feīzi lamented that rulers are unable to understand their laws and power,
control their ministers,
enrich the country and strengthen the military,
to resist enemies and defend against calamities.
They are deluded by the writings of foolish Confucians,
doubt the plans of worthy men,
promote the parasites of frivolous indulgence,
and place them above those with merit and substance,
yet they desire the state to be well-governed.
This is like removing the steps and expecting to climb high,
or controlling a runaway horse without reins and a bit.
Now that penal laws are fully prepared,
yet the people still violate them,
what if there were no laws?
Surely there would be chaos!"
The Wénxué said:
"Reins and bit are tools for controlling,
and they are adjusted by skilled craftsmen.
Laws and power are tools for governing,
and they are transformed by virtuous men.
If the reins are held by the wrong person,
the horse will run wild.
If the rudder is held by the wrong person,
the boat will capsize and be damaged.
In the past, the state of Wú sent Zǎi Pī to hold the rudder and he wrecked their boat,
the state of Qín sent Zhào Gāo to hold the reins and he overturned their carriage.
Now, if we abandon the arts of benevolence and righteousness
and employ those who focus on punishments and titles,
we will repeat the affairs of Wú and Qín.
As for being a ruler, one should emulate the Three Kings;
as for being a minister, one should emulate Zhōu Gōng;
as for methods, one should emulate Kǒngzǐ.
These are unchanging principles for generations.
Hán Feī rejected the former kings and did not follow them,
abandoned righteous commands and did not obey them,
and eventually fell into a trap,
was imprisoned,
and died as a guest in Qín.
He who does not understand the great way but is skilled in petty debates
will only harm himself."
10.2 Shēn Hán Fifth-sixth
The Yùshǐ said:
"If we wait for Zhōu Gōng to become a minister,
there would be no separate states.
If we wait for Kǒngzǐ to have learning,
there would be no Confucianism or Mohism.
If clothes have a small tear,
it can be mended, but you must wait for a whole piece to replace it;
if the government has a small defect,
laws can prevent it, but you must wait for the *Yǎ* and *Sòng* to govern it;
this is like dismissing the neighbor's doctor,
and seeking Yú Fū to treat the disease,
abandoning the water in the dirty pond,
and waiting for the rivers and seas to put out the fire.
Circuitous and not direct,
deficient and without purpose,
this is why teachings and orders are not followed and governance is troublesome.
Those who are good at governing
repair what is broken,
and stop what is overflowing,
therefore Wú Qǐ used law to govern Chǔ and Wèi, and Shēn Bùhài and Shāng Yāng used law to strengthen Qín and Hán.
The Wénxué said:
"Those who govern the state select the multitude and appoint the worthy,
those who study widely examine and achieve goodness,
why must it be Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ!
Therefore it is said to follow the law.
Now, Shāng Yāng violated the way of the sages,
disturbed the customs of Qín,
and afterwards the government declined and could not be governed,
lost and could not be recovered.
A foolish man sets fire to the marsh,
and cannot revive it;
a bee or scorpion stings a person,
releases death and cannot stop its poison.
Stopping it when it is troublesome,
calming it when it is agitated,
superiors and inferiors are weary and disturbed,
and the chaos increases.
Therefore, the sage's teachings
shine above with the sun and moon,
and flow below with heaven and earth,
how can it be said to be a small remedy!"
The Yùshǐ said:
"If clothes are torn and not mended,
they will worsen day by day;
if leaks are not stopped,
they will increase day by day.
The Great River's initial breach was at Hùzǐ,
a mere trickle,
but in the end,
it flooded and harmed the Central States,
devastated Liáng and Chǔ, broke Cáo and Wèi,
city walls were destroyed,
possessions floated away,
the people lived in trees,
for a thousand *lǐ* there were no dwellings,
causing the orphans and widows to have nothing to rely on,
and the old and weak to have nowhere to return.
Therefore, the late emperor mourned their calamity,
personally inspected the riverbanks,
and performed the work of Yǔ.
The river returned to its course,
and Cáo and Wèi were at peace.
The people wore his merit,
sang his virtue,
singing
'The Xuānfáng is blocked,
ten thousand blessings come',
it is the same,
how can it not be a small remedy!"
The Wénxué said:
"A river bursts like a jug's mouth,
and destroys a thousand *lǐ*,
how much more so when ritual bursts?
Its harm is also great!
Now, judging lawsuits amounts to tens of thousands a year,
and lawbreaking increases even more,
is the calamity limited only to Cáo and Wèi!
To know that blocking the Xuānfáng brings blessings,
but not to know that blocking the source of chaos brings order to the world.
When the state of Zhōu used it,
punishments were abandoned and not used,
the black-haired people were obedient,
the four seasons each fulfilled their order,
and the world was not lonely.
The *Sòng* says:
'Grant us long life,
with great blessings.'
This bestowing of blessings
is also not small!
If sincerity, trustworthiness, ritual, and righteousness are like the Xuānfáng,
then achievements have already been established,
and one can fold one's hands and do nothing.
What remedy is there for officials,
and what blocking is there for laws?"
The Yùshǐ said:
"Sharp sickles and hoes are beneficial to the five grains and eradicate the harm of weeds.
Understanding reason and rectifying the law is what the wicked hate and the good people bless.
Therefore, crooked wood hates straight lines,
and the wicked hate righteous laws.
Therefore, the sages are discerning in right and wrong,
and observant in order and chaos,
therefore they establish clear laws,
display strict punishments,
prevent wrongdoing and correct evil,
like the compass and square correcting crookedness.
Therefore, water is a preparation for fire,
and law is a prohibition to stop wickedness.
Without law and power,
even worthy men cannot govern;
without armor and weapons,
even Sūnzi and Wúqǐ cannot defeat the enemy.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ advocated benevolence and righteousness and the people followed like the wind,
but Bó Yí fled to Shǒuyáng and the people could not be transformed."
The Literary Man said:
"The law can punish people but cannot make them honest;
it can kill people but cannot make them benevolent.
What is valued in a good doctor
is that he carefully examines the condition and eliminates the pathogenic factors;
it is not that he applies needles and stones to puncture the skin.
What is valued in a good official
is that he eliminates evil before it sprouts,
making people not do wrong;
it is not that he imprisons and executes them.
The so-called good officials of today,
if they are meticulous in investigation, will bring disaster to their people;
if they are forceful, they will oppress their subordinates.
They do not seek the origin of the law,
but rely solely on their own cruel hearts.
They use literary accusations and fabricated laws
to entrap the innocent
and implicate those without guilt,
extending to sons and fathers,
and to younger and older brothers.
When one person is guilty,
the entire village is terrified,
and ten families flee in terror,
like carbuncles festering together,
or sexual licentiousness spreading.
One joint moves, and a hundred branches shake.
The *Shī* says:
'Those who are guilty, let them be punished for their crimes;
they have already received their due.
But if the innocent
are implicated and destroyed together,'
it is a painful grievance that the innocent are implicated.
It is not that we worry about the inadequacy of hoes and weeding tools,
but that we abandon weeding the grass and cultivate the seedlings.
It is not that we worry about the lack of level and plumb lines,
but that we abandon correcting the crooked and use the straight rope.
Therefore, relatives who err need not be punished;
this is like not using the hoe.
Those distant and estranged who have merit need not be rewarded;
this is like not nurturing the seedlings.
Therefore, the world does not worry about the lack of laws,
but worries about the lack of laws that are certainly enforced."
10.3 *Zhōu Qín Dì Wǔshíqī*
The Imperial Secretary said:
"The *Chūnqiū* does not give names to criminals;
they are referred to as 'cloud thieves,'
thereby despising those who are punished and severing them from human relationships.
Therefore, the ruler does not treat them as subjects,
and scholars do not treat them as friends;
they have no place in the community.
Thus, the people are ashamed to commit crimes.
Now, disobedient people
violate public laws to indulge each other,
abandon their relatives,
are unable to sacrifice themselves for principle,
flee and connect with each other,
and willingly fall into crime.
Is it not fitting that they be subjected to punishment and execution?
Within a room,
among fathers and elder brothers,
it is like limbs connected to the body;
when one joint moves, it is known in the heart.
Therefore, from now on, from guānnèi hóu downwards,
divide the land into groups of five,
observe each other at home,
supervise each other's comings and goings.
If the father does not teach his son,
and the elder brother does not correct the younger brother,
who else should be held responsible?"
The Literary Man said:
"In ancient times,
the Zhōu dynasty emphasized propriety and clarified its teachings.
When propriety was complete and teachings were clear,
only then were those who did not follow treated with punishment.
When punishments were just,
the people did not resent them.
Therefore, Shùn administered four punishments, and the world was in complete submission;
he punished the unkind.
Those of lighter or heavier offenses each accepted their punishment.
Punishment was certainly applied without pardon,
and pardons were only for those whose guilt was doubtful.
If this were the case,
how could the world have disobedient people to punish?
Now, murderers live,
and robbers and thieves become rich.
Therefore, good people become internally lax,
stop plowing, and lose heart.
In ancient times,
gentlemen did not associate with criminals;
criminals were not considered human.
Their bodies were exiled and they brought shame to future generations,
so whether wise or foolish,
all were ashamed.
Now, people without good conduct
covet profit and trap themselves,
enduring humiliation and abandoning propriety and righteousness,
constantly seeking to survive.
Why?
Because one day in the silkworm room,
before the wound is healed,
they guard the ruler,
entering and exiting the palace.
From this they receive salaries,
eat from the imperial kitchen, and enjoy rewards.
Their bodies become honored,
and their wives and children obtain abundance.
Therefore, some even join the ranks of high officials,
facing the knife and saw without pity.
How much more so the common people?
What shame is there!
Abandoning moral education
and demanding propriety and righteousness is to abuse the people.
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says:
'If a son is guilty, arrest his father;
if a subject is guilty, arrest his ruler.
This is the greatest mistake in judgment.'
Now, punishing the father for the son's crime,
and the elder brother for the younger brother's crime,
relatives are implicated,
and groups of ten and five are connected.
It is like pulling the roots to reach the flowers and leaves,
or injuring a small finger to burden the four limbs.
In this way,
punishing the innocent by punishing the guilty;
if the innocent are punished,
then the innocent in the world will be few.
Zāng Wénzhòng governed Lǔ,
overcoming its thieves but boasting about it.
Zǐgòng said:
'The people will deceive,
let alone thieves!'
Therefore, a good official is not one who makes many judgments,
and a good doctor is not one who performs many pricks.
Zǐchǎn punished two people
and killed one,
and people did not pick up lost items on the road
and the people had no deceitful intentions.
Therefore, being parents to the people
is like nurturing sick children,
increasing kindness and generosity.
Since the law of mutual accusation and self-reporting was established,
the kindness of flesh and blood has been abandoned,
and crimes and punishments have increased.
I have heard that parents hide their children,
even if they are guilty,
because they do not want them to confess.
The son hides his father,
and the father hides his son.
I have never heard of fathers and sons being mutually implicated.
I have heard of brothers being able to delay pursuit to spare a thief,
but I have never heard of brothers being mutually implicated.
I have heard of hating evil stopping with the person,
hating the origin and punishing the chief villain,
but I have never heard of groups of ten and five being mutually implicated.
Lǎozǐ said:
'When the ruler has no desires, the people are simple;
when the ruler is not busy, the people are naturally wealthy.'
Let rulers be rulers, and subjects be subjects;
let fathers be fathers, and sons be sons.
What is the purpose of dividing the land into groups of five,
and what responsibility does the government have?"
The Imperial Secretary said:
"Carrying the weight of a thousand *jūn*
to climb to the highest point,
descending the steep cliffs of a precipice,
looking down into an unfathomable abyss,
even with the agility of Qìng Jì,
and the courage of Bēn and Yù,
no one would not tremble in fear,
knowing that a fall would mean that their head and brains would be splattered on the rocks.
Therefore, those who have never been burned do not dare to hold fire,
seeing that it can burn.
Those who have never been injured do not dare to hold a blade,
seeing that it can injure.
Because they know it is wrong,
and the punishment will certainly be applied,
and execution will extend to fathers and elder brothers,
they will certainly fear and do good.
Therefore, establishing laws and regulations
is like facing a hundred-*rèn* deep ravine,
holding fire and stepping on a blade.
Then the people will fear and be cautious,
and dare not violate the prohibitions.
A kind mother has a spoiled son,
because she cannot bear to be strict.
A strict family has no rebellious servants,
because they are diligent in demanding accountability.
Now, not establishing the strictness that a family needs to control its subordinates,
but cultivating the kindness that spoils a son,
is truly a delusion."
The Literary Scholar said:
“Zhòu (紂) had the torture of the heated bronze pillar,
and Qín (秦) had the law of confiscating families into servitude.
Zhào Gāo (趙高) used harsh interpretations of the law to decide guilt within the court,
and officials used strict laws to judge and punish outside the court.
The dead lay pillowed upon each other,
and the punished were in constant view.
The common people looked askance and walked carefully,
trembling without cold.
The *Shī* (詩) says:
‘They say that Heaven is high;
I dare not but be contracted.
They say that Earth is thick;
I dare not but tread carefully.
Alas for the men of today,
Why are they like snakes and lizards!’
At such a time,
was it only risking fire and treading on blades?
Yet fathers and sons turned their backs on each other,
brothers were disrespectful to each other,
to the point where blood relatives slaughtered each other,
and superiors and inferiors murdered each other.
This was not because punishments were light and penalties uncertain,
but because decrees were too strict and kindness and grace were not extended.
Therefore, when the government is lenient, the people are close to their superiors;
when the government is strict, the people plot against their ruler.
Jìn Lì (晉厲) was imprisoned,
and the Second Emperor was killed.
Where was the failure to violate harsh laws,
or the absence of fierce slaves in a strict household?
The sage knew this,
and therefore strived for harmony and not for authority.
Therefore, Emperor Gāo (高) abolished the harsh laws of Qín (秦)
to appease the resentful and embittered people,
and to foster a spirit of lasting harmony,
fearing only that punishment would be severe and virtue thin.
Therefore, his kindness was boundless,
and his beneficence flowed to later generations.
Shāng Yāng (商鞅) and
Wú Qǐ (吳起) considered the laws of Qín (秦) and
Chǔ (楚) to be light and increased them,
endangering their lords
and ruining themselves.
Is this perhaps not like a cruel mother!”
10.4 *Zhào Shèng Dì Wǔshíbā* (詔聖第五十八)
The Imperial Secretary said:
“The Xiàhòu (夏后) clan did not go back on their word,
the Yīn (殷) made oaths,
and the Zhōu (周) formed alliances;
the integrity of their virtue waned more and more.
Without the men of Wén (文) and
Wǔ (武),
who wished to cultivate their laws,
this is why the Yīn (殷) and
Zhōu (周) lost power
and were seized by the feudal lords.
Therefore, when clothes are worn out, new leather is used;
when laws are broken, new regulations are made.
In the time of Emperor Gāo (高),
the empire was newly settled.
He issued benevolent decrees
and implemented sweeping orders;
this was expediency,
not the norm for correcting disorder and restoring order.
Afterwards,
the laws were gradually violated
and were not in accordance with reason.
Therefore, evil sprouted and the *Fǔ Xíng* (甫刑) was created;
the way of the king declined and the satire in the *Shī* (詩) became evident;
the feudal lords were violent and the *Chūnqiū* (春秋) criticized them.
A net with few meshes cannot catch fish,
and a law of three articles cannot govern.
Therefore, decrees must be increased,
and laws must be multiplied.
Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) drawing clothing patterns was not flattery,
Tāng (湯) and Wǔ (武) tattooing skin was not deliberate;
times and ages differ,
and the tasks of lightness and weight are different.”
The Literary Scholar said:
“The people's reliance on the law
is like a fish's reliance on water;
when the water is clear, it is still;
when it is muddy, it is disturbed.
When it is disturbed, they are uneasy in their dwellings;
when it is still, they enjoy their occupations.
When they enjoy their occupations, they become wealthy;
when they are wealthy, benevolence arises;
when they are sufficient, strife ceases.
Therefore, in the age of Chéng (成) and
Kāng (康),
there was no place to apply rewards,
and no place to add laws.
It was not that they could punish but did not punish;
it was that the people did not violate prohibitions.
It was not that they could reward but did not reward;
it was that the people were all benevolent.
If it were like this,
what could the officials do to govern?
Those who govern the people now
are like clumsy drivers of horses;
when they move, they hold them back;
when they stop, they whip them.
Their bodies are wounded by the whip,
and their mouths are injured by the bit,
and to demand that they make no mistakes,
how can that be possible?
In the campaign at Gān Xī (乾谿), the soil collapsed;
within the Liáng (梁) family, there was internal collapse.
Strict punishments could not prohibit it,
and harsh laws could not stop it.
Therefore, exhausted horses do not fear whips and lashes,
and exhausted people do not fear punishments and laws.
Even if they are increased and piled on,
what benefit would there be?”
The Imperial Secretary said:
“A wall with three blades is difficult for Lóu Jì (樓季);
a mountain so high it touches the clouds is climbed by a shepherd boy.
Therefore, when it is steep, Lóu Jì (樓季) finds the three blades difficult;
when it slopes gently, the shepherd boy easily reaches the mountain peak.
When metal is melted in a furnace,
Zhuāng Qiāo (莊蹻) does not look at it;
when coins and knives are on the road,
a common woman picks them up;
it is not that the common woman is greedy and Zhuāng Qiāo (莊蹻) is honest,
but that the system of weight and importance is different,
and the distinction between benefit and harm is clear.
Therefore, laws and decrees should be revered and not transgressed,
should be overseen and not entered into.
The *Shī* (詩) says:
‘Dare not rashly attack a tiger,
Dare not without a boat cross the river.’
This is because it is of no benefit.
Lǔ (魯) favored propriety but had the troubles of the Jì (季) and
Mèng (孟) families;
Yān Kuài (燕噲) favored abdication but had the disorder of Zǐ Zhī (子之).
Propriety and yielding are insufficient to prohibit evil,
but punishments and laws can stop violence.
An enlightened ruler relies on the law,
and therefore can long control the multitude below
and defend his state for a long time.”
The Literary Scholar said:
“In ancient times,
they made clear the oaths of benevolence and righteousness,
so that the people would not transgress.
To impose punishment above instruction
is to kill without teaching,
and that is tyranny.
Rather than punishments that cannot be transgressed,
it is better to have righteousness that cannot be transgressed.
I have heard of rites and righteousness being practiced and punishments being appropriate,
but I have never heard of punishments being practiced and filial piety and brotherly love flourishing.
A high wall on a narrow foundation
cannot stand.
Strict punishments and harsh laws
cannot last long.
The Second Emperor trusted the plans of Zhào Gāo (趙高),
assigned blame to the virtuous and entrusted execution and judgment to him.
Those being punished filled half the road,
and those dying accumulated daily.
Those who killed many people were considered loyal,
and those who rigorously exhausted the people were considered capable.
The common people could not bear their demands,
and the black-haired people could not bear their punishments.
The whole country shared their sorrow and could not live in peace.
Therefore, regarding matters of excessive labor,
fathers could not get it from their sons;
regarding endless demands,
rulers could not get it from their ministers.
Knowing that death comes but once,
cornered rats will bite weasels,
commoners will rush at ten thousand chariots,
servants will break their bows.
Chén Shèng (陳勝) and
Wú Guǎng (吳廣) are examples of this.
At that time,
the whole country rose up,
and attacked Qín (秦) from all sides.
Before a single year had passed, their altars and land were reduced to ruins.
Where was its ability to long control the multitude below
and defend its state for a long time?”
The Imperial Secretary was silent and did not reply.
An official said:
"Blind musicians do not know black from white but are good at hearing and understanding words.
Confucian scholars do not know how to govern the world but are good at criticizing and commenting.
Those who speak well of Heaven align with human affairs.
Those who speak well of the past examine it in light of the present.
Why are decrees implemented?
Why are laws added?
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武 preserved their full bodies, and the Yīn 殷 and
Zhōu 周 dynasties were well-governed.
The state of Qín 秦 used them,
but the laws failed and were violated.
The standard of two chi and four cun,
is the same in the past and present.
Sometimes it leads to order,
sometimes to chaos.
The *Chūn Qiū 春秋* traces the origins of crimes,
and the *Fǔ Xíng 甫刑* establishes punishments.
Now, I wish to hear about the root of order and chaos,
and the reasons for the success of Zhōu 周 and the failure of Qín 秦."
The Literary Scholar said:
"Spring and summer are seasons of growth,
and the sages modeled their decrees after them.
Autumn and winter are seasons of killing and storing,
and the sages used them as the basis for laws.
Therefore, decrees are
teachings,
used to guide the people;
laws are
punishments,
used to restrain the strong and violent.
These two
are tools for order and chaos,
and the evidence of survival and destruction.
It depends on what the ruler employs.
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武 governed through ritual propriety and righteousness,
clarifying what was good and evil,
and guiding their people with the Way.
Before punishments were applied,
the people themselves acted righteously.
This is why the Yīn 殷 and Zhōu 周 dynasties were well-governed.
When the ruler lacks virtuous teachings
and the people lack legal standards,
relying solely on harsh punishments,
with noses being cut off filling baskets,
and severed feet filling carts,
even the area west of the Yellow River
would be insufficient to contain the exiles of the world.
The one who ultimately perished
was the king of Qín 秦.
It was not that the standard of two chi and four cun was different,
but that his actions were contrary to the past and went against the people's hearts."
10.5 *Dà Lùn Dì Wǔ Shí Jiǔ 大論第五十九*
The official said:
"Moaning over dried bamboo slips,
and reciting the words of dead men,
then the officials are not like literary scholars.
Literary scholars know that prisons are behind the court but do not know what happens there,
they hear the affairs but do not know the affairs' essential business.
Governing the people
is like a master craftsman chiseling,
using an axe and adze to execute his craft,
stopping when the line is true.
Dù Dàfū 杜大夫,
Wáng Zhōngwèi 王中尉 and their like,
measured with law,
judged with punishment,
then banditry and villainy would stop.
Thus, archers rely on targets,
and rulers rely on laws.
Yú 虞 and Xià 夏 used culture,
Yīn 殷 and Zhōu 周 used military force,
different times call for different approaches.
Now to govern a worn-out and corrupt people
with the values of a simple and honest age,
is like delaying to rescue a drowning man,
or bowing and yielding while saving a fire."
The Literary Scholar said:
"When King Wén Wén Wáng arose, the people loved goodness,
when Yōu 幽 and Lì 厲 arose, the people loved violence.
It is not because of a difference in nature,
but because of the influence of customs.
Therefore, Shāng 商 and
Zhōu 周 flourished,
while Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂 perished.
Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武 did not govern with the people of Bó Yí 伯夷,
and Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂 did not bring chaos with the people of Zhí 跖 and
Qiāo 蹻.
Therefore, order and chaos do not depend on the people.
Confucius said:
'In hearing lawsuits, I am like anyone else;
what is necessary is to make it so that there are no lawsuits!'
Preventing lawsuits is difficult,
but hearing them is easy.
To not govern the root but attend to the branches,
is what the ancients called foolish,
and what the present call wise.
To correct disorder with a whip,
and to correct written documents with a knife and pen,
is what the ancients called thieves,
and what the present call worthy."
The official said:
"Customs are not like the times of Táng 唐 and
Yú 虞,
and the world is not populated with the people of Xǔ Yóu 許由,
and to want to govern by abolishing the law,
is like wanting to bend what is crooked without using compasses, squares, axes, and adzes.
Therefore, a ruler does not wait for inherently good people,
and a wheelwright does not wait for inherently bent wood.
In the past,
Yīng Shǎo 應少,
Bó Zhèng 伯正, and their like undermined Liáng 梁 and
Chǔ 楚. Kūn Lú 昆盧 and
Xú Gǔ 徐穀, and their gangs brought chaos to Qí 齊 and
Zhào 趙. The violent gangs of Shāndōng 山東
and Guān Nèi 關內
relied on people, obstructed with dangerous terrain.
At such times,
not relying on axes and adzes,
but crushing them with force,
and then beginning to establish rituals and cultivate culture,
would be like a hopeless doctor,
wanting to attack a tumor with a short needle,
or Kǒng Qiū 孔丘 using rituals to persuade Zhí 跖."
The Literary Scholar said:
"One who uses damaged timber to build a house
is not a good craftsman.
One who injures the people and wants to govern
is not a good official.
Thus, Gōngshū Zǐ 公輸子 adapts to the properties of wood,
and the sages do not waste the nature of the people.
Therefore, axes and adzes are used sparingly,
punishments are not relied upon,
and government is established and transformation is achieved.
Biǎn Què 扁鵲 treated illness in its early stages,
eliminating evil qi,
so that tumors could not form.
Sages work on things before they happen,
so that the source of chaos has no way to arise.
Therefore, stone needles are stored and not used,
and laws are established but not enforced.
To cut off what is already done,
and to chisel what has already sprouted,
is what ordinary people do.
To govern what is not yet formed,
and to see what is not yet sprouting,
is what gentlemen do."
The official said:
"The sage and wise man that the Literary Scholar refers to
is Kǒngzǐ 孔子.
His governance of Lǔ 魯 was not successful,
he was expelled from Qí 齊,
he was not employed by Wèi 衛,
he was surrounded in Kuàng 匡,
and he was trapped in Chén 陳 and
Cài 蔡. To know the times but not be used is like explaining,
which is forceful;
to know hardship but not stop,
is greedy;
to not know when one is being deceived and still go,
is foolish;
to not die when faced with hardship and disgrace,
is shameful.
If these four things
are what ordinary people would not do,
how much less a gentleman!
Shāng Jūn 商君 was introduced by Jǐng Jiān 景監,
and Yīng Hóu 應侯 was advanced by Wáng Jī 王稽.
Therefore, scholars rely on scholars,
and women rely on matchmakers.
When they become intimate and prominent,
it is not due to the strength of the matchmaker or scholar.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 not being able to go because of an introduction,
means he was neither a worthy scholar nor a talented woman."
The Literary Men said:
"Kǒngzǐ was born in a chaotic era.
He longed for the ways of Yáo
and Shùn.
He traveled east, west, north, and south,
with scorched head and soaking feet,
hoping that the ruler of the age might awaken.
All were negligent.
The ruler was foolish,
the high officials were jealous.
Who would agree to be a matchmaker?
Therefore, Mó Mǔ adorned herself and boasted,
while Xī Zǐ wandered about without a home.
It was not that he didn't know he was trapped and not employed,
but he grieved for the disasters of the world,
like a loving mother who would rather die for her child.
He knew it was impossible,
but hated to stop.
Therefore, when he went to Qí,
Jǐng Gōng deceived him;
when he went to Wèi,
Líng Gōng besieged him;
Yáng Hǔ slandered him;
Huán Tuí tried to harm him.
Those who deceive and harm sages
are foolish and deluded;
those who injure and destroy sages
are cunning and treacherous.
Cunning and deluded people
are not human beings.
What shame is there in that!
Mèngzǐ said:
'Observe close officials by what they uphold for their ruler;
observe distant officials by what they uphold for themselves.'
If the sage were to falsely accommodate and ingratiate himself,
not discussing conduct or choosing friends,
then how could he be Kǒngzǐ!"
The Grandee was dismayed and inwardly ashamed,
looking around and saying nothing.
At this time,
courtiers who followed the wind and catered to the ruler's wishes were like a woven mat,
mouths open but not closing,
tongues raised but not lowered,
silently bearing heavy burdens and facing blame.
The Grandee said:
"Yes,
like a glue-wheeled cart suddenly encountering rain,
I will explain this with you all."
10.6 《Zá Lún Dì Liù Shí》 (Miscellaneous Discourses, Number Sixty)
The Guest said:
"I have witnessed the discussions on salt
and iron,
observing the arguments of the dukes and ministers,
the Literary Men,
and Worthies and Good Men.
Their intentions point in different directions,
each having their own source.
Some extol benevolence and righteousness,
while others pursue power and profit."
"How different is what I have heard!
The Zhōu and Qín dynasties shone brightly,
both possessing the empire and ruling from the south,
yet their peace and danger, longevity and duration, differed across generations.
Once, Zhū Zǐbó of Rǔnán told me:
At that time,
outstanding talents advanced together,
and people from all directions gathered.
The Worthies and Good Men, like Táng Shēng of Mólíng,
and the Literary Men, like Wàn Shēng of Lǔ Country, more than sixty people in all, gathered at the palace gates,
spreading the influence of the Six Classics
and discussing the origins of peace.
The wise praised their deliberations,
the benevolent clarified their actions,
the brave demonstrated their decisiveness,
and the eloquent presented their arguments.
Earnest and respectful,
upright and forthright,
though not able to be fully comprehensive,
it was still possible to get a brief overview.
However, obscured by clouds and mists,
it was ultimately abandoned and not implemented,
alas!
The dukes and ministers know that relying on military force can expand territory,
but do not know that spreading virtue can attract those from afar;
they know that power and profit can be widely used,
but do not know that agriculture can enrich the country.
When those nearby are friendly and attached,
and those far away are persuaded by virtue,
what cannot be accomplished,
what cannot be obtained?
Not following this path,
but focusing on accumulating profit and increasing power,
is it not a mistake!
Liú Zǐyōng of Zhōngshān spoke of the Way of the King,
correcting the current age,
restoring things to correctness,
and striving to return to the root.
Upright without seeking favor,
incisive without being sharp,
balanced and refined, he can be called a broad-minded gentleman.
Zhù Shēng of Jiǔjiāng expressed the ideas of Fèn Yóu
and Lù,
promoted the integrity of Shǐ Yú,
expressed his indignation and resentment,
and criticized the dukes and ministers,
unyielding and upright,
he can be called unafraid of the powerful and tyrannical.
Grandee Sāng based himself on the current age,
conformed to the changes of the times,
promoted strategies,
and valued power and profit,
evading minor arguments.
Although not the correct method,
the great Confucian scholars and those with long-standing learning were ashamed
and unable to defend themselves.
He can be called a learned and well-informed man.
However, occupying the position of minister and chancellor,
he did not use the plumb line and ink rope,
to transform the people with the Way,
but indulged in the pursuit of profit,
not learning from the ancient beginnings.
The *Yì* says:
'Burning, casting aside.'
Occupying a position not suited for him,
acting in a way not suited for him,
he will surely ruin his nature
and bring ruin to his clan.
Chancellor Chē was in the ranks of Zhōu
and Lǚ,
holding power in the center,
keeping his mouth shut and saying nothing,
preserving himself and leaving.
Despicable!
Despicable!
As for the many chancellors
and officials of the two offices of Imperial Censors,
unable to offer proper advice to assist the prime minister,
becoming like-minded,
walking the same path,
catering and accommodating,
to please their superiors,
petty people,
a gang of flatterers,
how can they be counted!"
